handle: HASEL-vs-muscle benchmark table — Rothemund et al., 2021
citation: Rothemund, P., Kellaris, N., Mitchell, S. K., Acome, E., Keplinger, C. (2021). "HASEL Artificial Muscles for a New Generation of Lifelike Robots — Recent Progress and Future Opportunities." *Advanced Materials* 33, 2003375. (Online 2020.)
source: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202003375 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11469257/) and Semantic Scholar DOI record.
contribution: The authoritative side-by-side table of HASEL electrohydraulic artificial muscle performance against natural skeletal muscle, written by the group that invented the technology. It is the single best source for "how close is the best electrostatic soft actuator to muscle, honestly."
hard_numbers: Natural muscle: 0.35 MPa stress, 20% typical / 40% max strain, 50 W/kg avg and 200 W/kg peak specific power, 8 J/kg typical / 40 J/kg max specific energy, 40% efficiency, 500 %/s peak strain rate, ~10⁹ cycle life. HASEL: 0.3 MPa (planar), 0.21 MPa (Peano), 0.09 MPa (HS-Peano); strain up to 124% (planar) / 118% (quadrant donut) / 24% (HS-Peano); 614 W/kg at resonance (planar), 360 W/kg peak (Peano); 70 J/kg at resonance; 19–21% efficiency; 126 Hz bandwidth (quadrant donut), 7400 %/s peak strain rate; drive voltages 10 kV (Peano), 12 kV (quadrant donut), 22.5 kV (planar); cycle life 10⁶ (elastomeric) and 10⁴–10⁵ (thermoplastic).
design_relevance: Sets the ceiling. HASEL matches muscle in *stress* (0.3 vs 0.35 MPa) and beats it in specific power, but that stress is only achievable over tiny cross-sections at 10–22 kV. It tells the team that the electroactive family is not stress-limited — it is cross-section, voltage and packaging limited.
evidence_grade: D (review by the originating lab; underlying numbers are B)
limitations: Every number is per-actuator on a bench. Nothing here addresses carrying a static gravity load for minutes, backdriving under a 700 N leaning adult, or the 10–22 kV supply sitting inside a torso that a frail person touches. Cycle life of 10⁴–10⁵ for the thermoplastic variants is a few weeks of assistive duty at best. ---

handle: Electrohydraulic force/strain census — Tynan et al., 2025
citation: Tynan, L., Gunawardana, U., Liyanapathirana, R., Perera, O., Esposito, D., Centracchio, J., Gargiulo, G. (2025). "Review of Electrohydraulic Actuators Inspired by the HASEL Actuator." *Biomimetics* 10(3), 152.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics10030152 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11939893/).
contribution: A complete tabulated census of every published electrohydraulic / HASEL-derived actuator variant with force, strain, voltage and specific power. This is the "how much force has anyone ever actually gotten out of one of these" table.
hard_numbers: *Expanding:* elastomeric donut HASEL 2.45–3.92 N @ 21 kV, 40–50% strain; planar HASEL 2.45–14.72 N @ ~22.5 kV, 79% strain, 614 W/kg, 70 J/kg; quadrant HASEL (3-stack) ~60 N @ 12 kV, 118% strain, 121 W/kg, 12 J/kg; HEXEL <2 N; HAXEL 0.1–0.8 N @ 2 kV; LEAP 0.017 N. *Contracting:* Peano-HASEL (3-stack) 9.81–60 N @ 10 kV, 9–15% strain, 160 W/kg; HS Peano-HASEL 18 N @ 10 kV, 24% strain; HEXEL (contracting) 37.6 N @ 9.5 kV; EBM (6-series) ~7 N; electro-ribbon 0.172 N; EPP-BAM 0.981 N; HALVE 5 N @ 1.1 kV, 50.5 W/kg. Authors' conclusion quoted: *"low force and displacement still limit the viability of the soft actuators in real-life applications."*
design_relevance: Kills the electroactive family for this project outright. The maximum force ever reported from any electrohydraulic actuator is ~60 N from a multi-unit stack at 12 kV — that is the whole end-effector target, from an actuator that then has to be multiplied by a moment arm. There is no path from this table to 10–40 Nm at a shoulder.
evidence_grade: D (review; sources are B)
limitations: Review of bench characterisations only; no assembled limb, no sustained load-holding data, no contact-safety data. ---

handle: Soft shoulder actuator, measured at the joint — Zhang et al., 2024
citation: Zhang, H., Naquila, G. J., Bae, J., Wu, Z.-H., Hingwe, A., Deshpande, A. D. (2024). "Novel bio-inspired soft actuators for upper-limb exoskeletons: design, fabrication and feasibility study." *Frontiers in Robotics and AI* 11, 1451231.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2024.1451231 — verified via Frontiers full text and Semantic Scholar DOI record. Preprint mirror: arXiv:2509.01145.
contribution: Two purpose-built silicone pneumatic actuators — LISPER (elbow) and SCASPER (shoulder) — characterised for torque, ROM and bandwidth, with an analytical pressure→torque model. The authors explicitly built SCASPER because LISPER's output was too weak for the shoulder, and published both numbers.
hard_numbers: LISPER (elbow): 12.5 N max output force, **0.6 Nm max torque**, 112.2° ROM, 100 kPa max, 259 g, 132×55×92 mm. SCASPER (shoulder): 49.5 N max output force, **5.5 Nm max torque**, 122.5° ROM, 150 kPa max, 183 g, 122×91×132 mm. Bellows contribute ~35% of total output force. Authors state the LISPER "output force … is insufficient to support motions of shoulder."
design_relevance: This is the most direct measurement of the gap in the whole set. A purpose-designed, state-of-the-art, fully soft silicone shoulder actuator produces 5.5 Nm — roughly one seventh of the low end of a 10–40 Nm shoulder requirement, and it does so with no structural load path of its own.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated; "preliminary test on a dummy arm", no humans)
limitations: Wearable actuator mounted on a human skeleton that carries the load; the torque number is assistive torque added to a limb, not torque a freestanding structure must generate and react. Dummy-arm testing only. No durability or contact-safety data. ---

handle: Dual-DOF soft shoulder exosuit with human trial — Chen et al., 2026
citation: Chen, R., Chiaradia, D., Leonardis, D., Frisoli, A. (2026). "Design and Characterization of a Dual-DOF Soft Shoulder Exosuit with Volume-Optimized Pneumatic Actuator." arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.18212.
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18212 — verified by fetching both the arXiv abs page and the full HTML (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.18212).
contribution: A two-actuator soft pneumatic shoulder exosuit (curved abduction actuator + horizontal adduction actuator) with a geometry optimisation that cuts actuator volume while keeping torque, plus a 10-subject EMG study. It is currently the highest joint-level torque reported for a *fully soft pneumatic* shoulder actuator that has been on real people.
hard_numbers: CAA max moment **9.7 Nm at ~90° abduction, 90 kPa**. HAA modelled max torque **10.93 Nm at β=60°, 90 kPa**, falling to 4.64 Nm at β=120°. Operating pressures swept 10–90 kPa; demonstrations at 80 kPa (CAA) and 50 kPa (HAA). Actuator volume 357 mL vs 555 mL baseline (−35.7%) at 94.2% torque retention; fall time 35.2% faster at 90 kPa. Wearable mass 390 g. Ten healthy subjects (5 M / 5 F, 27.1 ± 3.0 y); EMG reduction up to 59% (abduction, HAA only) and 63.7% (flexion, dual actuator) across seven muscles.
design_relevance: This is the practical ceiling number to quote in the design review: ~10 Nm per soft pneumatic shoulder actuator at 90 kPa. It lands at the very bottom of the 10–40 Nm band and only with a tuned geometry, a tether, and a human skeleton underneath.
evidence_grade: A (hardware, 10 human subjects, EMG outcome measures) — with the caveat that this is a preprint.
limitations: Exosuit, not a freestanding arm: the torque is reacted through the wearer's torso. Healthy young subjects, not elderly or rehab patients. Tethered pneumatics. No leaning/impact load case. Preprint, unreviewed. ---

handle: Soft pneumatic bundles — highest verified torque from an all-soft module — Robertson et al., 2017
citation: Robertson, M. A., Sadeghi, H., Florez, J. M., Paik, J. (2017). "Soft Pneumatic Actuator Fascicles for High Force and Reliability." *Soft Robotics* 4(1), 23–32.
source: https://doi.org/10.1089/soro.2016.0029 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5346960/).
contribution: Bundling multiple thin fiber-reinforced soft pneumatic actuators into a "fascicle" beats a single actuator of equal volume on force, and scales to a multi-DOF platform. It is the clearest demonstration that soft pneumatics scale by *parallelism*, not by inflating one actuator bigger.
hard_numbers: Single SPA 26 N blocked force, 28 g, 145 mm × 17 mm, ~2 Hz bandwidth. 4Pack fascicle **112 N blocked force**, 185 g, ~0.61 N/g, ~2 Hz. Full platform 945 g, **468 N total force capacity, 18 N·m maximum moment**, 1.33 Hz bandwidth. Operating pressure 200 kPa gauge (2 bar max). Fiber angle 75.2°, 16 wraps. Fascicle gains 23% force over an equivalent single SPA.
design_relevance: The 18 Nm figure is the single strongest "yes it can" data point in this literature, and it is the number to defend a soft pneumatic shoulder with. It also fixes the scaling law for the design: to double torque, double the number of actuators and the mass and the air flow. Bandwidth of 1.3–2 Hz sets the control ceiling for D1.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: A bending platform, not a revolute shoulder — the 18 Nm is a bending moment over a short structure, with unknown behaviour under an off-axis leaning load. 2007-era silicone, no fatigue data at load. 200 kPa plumbing plus compressor is a large fraction of a freestanding torso's mass and noise budget, and 1.33 Hz is slow for reacting to a fall. ---

handle: Soft-rigid hybrid joint, the realistic fallback — Dimonte et al., 2026
citation: Dimonte, G., Gandolla, M., Proietti, T. (2026). "A bioinspired hybrid robotic joint for safer physical human–robot interaction." *Bioinspiration & Biomimetics* 21(4), 046004.
source: https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-3190/ae72db — verified via IOPscience article page.
contribution: A rigid frame driven by an antagonistic pair of thermoplastic-polyurethane pneumatic artificial muscles, with two model-free controllers that regulate joint angle and joint compliance independently. Demonstrates that you can keep a tuneable-compliance, human-safe joint while getting force levels a fully soft link cannot reach.
hard_numbers: PAM isometric force **400 N at 240 kPa**; stroke/stretchability 80 mm; material density 0.3 g/cm³. Position control <2° RMSE, <1% overshoot, rise time <1.3 s. **Stiffness modulation range 0.054–0.076 Nm/deg** (≈3.1–4.4 Nm/rad).
design_relevance: This is the architecture the project probably ends up with. 400 N of muscle force on a rigid moment arm of 50–100 mm gives 20–40 Nm directly — the target band — while antagonistic pressure still gives real, controllable compliance. It also supplies a measured stiffness range to quote in the safety case.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no human subjects)
limitations: Single joint on a bench, not a two-arm torso. The stiffness modulation range is narrow (about 40% span) — it will not go floppy on demand. 240 kPa PAMs mean a compressor, valves and a plumbing failure mode. No impact or leaning-load testing, and the rigid frame reintroduces exactly the hard edges and pinch points the "soft" premise is trying to avoid. ---

handle: The honesty framing — Hawkes, Majidi & Tolley, 2021
citation: Hawkes, E. W., Majidi, C., Tolley, M. T. (2021). "Hard questions for soft robotics." *Science Robotics* 6, eabg6049.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.abg6049 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API DOI record (publisher page returns 403 to automated fetch).
contribution: Three senior figures in the field argue that soft robotics has been coasting on "soft for soft's sake" and propose a three-tier test for whether a soft solution actually contributes: does softness enable something otherwise impossible, or is it decoration?
hard_numbers: none reported (position piece).
design_relevance: This is the paper to cite in the design review when justifying a soft-rigid hybrid over a fully soft arm. It gives the team permission — from the field's own leadership — to say "we went soft only where softness buys safety, and rigid where it buys torque," and it is the strongest defence against a reviewer asking why the arm isn't monolithically soft.
evidence_grade: D (review / position)
limitations: No data. Purely a framing device. ---

handle: Untethered soft pneumatic arm, whole-system numbers — Zuo et al., 2025
citation: Zuo, R., Han, D. H., Li, R., Jamal, S., Bruder, D. (2025). "UMArm: Untethered, Modular, Portable, Soft Pneumatic Arm." arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.11476 (v2, Dec 2025).
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11476 — verified via arXiv abs page and full HTML (https://arxiv.org/html/2505.11476v2).
contribution: A complete untethered soft arm: 24 valve-embedded self-regulated McKibben actuators, no external pressure regulators, directionally tunable compliance, demonstrated as a wearable assistive arm. It is the closest published system to "a soft arm you could bolt to a torso and run off-grid."
hard_numbers: **53.3 N blocked force at 1.15 kg arm mass** (regulators included). Max tested payload 2 kg. Input pressure 276 kPa (40 psi). 3 segments, 12 revolute joints, ±0.3 rad (±17.2°) per joint. 24 independently controlled McKibben actuators (8/segment). Antagonistic stiffness settings 14 / 55 / 110 kPa. Steady-state positional RMSE 0.85 mm at zero load, 110 kPa, 1× gain. Step settling 2–6 s depending on load and stiffness. Untethered runtime 11 min 45 s from a 1.11 L tank at 31 MPa.
design_relevance: Gives the team a system-level reality check that bench actuator specs never do: the *entire* soft arm produces 53 N — mid-band for the 10–100 N end-effector target — and runs for under 12 minutes untethered on a 310 bar tank. For a freestanding assistant, this says: plan for a tethered compressor, not bottled gas.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no human-subject study)
limitations: Preprint. ±17° per joint is a small range. 2–6 s settling is far too slow to catch a stumbling person. No contact-safety or leaning-load characterisation. Runtime number effectively rules out an untethered pneumatic torso. ---

handle: Electrohydraulic joint torque, measured — Kellaris et al., 2021
citation: Kellaris, N., Rothemund, P., Zeng, Y., Mitchell, S. K., Smith, G. M., Jayaram, K., Keplinger, C. (2021). "Spider-Inspired Electrohydraulic Actuators for Fast, Soft-Actuated Joints." *Advanced Science* 8(14), 2100916.
source: https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202100916 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8292915/).
contribution: The best-performing electrohydraulic *rotary joint* published — a spider-inspired soft joint combining Peano-HASEL and pouch-motor principles, characterised directly in torque rather than linear force.
hard_numbers: **Blocked torque up to 70 mN·m.** Specific torque up to 21.2 N·m/kg (actuator mass only). Roll-off frequency up to 24 Hz. 6–9 kV DC. Actuator mass 1.36 g (2×4×1 cm). 70° range at 9 kV, ~180° in series. Specific power up to 230 W/kg. Rise time 12 ms, fall time 31 ms. >2000 cycles with <3% degradation. Holding power <1 mW vs 140 mW for a comparable servo.
design_relevance: The decisive negative result for the electroactive route. 70 mN·m is **~150–570× short** of a 10–40 Nm shoulder. The 21.2 N·m/kg specific torque is genuinely servo-class, but only if you ignore the kV supply mass; scaling the actuator mass to reach 40 Nm implies ~1.9 kg of actuator plus high-voltage electronics at the joint.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: 6–9 kV at a joint a frail person may grab. >2000 cycles is not a service life. Specific torque excludes driver mass, which dominates at this scale. ---

handle: Canonical HASEL — Acome et al., 2018
citation: Acome, E., Mitchell, S. K., Morrissey, T. G., Emmett, M. B., Benjamin, C. E., King, M., Radakovitz, M., Keplinger, C. (2018). "Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic actuators with muscle-like performance." *Science* 359(6371), 61–65.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao6139 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API DOI record (title, authors, venue, volume 359, pages 61–65, year 2018).
contribution: The founding HASEL paper: electrostatic Maxwell stress pumps a liquid dielectric to produce large-strain, self-healing, muscle-like actuation.
hard_numbers: Single-unit actuator 107% linear strain under a **250 g load**; two-unit actuator 124% linear strain under a **700 g load**. Peak specific power during contraction 614 W/kg, specific work 70 J/kg (two-unit), ~2× natural muscle peak specific power. (Cross-checked against Rothemund 2021 and Tynan 2025, which report the same values; the Science page itself is paywalled to automated fetch.)
design_relevance: The headline "muscle-like" claim that will come up in any design review — and the numbers that deflate it for this application. 700 g of load is ~7 N. Cite this with the load figure attached, not the power-density figure.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: Load figures are grams, not tens of newtons. Liquid dielectric plus ~20 kV inside an assistive device that contacts skin is a hazard analysis the team does not want. ---

handle: Where the power-density gap actually sits — Kim et al., 2025
citation: Kim, T., Dunn, E. A., Chen, M., Truby, R. L. (2025). "Architected Soft Actuators for Artificial Musculoskeletal Systems." *Advanced Materials* 37(43), e2501290.
source: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202501290 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12574648/).
contribution: Low-voltage motorised-tendon soft actuators built into architected musculoskeletal assemblies, with an unusually candid comparison against muscle — including the authors admitting their own actuators sit an order of magnitude below muscle.
hard_numbers: Actuators: 29.5% linear strain, **75 N max force**, 22.8 W/kg peak power density (pulling), ~3.7 J/kg peak energy density, **<10 V drive**. Quoted directly: *"The maximum power and energy densities of muscle (200 W kg⁻¹ and 40 J kg⁻¹) are still an order of magnitude higher than our actuators' (40 W kg⁻¹ and ≈4 J kg⁻¹)."* Authors also note that once auxiliary hardware mass is counted, motorised actuators beat other soft actuators' power and energy density by four orders of magnitude.
design_relevance: Two things the team should take: (1) the honest muscle-vs-soft-actuator gap number to quote — one order of magnitude on power, ten on energy; (2) the auxiliary-hardware argument, which is the strongest technical case for a motor-plus-compliance (SEA/VSA) architecture over fully soft. Once you count the compressor, tank, valves or the kV driver, "soft" actuators lose their power-density advantage outright.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: 75 N is a tendon force, not a joint torque; no shoulder-scale demonstration. Comparative claims rest on supplementary tables not reproduced in the main text. ---

handle: SMA reality check — Shami, Arslan & Lomax, 2025
citation: Shami, Z., Arslan, T., Lomax, P. (2025). "Wearable Soft Robots: Case Study of Using Shape Memory Alloys in Rehabilitation." *Bioengineering* 12(3), 276.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/bioengineering12030276 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11939777/).
contribution: A tabulated review of every significant SMA-actuated rehabilitation device, with force, cooling time, current draw and efficiency for each. It is the fastest way to conclude that SMA is not viable here.
hard_numbers: 0.38 mm NiTi wire: 22.06 N (22.5 N heating / 9 N cooling), 2.2 A drive. SMA spring 0.25 N each; 3 in parallel 0.75 N. Hand exoskeleton 10 N per fingertip, 40 N grip. AAFO 8-wire 70 N. Platform ankle robot 110 N max force. SHADE ankle 13 N/actuator, 200 N·cm (**2 Nm**) max torque; Leia ankle 100 N·cm (**1 Nm**). Nitinol max contraction 4.5% (wires 3–5%); springs >100%; knitted actuators >40%. Stress limits 266–300 MPa. **Cooling: 2.0 s (0.15 mm wire) to 16.8 s (0.51 mm wire) at 70 °C; 40–50 s for a knee orthosis on natural convection; 3.57 s with forced convection.** Actuation frequency 0.143–0.5 Hz. Efficiency **10–15%**. Work density 10 J/cm³ (25× electric motors). Power draw e.g. 28.8 W for a knee+ ankle device; 10.2 A at 14.7 V for a fabric muscle.
design_relevance: Eliminates SMA. Highest joint torque anyone has published in a wearable SMA device is 2 Nm, at 0.14–0.5 Hz, at 10–15% efficiency, with cooling times measured in tens of seconds. A torso a person leans on needs to hold load continuously — which for SMA means continuous heating at ~10% efficiency, i.e. a hot device against skin.
evidence_grade: D (review; underlying devices are A/B)
limitations: Review, not primary data. All devices are wearables with the load path through the human skeleton. ---

handle: Twisted/coiled polymer — the canonical claim — Haines et al., 2014
citation: Haines, C. S., Lima, M. D., Li, N., Spinks, G. M., Foroughi, J., Madden, J. D. W., Kim, S. H., Fang, S., Jung de Andrade, M., Göktepe, F., Göktepe, Ö., Mirvakili, S. M., Naficy, S., Lepró, X., Oh, J., Kozlov, M. E., Kim, S. J., Xu, X., Swedlove, B. J., Wallace, G. G., Baughman, R. H. (2014). "Artificial Muscles from Fishing Line and Sewing Thread." *Science* 343(6173), 868–872.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1246906 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API DOI record including full abstract. Green OA copy on figshare.
contribution: Twisting commodity nylon fibre past the coiling point produces a thermally driven tensile actuator with very large stroke and extreme specific work. The origin of every "artificial muscle from fishing line" headline.
hard_numbers: 49% contraction; lifts loads **>100× heavier than human muscle of the same length and weight**; **5.3 kW/kg mechanical work per kg of muscle**; long cycle life, non-hysteretic, scalable by twist insertion.
design_relevance: Sets the aspirational upper bound for TCP, and is the number a reviewer will quote at the team. The honest counter is in the next entry: per-actuator absolute force and bandwidth, not specific work, are what a shoulder needs.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: Thermally driven — heating and cooling set the bandwidth, and cooling is uncontrolled. 5.3 kW/kg is a *peak* figure at resonance-like conditions, not sustained load-holding. No joint, no robot, no load path. ---

handle: Twisted/coiled polymer — what it actually delivers today — Sun et al., 2025
citation: Sun, J., Zhang, S., Deng, J., Li, J., Zhou, D., Wang, D., Liu, J., Chen, W., Liu, Y. (2025). "High-Performance Twisted Nylon Actuators for Soft Robots." *Research* 8, 0642.
source: https://doi.org/10.34133/research.0642 — verified via PMC full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11912876/) and the NCBI eSummary record for PMID 40099267 (confirms 2025, vol 8, pages 0642).
contribution: A current best-effort attempt to push twisted nylon actuators toward useful absolute force via parallel-twisted and untwisted-parallel architectures, with the structural trade-off stated explicitly.
hard_numbers: PTNA (parallel-twisted) **11.0 N output force**, 12.1% contraction under 15 N load (≈10,000× its own weight), 20.3% contraction at 9 N, 0.25 s heating cycle. PTUNA 3.67 N, 53.7% contraction at 2 N. TUNA 60.2% contraction (vertical), ~100% horizontal, ~10 s to reach 110 °C, 0.5 N load. Five TUNAs launched a ball to 131 cm in 0.05 s (4.0 m/s). Stated trade-off: *"increasing the diameter enhances deformation but also reduces stiffness, thereby decreasing the output force."*
design_relevance: Eliminates TCP. Eleven newtons from a state-of-the-art 2025 bundle, with a thermal actuation cycle, against a 10–100 N end-effector requirement and a shoulder joint. The quoted diameter/stiffness trade-off explains why this family does not scale up by making the actuator bigger.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: Thermal, so bandwidth and duty cycle are poor, and sustained load-holding means sustained heating. No joint, no assistive demonstration, no safety analysis. ---

handle: Low-voltage DEA — the best case for dielectric elastomers — Peng et al., 2026
citation: Peng, J.-B., Zhuo, J.-S., Qiu, H., Normahmedov, O., Shi, M.-K., Dong, H.-F., Wang, L., Jiang, S.-C., Zou, J., Gu, G.-Y., Li, T.-F., Fu, W.-F., Peng, B., Ma, H.-Z., Shi, Y. (2026). "Low-voltage and high-output dielectric elastomer actuators for untethered soft machines working at 200 volts." *Science Robotics* 11(111), eady9635.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.ady9635 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API DOI record including full abstract.
contribution: A new high-permittivity elastomer plus dry-stacked multilayering drops DEA drive voltage from kilovolts to 200 V while keeping useful energy and power density — the single biggest obstacle to DEAs in human-contact devices, directly addressed.
hard_numbers: **38.4 J/kg energy density, 452 W/kg power density at 20 V/µm nominal field**, no prestretch, no resonance. Operation demonstrated at **200 V**. Untethered wearable devices and soft robots built and run.
design_relevance: The only credible path by which DEAs become safe enough to sit in a torso a person touches. Worth tracking, not worth designing around for a senior design cycle: the paper reports energy/power density, not force or torque, so there is no number the team can put in a torque budget. Note 38.4 J/kg is still below muscle's 40 J/kg maximum.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, no humans)
limitations: No force or torque figure reported at all — this is the single most important omission for this project. Multilayer dry stacking at scale is a manufacturing research problem. Published 2026; no independent replication. --- These were verified but are lower value for the actuation decision. Full BibTeX in `A1.bib`. - **Gravert et al. (2024), "Low-voltage electrohydraulic actuators for untethered robotics," *Science Advances* 10, eadi9319, doi:10.1126/sciadv.adi9319** (verified via S2 DOI record; CC-BY). HALVE actuators match mammalian skeletal muscle in average power density (**50.5 W/kg**) and peak strain rate (**971 %/s**) at **1100 V**, 4.9× lower than prior art. Per Tynan 2025, HALVE force is **5 N**. Safe-to-touch and waterproof — relevant to C1/C2 — but 5 N is nowhere near this project's needs. Grade B. - **Li, Vogt, Rus & Wood (2017), "Fluid-driven origami-inspired artificial muscles," *PNAS* 114(50), 13132–13137, doi:10.1073/pnas.1713450114** (verified via S2 DOI record with full abstract; hybrid OA). >90% contraction, **~600 kPa stress, >2 kW/kg peak power density**, driven at *negative* pressure (safer than positive-pressure fluidics). The famous "1000× own weight" claim comes from here. Relevant as a vacuum-actuation option for C1 safety, but the absolute forces are small and the architecture is contractile-linear, not a shoulder. Grade B. - **Bruder, Graule, Teeple & Wood (2023), "Increasing the payload capacity of soft robot arms by localized stiffening," *Science Robotics* 8, eadf9001, doi:10.1126/scirobotics.adf9001** (verified via S2 DOI record with full abstract; paywalled — NASA NTRS mirror ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250001131 was 503 on three attempts, so **I did not extract its numeric results**). Model-based method: stiffen localised body regions to cut end-effector compliance without losing ROM, raising the height at which an arm can lift a payload. Directly relevant to B1/A2. **Hard numbers: not extracted — do not cite numerically until someone opens the PDF.** Grade B. - **Zhang, Long, Chen, Wu, Wang & Jiang (2023), "Soft and lightweight fabric enables powerful and high-range pneumatic actuation," *Science Advances* 9, eadg1203, doi:10.1126/sciadv.adg1203** (verified via S2 DOI record with full abstract; CC-BY-NC). Less-stretchable fabric pneumatic actuators; three-actuator gripper with **>150 N grasping force**, 70–350 mm range, low input pressure, fast response. The material argument (low stretchability → higher payload) transfers to the arm even though the demo is a gripper. Grade B. - **Pan, M. et al. (2022), "Soft Actuators and Robotic Devices for Rehabilitation and Assistance," *Advanced Intelligent Systems* 4, 2100140, doi:10.1002/aisy.202100140** (verified via S2 DOI record with full abstract; gold OA, CC-BY). The canonical review covering the whole assistive soft-actuator space by actuation principle. Authors state the field "is in its infancy." Use as the survey citation; it is not a source of hard numbers. Grade D. - **Mirvakili & Hunter (2018), "Artificial Muscles: Mechanisms, Applications, and Challenges," *Advanced Materials* 30, 1704407, doi:10.1002/adma.201704407** (verified via S2 DOI record; abstract elided by publisher; closed access). The standard cross-technology artificial-muscle review. Cited for completeness; Rothemund 2021 and Tynan 2025 above give the team better, open-access numbers. Grade D. - **Madden, J. D. W. et al. (2004), "Artificial muscle technology: physical principles and naval prospects," *IEEE Journal of Oceanic Engineering* 29(3), 706–728, doi:10.1109/JOE.2004.833135** (verified via S2 DOI record: title, all nine authors, venue, vol 29, pp. 706–728; abstract elided; closed access). The original cross-technology comparison table (stress, strain, efficiency, bandwidth) that every later review descends from. Historically canonical; twenty years stale on HASEL/TCP. Grade D. --- No genuinely soft actuator technology reaches a 10–40 Nm shoulder, and only one family gets close enough to argue about. Every electroactive option is out by two to three orders of magnitude: the highest joint torque ever published from an electrohydraulic soft joint is 70 mN·m (Kellaris 2021), the highest force from any HASEL-family actuator ever is ~60 N from a multi-unit stack at 12 kV (Tynan 2025), and the DEA state of the art (Peng 2026) reports no force figure at all — it reports 38.4 J/kg, still under muscle's 40 J/kg. SMA tops out at 2 Nm in a published wearable at 10–15% efficiency with 3–17 s cooling and 0.14–0.5 Hz bandwidth (Shami 2025); twisted/coiled polymer tops out at 11 N per bundle and gets weaker as you make it bigger (Sun 2025). Both are thermal, which means holding a static gravity load means holding a heater against a frail person's arm — that is a disqualifying failure mode, not a tuning problem. Fluidic soft actuation is the only family in range: purpose-built soft pneumatic shoulder actuators deliver 5.5 Nm (Zhang 2024) and 9.7–10.9 Nm at 90 kPa (Chen 2026, 10 human subjects), and a bundled soft pneumatic platform reached 18 Nm at 2 bar (Robertson 2017) — so the bottom of the target band is reachable with all-soft pneumatics, the top of it is not, and the price is a compressor, valves, 1.3–2 Hz bandwidth and 2–6 s settling times (Zuo 2025) that are far too slow to catch someone falling. The architecture that actually clears 10–40 Nm is the soft-rigid hybrid: 400 N TPU pneumatic muscles at 240 kPa on a rigid antagonistic frame, with measured stiffness modulation of 0.054–0.076 Nm/deg (Dimonte 2026), which is 20–40 Nm on a 50–100 mm moment arm. One further caveat the team must not skip: every torque number above comes from a *wearable*, where the human skeleton carries the reaction load — a freestanding torso must generate that torque **and** react a leaning adult's body weight through its own structure, and no paper in this set characterises that case, which pushes the real problem into B1 (structure) as much as A1 (actuation). Plan on a hybrid, spend the softness budget on the contact surfaces and the outer 100 mm of the arm, and treat "fully soft arm" as a claim the evidence does not support. ---

handle: Crash-test HIC — Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer & Hirzinger, 2007
citation: S. Haddadin, A. Albu-Schäffer, G. Hirzinger, "Safety Evaluation of Physical Human-Robot Interaction via Crash-Testing," *Robotics: Science and Systems III*, Atlanta, GA, 2007, pp. 217–224.
source: 10.15607/RSS.2007.III.028 — verified by fetching and text-extracting the full PDF at https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss03/p28.pdf (also reissued as MIT Press chapter 10.7551/mitpress/7830.003.0029).
contribution: DLR LWR-III driven into certified ADAC automotive crash-test dummies (head, neck, chest) at controlled TCP speeds, scored against the EuroNCAP protocol. It is the only paper in this set that puts a compliant robot arm against a standardized injury protocol.
hard_numbers: robot 14 kg, 7-DOF, ~4 kg effective mass at TCP, 1 kg aluminium impactor. TCP speeds tested 0.2 / 0.7 / 1.0 / 1.5 / 2.0 m/s. **HIC36 < 25 at 2 m/s**, against a EuroNCAP limit of 650 (= 5% probability of AIS≥3). Chest 3 ms criterion at 2 m/s reached **< 20% of the 72 g limit**. Simulation sweep (fitted to the measured impact data, Hunt-Crossley contact) over robot masses 1/4/10/50/100/500 kg and speeds to 10 m/s shows **HIC saturates with increasing robot mass** — beyond a point, more mass does not raise HIC. Quoted ISO-10218 collaborative limits: TCP ≤ 0.25 m/s, dynamic power ≤ 80 W, static force ≤ 150 N. Paper's own conclusion: "no robot whatever mass it has could become dangerous at 2 m/s by means of the presented criteria as long as clamping and impacts with sharp surfaces can be excluded."
design_relevance: This is the paper that tells the design team where the safety argument actually lives. Free-flight blunt impact from a low-speed arm is **not** the dominant hazard and is already survivable; the hazard is **clamping / quasi-static constrained contact**, where inertia stops helping and only force limiting and release behaviour matter. For a torso a person leans on, essentially every dangerous contact is the constrained kind.
evidence_grade: A — hardware, certified crash facility, standardized (EuroNCAP) protocol, instrumented dummies.
limitations: Dummies, not people; unconstrained frontal impacts only; sharp edges and tools explicitly excluded; head/neck/chest only, no lean-on or entrapment loading; the LWR-III is a serial arm, not a torso with a person's weight on it. The paper itself notes dummy response over-predicts real injury severity at these speeds. ---

handle: Compliance does not reduce HIC — Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer, Eiberger & Hirzinger, 2010
citation: S. Haddadin, A. Albu-Schäffer, O. Eiberger, G. Hirzinger, "New insights concerning intrinsic joint elasticity for safety," *Proc. IEEE/RSJ Int. Conf. on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)*, Taipei, 2010, pp. 2181–2187.
source: 10.1109/IROS.2010.5652037 — verified via Crossref (authors/pages/venue) and OpenAlex (full abstract retrieved); IEEE listing https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5652037/.
open_access: partial (TUM mediaTUM record 1438559 is listed as the OA location; the landing page was behind a bot filter when I fetched it).
contribution: The most important counter-evidence in this whole topic. From the verified abstract: intrinsic joint elasticity **does not reduce HIC or impact forces** compared to conventional actuation that already has some joint elasticity, for full-scale robots — and the authors "elaborate conditions under which intrinsically compliant actuation is potentially *more dangerous* than rigid one."
hard_numbers: none verified. I retrieved the abstract, not the full text; the numerical conditions and thresholds are in the body and I will not paraphrase numbers I did not read.
design_relevance: Kills the lazy version of this project's safety argument. "We put springs in it, therefore it is safe" is not a defensible claim, and this is the paper a reviewer will hit you with. If the team goes SEA/VSA, the safety case must be built on **measured contact force limits and reaction behaviour**, not on the presence of a spring. Also flags the real compliant-actuator hazard: stored spring energy released on the human.
evidence_grade: B — hardware experiments plus analysis; the collision detection/reaction schemes are experimentally verified, but there is no human or standardized-protocol testing.
limitations: "Full scale robots" is the stated scope; a low-speed, low-inertia assistive torso is exactly the regime where the conclusion might not hold, and the paper does not test that regime. Conference-length treatment. ---

handle: Foundational SEA — Pratt & Williamson, 1995
citation: G. A. Pratt, M. M. Williamson, "Series elastic actuators," *Proc. 1995 IEEE/RSJ Int. Conf. on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS): Human Robot Interaction and Cooperative Robots*, Pittsburgh, PA, vol. 1, pp. 399–406.
source: 10.1109/IROS.1995.525827 — verified via Crossref (Pratt, G.A.; Williamson, M.M.; vol 1, pp. 399–406) and OpenAlex (abstract retrieved, 2211 citations).
open_access: no (IEEE paywalled; the widely circulated copy is an author preprint).
contribution: States the entire tradeoff the design team is about to make. Deliberately softening the actuator-load interface buys shock tolerance, lower reflected inertia, accurate and stable force control, less damage to the environment, and energy storage — and **costs zero-motion force bandwidth**. Validated on a revolute SEA for the MIT Cog humanoid arms and a small planetary rover.
hard_numbers: none verified. The abstract is qualitative; the bench results are in the body, which I did not access. Do not cite a bandwidth figure to this paper without reading it.
design_relevance: The canonical citation for why a spring in series is a design choice and not a compromise. Also the source of the argument the team will lean on: for contact-rich "natural" tasks, zero-motion force bandwidth is the wrong figure of merit — which is exactly the argument this project needs, because an assistive torso does slow, high-force, contact-rich work.
evidence_grade: B — hardware testbed, no humans, no standardized protocol.
limitations: 1995 componentry; the reflected-inertia argument was written for geared electric drives in a lab arm, not for a structure supporting a person's body weight; bandwidth loss claims predate modern disturbance-observer control which partly recovers it (see Paine below). ---

handle: UT-SEA, the design-tradeoff numbers — Paine, Oh & Sentis, 2014
citation: N. Paine, S. Oh, L. Sentis, "Design and Control Considerations for High-Performance Series Elastic Actuators," *IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics*, vol. 19, no. 3, pp. 1080–1091, June 2014. Companion with the same hardware: N. Paine, L. Sentis, "A new prismatic series elastic actuator with compact size and high performance," *Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. on Robotics and Biomimetics (ROBIO)*, 2012, pp. 1759--1766, DOI 10.1109/ROBIO.2012.6491222 (Crossref-verified).
source: 10.1109/TMECH.2013.2270435 — verified via Crossref (Paine, Nicholas; Oh, Sehoon; Sentis, Luis; vol 19, iss 3, pp 1080–1091) and OpenAlex. Numbers below were extracted by me from the companion full text at https://sites.utexas.edu/hcrl/files/2016/01/prismatic-sea-paine.pdf.
open_access: partial — journal version paywalled, companion preprint and the dissertation are free.
contribution: A compact ball-screw SEA pushed to the performance limit of electric SEA, with a full spring-selection rationale (soft springs store more energy for a given force; stiffness chosen to maximise energy storage within a deflection budget) and force/position controllers combining PID, model-based and disturbance-observer structures.
hard_numbers: mass **1013 g** (2.23 lb); continuous force **848 N**; intermittent force **2800 N**; spring rate 138 N/mm per spring, **278 N/mm** effective (two precompressed springs); stroke 6 cm; max speed 32.5 cm/s; force resolution 0.31 N; **94 W/kg** measured power-to-weight and **77% mechanical efficiency** — against 64 W/kg cited for the prior SEA benchmark.
design_relevance: This is the sizing reality check. A ~1 kg actuator delivering 848 N continuous is the realistic performance envelope for a good electric SEA today. If the torso needs N joints at that class, the mass budget follows directly, and it is not small. Also the reference for how spring rate is actually chosen — it is an energy-storage and deflection-resolution decision, not a "feels compliant" decision.
evidence_grade: B — hardware, bench-validated at the limits of its capability, no humans.
limitations: Designed for legged locomotion (high force, fixed range of motion, passively cooled, short duty cycles). An assistive torso holds load **continuously**, which is a thermal problem this actuator was not characterised for. Prismatic, so it needs a linkage to make a joint, and the linkage moment arm is angle-dependent. ---

handle: The price of force bandwidth — Paine, 2014 (dissertation, Valkyrie SEA data)
citation: N. A. Paine, "High-Performance Series Elastic Actuation," Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Texas at Austin, 2014.
source: https://sites.utexas.edu/hcrl/wp-content/uploads/sites/3888/2016/01/nick-paine-thesis-dissertation-2014.pdf — verified by fetching and text-extracting the full PDF myself.
contribution: Measured, on NASA Valkyrie's SEA joints, exactly what it costs to claw back the bandwidth that series elasticity gives away.
hard_numbers: Valkyrie elbow SEA **passive torque bandwidth 13 Hz**, extended to **70 Hz** closed-loop with PD feedback (factor 5.3). Torque tracking error ~**1.0 Nm on a 10 Nm reference**, with and without injected disturbances. Critically: raising closed-loop torque bandwidth from **30 Hz to 82 Hz raised average power consumption at the passive bandwidth frequency from 27 W to 97 W — a factor of 3.6 (+260%)**, with the corresponding motor heating. Passive system cutoff quoted as 11 Hz for the knee case.
design_relevance: Settles the "just turn the gains up" argument before someone makes it. Every Hz of force-control bandwidth recovered above the spring's passive cutoff is paid for in current, heat and battery. For a torso that must hold a leaning adult for minutes at a time, thermal headroom is the binding constraint, so the spring should be chosen so the **passive** cutoff is already close to what the task needs — not soft-and-then-compensated.
evidence_grade: B — hardware (Valkyrie), measured, no humans.
limitations: Humanoid limb joints under locomotion-style loading, not sustained static support. Dissertation, so peer review is the committee rather than a journal; the same lab's T-Mech and ICRA papers are the citable form for the design content. ---

handle: Distributed macro-mini (DM²) — Zinn, Roth, Khatib & Salisbury, 2004
citation: M. Zinn, B. Roth, O. Khatib, J. K. Salisbury, "A New Actuation Approach for Human Friendly Robot Design," *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, vol. 23, no. 4–5, pp. 379–398, April–May 2004.
source: 10.1177/0278364904042193 — verified via Crossref; numbers below extracted by me from the full PDF at https://cs.stanford.edu/group/manips/publications/pdfs/Zinn_2004_IJRR.pdf.
contribution: Splits joint torque into a low-frequency component from a large base-mounted actuator (through a cable/SEA transmission) and a high-frequency component from a small low-inertia joint motor in parallel. The point is to strip reflected inertia out of the arm entirely rather than to hide it behind a spring.
hard_numbers: PUMA 560 at 1 m/s impact produces **HIC > 500**. To get that down to HIC ≤ 100 with padding alone would need **more than five inches of compliant cover**. The two-axis DM² prototype reduced **effective joint inertia by almost a factor of 10** and impact loading **by an order of magnitude**. Closed-loop position bandwidth **5 Hz with DM² vs 2 Hz with the base SEA alone**, with position tracking error cut by more than 10×. SEA output impedance reduction by control quoted at **10× to 100×**. Pneumatics noted as limited to <20 Hz control bandwidth; conventional gear reduction more than doubles effective inertia.
design_relevance: Directly relevant to a **freestanding torso**, and probably underrated by the team. A torso has something an arm does not: a big, grounded, non-moving base you can bolt heavy actuators to. Moving actuator mass off the arms and into the torso — via cable or Bowden transmission — reduces the arms' reflected inertia, which is the one quantity that genuinely reduces impact severity. The five-inch-of-foam number is also the honest answer to "can't we just pad it?"
evidence_grade: B for the prototype and bandwidth results (two-axis hardware testbed); **C for the impact-reduction claim**, which is computed from effective-inertia ellipsoids and a 2-DOF mass-spring HIC model, not measured against dummies. Do not present the order-of-magnitude figure as a measurement.
limitations: Impact severity is modelled, not measured; a 2-DOF planar testbed is a long way from a two-armed torso; and the HIC framing is exactly the metric Haddadin 2007/2010 shows is the wrong one at these speeds. Cable/Bowden routing adds friction and hysteresis (see Veneman). ---

handle: Safety-performance co-design — Bicchi & Tonietti, 2004
citation: A. Bicchi, G. Tonietti, "Fast and 'Soft-Arm' Tactics: Dealing with the Safety-Performance Tradeoff in Robot Arms Design and Control," *IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine*, vol. 11, no. 2, pp. 22–33, June 2004. Companion with the worked numbers: A. Bicchi, G. Tonietti, M. Bavaro, M. Piccigallo, "Variable Stiffness Actuators for Fast and Safe Motion Control," *Robotics Research: The Eleventh Int. Symp. (ISRR)*, Springer STAR, 2005, pp. 527–536.
source: 10.1109/MRA.2004.1310939 (Crossref-verified: Bicchi, A.; Tonietti, G.; vol 11, iss 2, pp 22–33; abstract retrieved via OpenAlex). Companion 10.1007/11008941_56, Crossref-verified; numbers below extracted by me from the full PDF at https://www.centropiaggio.unipi.it/sites/default/files/anthropic-ISRR03.pdf.
open_access: partial — magazine article paywalled, ISRR companion free.
contribution: Formalises the tradeoff as minimum-time optimal control subject to an injury-risk constraint, and shows that a variable-stiffness transmission dominates both the fixed-stiff and fixed-soft options because it can be stiff when slow and soft when fast.
hard_numbers: worked example with rotor inertia **M_rot = 1.2 kg**, link **M_link = 0.1 kg**, soft rubber cover **K_cov = 5 kN/m**, operator head **M_oper = 4 kg**: accepting **HIC = 100** implies a velocity ceiling of **v_safe ≈ 2 m/s** for the rigid-joint case. A second study sweeps transmission stiffness at a 10 m/s pre-impact link velocity and shows HIC tending to the rigid-link value as K→∞ and to the link-inertia-only value as K→0, with an **optimum intermediate transmission stiffness** for minimum-time performance under the safety constraint.
design_relevance: This is the argument for VSA over fixed SEA, and also the argument against reflexively choosing "as soft as possible." There is an optimum, and softer than optimum makes the arm slow and floppy without buying more safety. If the team is choosing a spring rate, this is the framing to use.
evidence_grade: C — analysis, optimal control and simulation; the hardware realisation is the separate VSA-II paper (Tonietti, Schiavi & Bicchi, ICRA 2005, DOI 10.1109/ROBOT.2005.1570172, Crossref-verified, one-link arm).
limitations: Single-DOF rest-to-rest motion, HIC as the objective, and a free-flight impact model. All three assumptions are wrong for a torso under a leaning person: the hazard is constrained and quasi-static, HIC does not apply, and the motion is not a fast point-to-point slew. ---

handle: SEA in a rehab exoskeleton, with measured bandwidth — Veneman et al., 2006
citation: J. F. Veneman, R. Ekkelenkamp, R. Kruidhof, F. C. T. van der Helm, H. van der Kooij, "A Series Elastic- and Bowden-Cable-Based Actuation System for Use as Torque Actuator in Exoskeleton-Type Robots," *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, vol. 25, no. 3, pp. 261–281, March 2006.
source: 10.1177/0278364906063829 — verified via Crossref (full author list, vol/iss/pages) and OpenAlex (full abstract retrieved, 436 citations). Sage full text returned 403 to me.
contribution: The actuator behind LOPES. Motor sits off-board, torque goes to the joint through a flexible Bowden cable, and a series elastic element closes the force loop. Explicitly engineered so that the limb-worn structure stays light while the actuator still behaves as a decent torque source.
hard_numbers: **11 Hz** force-tracking bandwidth over the full force range (requirement was 4 Hz); **20 Hz** over a smaller force range (requirement 12 Hz). Residual output impedance: peaks of about **0.7 Nm under 4 Hz imposed motion, < 2.5% of maximum force output**, attributed to stick friction in the Bowden cables. Spring-stiffness sweep showed **both too stiff and too compliant degrade performance** — a stiff spring lowers the maximum stable controller gain.
design_relevance: The closest architectural analogue to what this project probably wants. It is DM²'s "put the mass at the base" idea, executed in a rehabilitation device with people in it, and with the transmission penalty honestly quantified (stick friction shows up as parasitic output impedance, which is exactly what a patient feels when leaning). The both-ends-are-bad spring result independently confirms Bicchi's optimum.
evidence_grade: B — hardware, bench-characterised. (The LOPES system built on it was later used with patients, but that is downstream work, not this paper.)
limitations: Gait/lower limb, cyclic motion, not sustained static support; Bowden routing friction scales with path curvature and will be worse in a torso with two articulated arms; no injury or contact-force testing at all. ---

handle: SEA for human assistance, tested on a person — Kong, Bae & Tomizuka, 2012
citation: K. Kong, J. Bae, M. Tomizuka, "A Compact Rotary Series Elastic Actuator for Human Assistive Systems," *IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics*, vol. 17, no. 2, pp. 288–297, April 2012.
source: 10.1109/TMECH.2010.2100046 — verified via Crossref (Kong, Kyoungchul; Bae, Joonbum; Tomizuka, Masayoshi; vol 17, iss 2, pp 288–297) and OpenAlex (abstract retrieved, 325 citations).
contribution: A rotary SEA sized specifically for human assistive devices, using a worm gear to get torque density in a small package, with a robust controller that explicitly models the worm gear friction (the actual amplification ratio departs from the nominal reduction ratio because of it). Includes experiments with a human subject.
hard_numbers: none verified. I retrieved the abstract only; the torque, impedance and mass figures are in the body and I did not read them. The abstract states the requirements it targets — precise large torque, backdrivability, low output impedance, compactness — without numbers.
design_relevance: Two things. First, it is one of the few SEA papers whose validation includes a human in the loop, which is the grade of evidence this project's safety argument needs. Second, the worm-gear finding is a direct warning: a non-backdrivable or friction-dominated reduction destroys the force-control fidelity that was the whole reason to fit a spring. If the team reaches for a worm or high-ratio harmonic drive to hit the torque target, the compliance argument degrades with it.
evidence_grade: A — hardware validated including experiments with a human subject (not a standardized injury protocol).
limitations: Single joint, knee/limb assistance geometry; worm gearing is a poor fit for a torso joint that must yield when a person pushes it; no impact or clamping characterisation. ---

handle: Interaction control for compliant rehab robots — Yu, Huang, Chen, Pan & Guo, 2015
citation: H. Yu, S. Huang, G. Chen, Y. Pan, Z. Guo, "Human–Robot Interaction Control of Rehabilitation Robots With Series Elastic Actuators," *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*, vol. 31, no. 5, pp. 1089–1100, October 2015.
source: 10.1109/TRO.2015.2457314 — verified via Crossref (full author list, vol/iss/pages) and OpenAlex (abstract retrieved, 360 citations).
contribution: Control design for an SEA-driven rehabilitation robot that must switch between a **human-in-charge mode** (robot must present near-zero output impedance and get out of the way) and a **force-control mode** (robot must track a commanded assistive force). Includes human-interaction compensation, friction compensation, a disturbance observer, and a stability proof for the closed loop under physical interaction. Verified in walking experiments with an ankle robot.
hard_numbers: none verified — abstract only; the impedance and force-tracking figures are in the body.
design_relevance: This is the control architecture the project actually needs, and it names the failure mode the team has probably not thought about: **physical interaction changes the controlled variables and can destabilise the system**. A person leaning on a torso is a large, unmodelled, time-varying impedance in the loop. A compliant actuator does not make that stable; a controller with a stability proof under interaction does. Also the right reference for the dual-mode requirement (transparent when the user leads, forceful when assisting).
evidence_grade: A — hardware, walking experiments with human subjects.
limitations: Ankle, single DOF, gait. The stability proof is for that plant; a two-arm torso is multi-DOF with contact at arbitrary points, and the authors' claim that results extend "without much difficulty" is an assertion, not a demonstration. ---

handle: VSA design guide — Wolf et al., 2016
citation: S. Wolf, G. Grioli, O. Eiberger, W. Friedl, M. Grebenstein, H. Höppner, E. Burdet, D. G. Caldwell, R. Carloni, M. G. Catalano, D. Lefeber, S. Stramigioli, N. Tsagarakis, M. Van Damme, R. Van Ham, B. Vanderborght, L. C. Visser, A. Bicchi, A. Albu-Schäffer, "Variable Stiffness Actuators: Review on Design and Components," *IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics*, vol. 21, no. 5, pp. 2418–2430, October 2016.
source: 10.1109/TMECH.2015.2501019 — verified via Crossref (full 19-author list, vol/iss/pages) and by fetching and text-extracting the accepted manuscript PDF at https://arpi.unipi.it/retrieve/handle/11568/842829/738859/VIA_review.pdf.
open_access: yes (accepted manuscript in the Pisa and Twente repositories).
contribution: A design-process guide rather than a catalogue: how the task determines the required attributes, and how those attributes drive motor, sensor and spring selection. Its most useful content is the explicit statement of the design contradiction — **size, weight and cost pull against output power, potential energy capacity, stiffness range, efficiency and accuracy** — so any VSA is a point on that surface and cannot be good at everything.
hard_numbers: **none reported** in a form I could extract. I read the full accepted manuscript; the treatment is analytical and qualitative (stiffness defined as k(φ,σ) = dτ/dφ, energy-capacity curves parameterised by stiffness setting) with no comparison table of device specifications. Anyone wanting per-device numbers should go to Grioli 2015 below.
design_relevance: The right document to hand a student team before they design a joint, because it prevents the standard mistake of specifying a stiffness range without noticing what it costs in mass and efficiency. Useful for justifying *why* the project did not build a VSA, if that is the conclusion.
evidence_grade: D — review.
limitations: Written by and for the VSA community, so it assumes a VSA is the answer. Nothing about sustained static load holding, nothing about safety validation, nothing about cost at student-project scale. ---

handle: VIA taxonomy — Vanderborght et al., 2013 (VIACTORS)
citation: B. Vanderborght, A. Albu-Schaeffer, A. Bicchi, E. Burdet, D. G. Caldwell, R. Carloni, M. Catalano, O. Eiberger, W. Friedl, G. Ganesh, M. Garabini, M. Grebenstein, G. Grioli, S. Haddadin, H. Hoppner, A. Jafari, M. Laffranchi, D. Lefeber, F. Petit, S. Stramigioli, N. Tsagarakis, M. Van Damme, R. Van Ham, L. C. Visser, S. Wolf, "Variable impedance actuators: A review," *Robotics and Autonomous Systems*, vol. 61, no. 12, pp. 1601–1614, December 2013.
source: 10.1016/j.robot.2013.06.009 — verified via Crossref (full 25-author list, vol/iss/pages) and by fetching and text-extracting the accepted manuscript at https://www.centropiaggio.unipi.it/sites/default/files/2013_VABBCCCEFGGGGHHJLLPSTVVVW_RAS.pdf.
contribution: The reference taxonomy and the principal published output of the EU VIACTORS project. Classifies by *how* variable stiffness and damping are obtained: active impedance by control, inherent compliance/damping, inertial actuators, and combinations.
hard_numbers: **none reported** that I could extract from the accepted manuscript. It is a classification paper. (The most-cited work in this set — >1000 citations — and still it gives the design team no numbers, which is itself worth knowing.)
design_relevance: Use it to place whatever the team builds on a recognised map, and to make the one decision it actually forces: **active impedance by control vs inherent physical compliance**. Active impedance is far cheaper in mass and parts but fails safe-open — power loss, sensor fault or a controller hang leaves a rigid arm. For a device a frail person leans on, that distinction is the whole argument.
evidence_grade: D — review.
limitations: No performance data, no safety data, no cost data. A taxonomy, not a selection tool. ---

handle: VSA datasheets and benchmarking — Grioli et al., 2015
citation: G. Grioli, S. Wolf, M. Garabini, M. Catalano, E. Burdet, D. Caldwell, R. Carloni, W. Friedl, M. Grebenstein, M. Laffranchi, D. Lefeber, S. Stramigioli, N. Tsagarakis, M. van Damme, B. Vanderborght, A. Albu-Schaeffer, A. Bicchi, "Variable stiffness actuators: The user's point of view," *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, vol. 34, no. 6, pp. 727–743, 2015.
source: 10.1177/0278364914566515 — verified via Crossref (full 17-author list, vol/iss/pages) and OpenAlex (abstract retrieved, listed OA at the Twente repository).
open_access: partial (Twente repository record listed as best OA location; the file itself did not resolve for me).
contribution: The VIACTORS consortium's attempt to fix the problem that VSA data is scattered and non-comparable. Proposes a standard **VSA datasheet** — the parameter set an engineer needs to select a VSA the way they would select a conventional electric actuator, extending the usual motor parameters with quantities describing stiffness-change capability.
hard_numbers: none verified. The paper defines *which* quantities should be reported (stiffness range, stiffness-change time, energy capacity, and so on); I could not retrieve the populated tables, so I will not quote device figures.
design_relevance: This is the specification checklist for the fallback decision. If the team goes VSA, this is the list of quantities that must appear in the design report — and if a candidate off-the-shelf unit cannot supply them, that is a reason to reject it. Also the honest answer to "which VSA should we buy": the literature is not organised well enough to answer that, and this paper says so.
evidence_grade: D — methodology/standardisation proposal.
limitations: Proposes a convention; it did not become one. No device in this project's price range is likely to publish a compliant datasheet. ---

handle: Low-cost modular VSA — Catalano et al., 2011 (VSA-Cube / VSA-CubeBot)
citation: M. G. Catalano, G. Grioli, M. Garabini, F. Bonomo, M. Mancini, N. Tsagarakis, A. Bicchi, "VSA-CubeBot: A modular variable stiffness platform for multiple degrees of freedom robots," *Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)*, Shanghai, 2011, pp. 5090–5095.
source: 10.1109/ICRA.2011.5980457 — verified via Crossref (full author list, pp. 5090–5095) and OpenAlex (abstract retrieved, 149 citations).
open_access: partial (an OA record is listed at openaccessrepository.it; it returned 404 when I fetched it).
contribution: The only VSA in this set designed with **low cost as the primary goal**, built from hobby servos into a modular unit, with single-actuator characterisation (theoretical and experimental) and five units chained into an arm.
hard_numbers: none verified — abstract only. The per-unit torque and stiffness-range figures are in the body and I did not read them. Expect hobby-servo class torque, i.e. roughly two orders of magnitude below what an assistive torso needs.
design_relevance: The realistic *prototyping* path, not the product path. If the team wants to test a variable-stiffness control strategy and a safety protocol on a bench rig this semester, this is the architecture that fits a student budget. It is not a candidate for the torque target.
evidence_grade: B — hardware, characterised, no humans.
limitations: Torque class is nowhere near a person leaning on a torso; hobby-servo internals mean poor repeatability, backlash and no meaningful duty rating; 2011 componentry. ---

handle: Torque-controlled rigid arm as the baseline — Albu-Schäffer et al., 2007 (DLR LWR → KUKA iiwa)
citation: A. Albu-Schäffer, S. Haddadin, Ch. Ott, A. Stemmer, T. Wimböck, G. Hirzinger, "The DLR lightweight robot: design and control concepts for robots in human environments," *Industrial Robot: An International Journal*, vol. 34, no. 5, pp. 376–385, 2007.
source: 10.1108/01439910710774386 — verified via Crossref (full author list, vol/iss/pages) and OpenAlex (abstract retrieved, 622 citations; OA record at TUM mediaTUM 1438494).
contribution: The mechatronic design that became the KUKA LBR iiwa: **joint torque sensing in every joint**, load-to-weight ratio 1:1, active vibration damping, sensitive collision detection, and compliant (impedance) control at joint and Cartesian level, made robust by passivity-based control and sensor redundancy.
hard_numbers: **load-to-weight ratio 1:1** is the only figure in the verified abstract. Other specifications are in the body, which I did not read.
design_relevance: The honest alternative the team must argue against. This machine is not intrinsically compliant — it is stiff hardware with torque sensors and impedance control — and it is the arm that actually got certified, sold, and deployed next to people. It is also the arm used in the crash tests above. Two consequences: (1) **torque sensing plus impedance control, without any spring, is a commercially validated route to safe pHRI**, and it is lighter and stiffer than SEA; (2) it fails unsafe on power loss, which is the specific gap a spring closes. That is the real trade, and the design report should state it in those terms.
evidence_grade: B — hardware, extensively deployed; safety validation is in the separate crash-test papers above.
limitations: An industrial serial arm, not a torso; the safety case depends on continuously powered, correctly functioning sensing and control; joint torque sensors at this quality are expensive and outside a student BOM. --- All Crossref-verified; not expanded above because they duplicate or narrow the entries already given. Full BibTeX for each is in `A2.bib`. - **Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer & Hirzinger, "Requirements for Safe Robots: Measurements, Analysis and New Insights," IJRR 28(11–12):1507–1527, 2009** — DOI 10.1177/0278364909343970 (Crossref + OpenAlex abstract verified; OA at TUM mediaTUM 1438496). The journal extension of the RSS 2007 crash-test paper, adding the **quasi-static constrained impact** analysis — "a serious threat to the human even for low-inertia robots." If the team cites one Haddadin paper in the report, this is arguably the one, because the constrained case is this project's case. I verified the record and abstract but not the full text, so I quote no numbers from it here. Grade A. - **Van Ham, Sugar, Vanderborght, Hollander & Lefeber, "Compliant actuator designs," IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine 16(3):81–94, 2009** — DOI 10.1109/MRA.2009.933629 (Crossref + OpenAlex abstract verified). The earlier and more readable compliant-actuator review; gives the four-way split (equilibrium-controlled, antagonistic-controlled, structure-controlled, mechanically-controlled stiffness) that the later reviews assume. Grade D. - **Wolf, Eiberger & Hirzinger, "The DLR FSJ: Energy based design of a variable stiffness joint," ICRA 2011, pp. 5082–5089** — DOI 10.1109/ICRA.2011.5980303 (Crossref + OpenAlex abstract verified). Energy-first VSA design for the DLR Hand Arm System arm axes; abstract explicitly reports "a demonstration of robustness... by the investigation of a blunt impact to the tip of the arm," but the numbers are behind IEEE. Grade B.

handle: McKibben design review — Kortman, Jovanova, Nabae, Endo, Suzumori & Sakes, 2026
citation: V. G. Kortman, J. Jovanova, H. Nabae, G. Endo, K. Suzumori, A. Sakes, "Designing McKibben muscles: a critical review for practical implementation," *Bioinspiration & Biomimetics*, vol. 21, no. 3, art. 031002, 2026.
source: https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-3190/ae66c0 — **fetched:** Crossref record + IOPscience article page (full text readable).
contribution: Systematic review of 146 Scopus-indexed McKibben papers, organised as a *design* reference: bladder/sleeve choices, bundling topologies (serial, parallel, braided, convergent, pennate), and the performance envelope you actually get.
hard_numbers: axial strain 20–35% typical, 30–35% for best designs; braided configurations reach contraction ratio 0.34–0.41; smallest unit cited 1.5 mm dia. at 15% strain and 350 mm/s; largest hydraulic unit 40 mm dia. at up to 28 kN. **Typical driving frequency in the literature clusters around 0.3 Hz; above ~1 Hz the muscle cannot fully inflate/deflate.** Bandwidth improvable by up to 400% by cutting internal dead volume. Tension intensity 88–144 N/cm² (biological muscle 35 N/cm²); energy efficiency 0.32–0.49 (muscle 0.2–0.25); work density 0.13–0.20 J/cm³; peak power density 2.65 W/cm³ (muscle 0.70 W/cm³); one optimised inelastic-bladder design ~80% efficiency. Hysteresis grows with driving frequency from bladder viscoelasticity. Latex bladder fatigue life ~24× silicone at large strain; leakage is the common failure mode. Review states no comprehensive untethered-supply solution is established.
design_relevance: This is the single most useful document for A3. It sets the honest bandwidth ceiling (~0.3–1 Hz for a normal build), gives the force-density argument *for* PAMs, and names the failure mode (leaks) and the unsolved problem (untethered supply). Use its strain/pressure envelope directly in the actuator trade table.
evidence_grade: D (review), but the highest-quality D available.
limitations: A review of unit actuators, not of loaded joints. Nothing here tells you what happens when a 70 kg person leans on the arm and the muscle is back-driven; the quoted efficiency numbers are actuator-level, not system-level including compressor. ---

handle: Foundational McKibben model — Chou & Hannaford, 1996
citation: C.-P. Chou and B. Hannaford, "Measurement and modeling of McKibben pneumatic artificial muscles," *IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation*, vol. 12, no. 1, pp. 90–102, 1996.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/70.481753 — **fetched:** Crossref record (title, authors, venue, vol/iss/pages, year all confirmed) and the Semantic Scholar record (1554 citations).
open_access: no. (A DTIC technical-report version exists at apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA299458.pdf but returned HTTP 403 to my fetch — I could not read it, so I am not quoting numbers from it.)
contribution: The static geometric force model F = f(P, contraction) for braided-sleeve muscles plus static and dynamic length–tension measurement, and the explicit comparison against human skeletal muscle.
hard_numbers: **Not verified first-hand** — the paywall and the DTIC 403 blocked me. The numbers routinely attributed to this paper (max contraction stress ~0.3 MPa, contraction ratio 25–30%) appear in secondary sources I did not treat as authoritative. The *verified* equivalent figures are the tension-intensity/efficiency/work-density ranges in Kortman et al. 2026 above, which cite this model. Note the paper's well-known qualitative result: PAM force does **not** fall with shortening velocity the way muscle force does.
design_relevance: It is the equation you will actually sizing-calculate with. Cite it for the model; cite Kortman for the numbers.
evidence_grade: B (hardware characterisation, no humans).
limitations: Ideal-cylinder assumption, ignores bladder wall thickness and friction — i.e. it deliberately omits the hysteresis that will dominate your control problem. 1996 materials. ---

handle: X-PAM — Feng, Yang, Ren, Wei & Gu, 2023
citation: M. Feng, D. Yang, L. Ren, G. Wei, G. Gu, "X-crossing pneumatic artificial muscles," *Science Advances*, vol. 9, no. 38, 2023.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adi7133 — **fetched:** Crossref record + Semantic Scholar abstract (science.org itself 403'd).
contribution: A non-braided positive-pressure muscle using an X-crossing linkage that breaks the PAM trade-off between contraction ratio, force, and speed.
hard_numbers: contraction ratio 92.9%; output force 207.9 N·kg⁻¹·kPa⁻¹; strain rate 1603.0 %/s; specific power 5.7 kW/kg; work density 842.9 kJ/m³. Demonstrated on a robotic elbow, a jumping robot and a gripper. Explicitly framed as overcoming "the slow actuation of conventional PAMs."
design_relevance: Two uses. (1) If the team wants a fluidic arm that is actually fast, the braided McKibben is not the state of the art. (2) More usefully as a rhetorical baseline in the design review: a *Science Advances* paper exists whose entire premise is that conventional PAMs are too slow. That is the argument against McKibben, from the pro-fluidic camp.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Bench actuators and small demos, not a loaded human-scale arm. The X-crossing mechanism has rigid linkages — it is less intrinsically safe on contact than a soft braided muscle, which cuts against this project's whole premise. No fatigue/durability data at the scale a torso needs. ---

handle: Pneumatic upper-limb rehab review — Zhao, Zhang, Cai & Wei, 2026
citation: Y. Zhao, Y.-M. Zhang, M.-L. Cai, F. Wei, "Advances in Pneumatic Upper-Limb Rehabilitation Robots: A Critical Review of Structural Design, Human–Robot Interaction, and Clinical Translation," *Robotics*, vol. 15, no. 8, art. 159, 2026.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/robotics15080159 — **fetched:** Crossref record + Semantic Scholar abstract (mdpi.com 403'd my fetch, but the DOI and full abstract are confirmed and it is CC BY).
contribution: Current-decade survey of pneumatically actuated upper-limb rehab robots, comparing rigid exoskeletons vs. soft wearables vs. rigid–soft hybrids on output capability, motion accuracy, comfort and clinical applicability.
hard_numbers: none extractable without the full text (MDPI blocked). The verified abstract-level findings are qualitative but load-bearing: clinical translation "remains hindered by challenges including actuator hysteresis, nonlinear dynamics, limited accuracy in intention recognition, and inconsistent clinical evaluation metrics"; existing trials are "constrained by small sample sizes, short interventions, and heterogeneous protocols"; the field's conclusion is that **rigid–soft hybrid** architectures are the developmental trend, because rigid gives precision and soft gives safety.
design_relevance: Direct support for a hybrid architecture rather than a purist "all soft" torso — rigid skeleton, compliant actuation. Also the citation to use when a reviewer asks "why isn't everyone doing PAMs already?"
evidence_grade: D.
limitations: 2026 review of a field where the underlying trials are weak; it inherits their weakness. Wearable exoskeletons, not freestanding torsos — the load path is completely different (their reaction force goes into the user's own body; yours goes into a base). ---

handle: PASE soft elbow exosuit, 19 subjects — Sridhar, Erel, Nasirian, Wijesundara & Rahman, 2025
citation: E. P. Sridhar, V. Erel, A. Nasirian, M. B. J. Wijesundara, M. Rahman, "Design, development, and evaluation of a pneumatically actuated soft wearable robotic elbow exoskeleton for reducing muscle activity and perceived workload," *Journal of Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies Engineering*, vol. 12, art. 20556683251347517, 2025.
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/20556683251347517 — **fetched:** PubMed esummary (PMID 40463354) and PMC full text (PMC12130663).
contribution: A fabric/silicone pneumatic elbow exosuit measured on humans for EMG reduction and subjective workload across three realistic tasks.
hard_numbers: n = 19 (14 M, 5 F, 18–45). Operating pressure 18 psi (124 kPa) nominal, tested 15–25 psi, max 21 psi (145 kPa). **Max torque 4.39 N·m at 21 psi, 30° elbow angle**; at 18 psi: 3.15 N·m (30°), 1.90 N·m (60°), 1.45 N·m (90°). EMG reduction: biceps 22.4% / triceps 18.2% (static hold), down to 10.2% / 5.2% on the power-tool task; variable-weight test biceps 24.2%. NASA-TLX reduced by 8.9–9.6 points. Device mass 638 g. **Inflation was manual during trials** — no compressor in the loop.
design_relevance: This is the most honest "what does a soft pneumatic joint actually deliver to a human" datapoint in the set. Note the torque: **~1.5–4.4 N·m at the elbow, and it falls by ~55% as the joint extends from 30° to 90°.** If your spec needs to support a leaning adult, a single fluidic actuator of this class is roughly an order of magnitude short, and its torque is strongly configuration-dependent. Also note the authors dodged the supply problem entirely by hand-pumping.
evidence_grade: A (hardware + 19 human subjects, standardised NASA-TLX + EMG).
limitations: Wearable, so the suit borrows the human skeleton as its structure; a freestanding torso has no such luxury. Healthy young adults, not elderly or impaired. Torque falls off steeply with angle — a leaning patient will load the arm at exactly the extended angles where it is weakest. And the manual inflation means this paper contains *no* evidence about continuous pneumatic supply. ---

handle: PAM assist suits in real nursing facilities — Kato et al., 2021
citation: K. Kato, T. Yoshimi, S. Tsuchimoto, N. Mizuguchi, K. Aimoto, N. Itoh, I. Kondo, "Identification of care tasks for the use of wearable transfer support robots – an observational study at nursing facilities using robots on a daily basis," *BMC Health Services Research*, vol. 21, art. 665, 2021.
source: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-021-06639-2 — **fetched:** Semantic Scholar record (abstract, PMC8256590, PMID 34225718).
contribution: Time-motion observation of caregivers at two Japanese nursing facilities that have used PAM-driven Muscle Suit (INNOPHYS) and HAL Lumbar for >24 months as routine equipment.
hard_numbers: two facilities; 1-minute observational time-motion sampling; robots used for direct care in **>70% of transits**, concentrated in transfer assistance and toileting; heaviest use in the morning wake-up block. UMIN000039204. No force/pressure/bandwidth numbers — it is a services-research paper.
design_relevance: The only evidence I found that PAM actuation has *survived contact with an actual care setting over years*. Critically, the Muscle Suit is compressor-free in service (hand pump / gas cartridge). That is the deployment pattern that worked. It is an argument that PAMs are acceptable in elder care **when the air supply is not a running compressor**.
evidence_grade: A (real-world deployment with human data), but soft outcomes.
limitations: Observational, no control condition, no injury or force data, two sites. It tells you about a worn lumbar assist device, not a freestanding robot that contacts a frail patient. Transfers nothing about actuator dynamics. ---

handle: EMG-controlled pneumatic rubber muscle assist suit — Ogawa, Ono, Fukuda, Tsuneyasu & Kurita, 2018
citation: K. Ogawa, A. Ono, Y. Fukuda, K. Tsuneyasu, Y. Kurita, "Development of a Lightweight Flexible Construction Work Assist Suit Using Pneumatic Rubber Artificial Muscles," in *Proc. 40th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC)*, 2018.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/EMBC.2018.8513402 — **fetched:** Semantic Scholar record (abstract, PMID 30441325).
contribution: A lumbar assist suit with lightweight pneumatic rubber muscles whose assist force is PWM-modulated from spinal-erector EMG and an estimated hip torque; experimentally reduced measured muscle activity during bend/stretch. Also proposes a temple-mounted EMG for intent detection.
hard_numbers: none reported in the verified abstract (force, pressure, mass, participant count all absent from what I could read; full text paywalled).
design_relevance: Relevant for the *intent-detection + PAM* control pattern (D1 overlap): if the robot must decide when to assist a patient who is leaning, EMG-triggered PWM on the muscle is a demonstrated, simple approach that does not require solving the PAM inverse model.
evidence_grade: A (human EMG measurement) — but downgrade in practice because I could not verify sample size.
limitations: Conference paper, unverified n, worn device. EMG on a frail elderly user is far noisier and less ethically simple than on a construction worker. ---

handle: RUPERT + FES with iterative learning control — Tu et al., 2017
citation: X. Tu, H. Han, J. Huang, J. Li, C. Su, X. Jiang, J. He, "Upper Limb Rehabilitation Robot Powered by PAMs Cooperates with FES Arrays to Realize Reach-to-Grasp Trainings," *Journal of Healthcare Engineering*, vol. 2017, art. 1282934, pp. 1–15, 2017.
source: https://doi.org/10.1155/2017/1282934 — **fetched:** Crossref record and Europe PMC full-text XML (PMC5494786).
contribution: RUPERT — a lightweight portable exoskeleton whose joints are **unidirectionally** actuated by PAMs — paired with FES arrays to get the missing return direction, controlled by iterative learning control because neither the PAM nor the stimulated muscle is tractable with a fixed model.
hard_numbers: 3 healthy subjects (ages 32, 34, 29), ethics-approved. Target angles [60°, 45°], 10 s task, RMS tracking error < 2°. The PAM model used is an explicitly **asymmetric three-element model with separate inflation and deflation damping coefficients (B₀ⁱ/B₁ⁱ vs B₀ᵈ/B₁ᵈ)** — i.e. the hysteresis is baked into the plant model as two different systems. EMG leads muscle force by 20–30 ms (their justification for bioelectric intent sensing). No force, pressure or mass figures given.
design_relevance: Two hard lessons. (1) A real PAM arm went **unidirectional** and needed an entirely separate actuation modality (FES) to get the other direction — antagonistic pairs are not free. (2) The team resorted to iterative learning control, which works only for repeated trajectories. A robot a patient leans on unpredictably cannot use ILC. That is a direct warning about PAM controllability under unscripted contact.
evidence_grade: A (human subjects) — but n = 3, healthy, no patients. Treat as A-with-an-asterisk.
limitations: n = 3 healthy adults, scripted trajectories, treadmill/bench context. Nothing about contact forces or disturbance rejection. Being honest: this is weak evidence dressed as a clinical paper. ---

handle: Thin McKibben muscle and multifilament bundles — Kurumaya, Nabae, Endo & Suzumori, 2017
citation: S. Kurumaya, H. Nabae, G. Endo, K. Suzumori, "Design of thin McKibben muscle and multifilament structure," *Sensors and Actuators A: Physical*, vol. 261, pp. 66–74, 2017.
source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sna.2017.04.047 — **fetched:** Crossref record (title/authors/venue/vol/pages/year confirmed) + Semantic Scholar record (136 citations).
