contribution: Sub-2 mm-diameter McKibben muscles that are flexible enough to be woven, and the demonstration that bundling them into "multifilament" muscles gives force that **scales linearly with filament count** while keeping the bundle routable like a tendon.
hard_numbers: filament diameter ~1.8 mm (2–3 mm variants), durable to 0.5 MPa; a 60-filament demonstration bundle behaved as a linear actuator; output force proportional to filament count. Companion OA paper (Kurumaya, Suzumori, Nabae & Wakimoto, *ROBOMECH Journal* 3:25, 2016, DOI 10.1186/s40648-016-0061-3, Crossref-verified) applies the bundles to a musculoskeletal lower-limb robot — but Springer blocked my full-text fetch so I have no numbers from it.
design_relevance: The most practical route to a *human-scale* PAM arm on a student budget. You size force by adding filaments rather than by making one fat muscle, and the bundle can be routed around a compliant torso structure the way a tendon is. Also directly informs B1: thin muscles can be embedded in fabric/structure rather than bolted on.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Force scales linearly with filaments; so does **air volume, and therefore compressor duty and response time**. 60 filaments is 60 potential leak points and 60 terminations to crimp. No human contact, no safety data. A senior design team will underestimate the fabrication labour here badly. ---

handle: Recurrent braiding to raise contraction ratio — Koizumi, Kurumaya, Nabae, Endo & Suzumori, 2020
citation: S. Koizumi, S. Kurumaya, H. Nabae, G. Endo, K. Suzumori, "Recurrent Braiding of Thin McKibben Muscles to Overcome Their Limitation of Contraction," *Soft Robotics*, vol. 7, no. 2, pp. 251–258, 2020.
source: https://doi.org/10.1089/soro.2019.0022 — **fetched:** Crossref record + Semantic Scholar full abstract.
contribution: Braiding thin McKibben muscles out of thin McKibben muscles, recursively, raises stroke beyond the geometric limit of a single muscle.
hard_numbers: single thin McKibben contraction ratio **28%**; braided once **37%**; braided twice **41%**. Theory and experiment agree; ratio keeps rising with more braiding levels.
design_relevance: This is the number to quote when someone claims PAMs "only give 25%." A shoulder needing large joint excursion can get ~40% stroke from a bundled architecture. Conversely it confirms that a plain McKibben tops out near 28% — which sets your moment-arm and muscle-length geometry, and a long muscle needs a long torso to live in.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Contraction ratio is bought with force and with more air volume per unit stroke; the abstract does not report the force penalty, and I could not read the full text to check. Bench actuators only. Recursive braiding is a serious fabrication skill, not a weekend job. ---

handle: Silent electrically driven thin McKibben muscles — Cacucciolo, Nabae, Suzumori & Shea, 2020
citation: V. Cacucciolo, H. Nabae, K. Suzumori, H. Shea, "Electrically-Driven Soft Fluidic Actuators Combining Stretchable Pumps With Thin McKibben Muscles," *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, vol. 6, art. 146, 2020.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2019.00146 — **fetched:** Crossref record + the Frontiers full-text page.
contribution: Pairing a 1 g solid-state electrohydrodynamic stretchable pump with a low-pressure thin McKibben muscle to get a **completely silent, compressor-free, tube-free** fluidic actuator — and quantifies the price.
hard_numbers: muscle blocked force 0.84 N; stroke 4 mm on 180 mm length = **2.2% contraction**; operating pressure 10–20 kPa (vs. standard 100–200 kPa); inner tube ~1 mm dia., 0.15 mm wall; 0.0424 N/kPa. Pump 1 g, 1.5 × 10 mm cross-section, 5–8 kV, ~100 µL/s, ~19 kPa at 7.2 kV. Combined mass 2 g. **Response 10–90%: rise ~14 s, fall ~6.6 s.** Pump efficiency 0.65%; full system efficiency **0.0052%**. Silent operation explicitly claimed.
design_relevance: This is the honest answer to "can we get rid of the compressor?" for the noise constraint. Yes — and the actuator then produces 0.84 N with a 14-second rise time at 0.005% efficiency. The silent-supply route is nowhere near human-scale assistive force. Use this to close off a tempting-but-dead design branch in one slide.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Milli-newton scale, kilovolt drive (a new safety problem next to a patient), 14 s response. Zero transfer to a torso a person leans on, which is precisely why it is worth citing. ---

handle: Electro-pneumatic pumps — Diteesawat, Helps, Taghavi & Rossiter, 2021
citation: R. S. Diteesawat, T. Helps, M. Taghavi, J. Rossiter, "Electro-pneumatic pumps for soft robotics," *Science Robotics*, vol. 6, no. 51, eabc3721, 2021.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.abc3721 — **fetched:** Crossref record + Semantic Scholar abstract; OA author manuscript at research-information.bris.ac.uk.
open_access: partial (accepted author manuscript OA via Bristol; publisher version paywalled).
contribution: A flexible dielectric-fluid electrostatic-zipping pump, 1.1 mm thick and 5.3 g, that silently supplies pressure locally — framed explicitly against "large, heavy pressure vessels or **noisy, inefficient air pumps**."
hard_numbers: pressure up to 2.34 kPa; volumetric flow up to 161 mL/s; under 0.5 W; thickness 1.1 mm; mass 5.3 g. Drove a soft actuator to 32.40% contraction change at 54.43 %/s. Demonstrated in an antagonistic mechanism, an arm-flexing wearable, and a continuous-pumping system.
design_relevance: The peer-reviewed statement that conventional pneumatic supplies are noisy — useful to cite for the elder-care noise constraint rather than asserting it. But 2.34 kPa is ~50–100× below McKibben operating pressure, so it cannot be your supply. Keep it as the "state of the art in silent supply" bound.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Pressure two orders of magnitude short of what a load-bearing McKibben needs. High-voltage drive. No human-contact data. ---

handle: phloSAR portable supply — Ahlquist, Jitosho, Bao & Okamura, 2024
citation: M. Ahlquist, R. Jitosho, J. Bao, A. M. Okamura, "phloSAR: a Portable, High-Flow Pressure Supply and Regulator Enabling Untethered Operation of Large Pneumatic Soft Robots," arXiv:2403.01086, 2024.
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01086 — **fetched:** arXiv abstract page and the full PDF (text extracted locally).
contribution: A 0.84 kg portable supply built from high-flow proportional valves, a 2 L PET reservoir and a Venturi vacuum generator, quantifying exactly what it costs to cut the air tether on a large soft robot.
hard_numbers: phloSAR mass 0.84 kg; total with soft robot 1.4 kg. Reservoir: 2 L PET bottle, operating reservoir pressure 690 kPa, burst >900 kPa. Valve flow: EVP 23.5 SLPM, DVP 67.0 SLPM; valve inlet limit 690 kPa. Control error cutoff 1 kPa. Key comparative figure: **micropumps for untethered soft robots cap out around 10 SLPM** and their flow drops as outlet pressure builds; single-use CO₂ cartridges hold ~6000 kPa but freeze the regulator on sustained draw. A reservoir has inherently finite operable duration; refilling it onboard means adding a compressor, which "increases system weight, size, and cost."
design_relevance: This is the plumbing-cost paper. It says in print: for a *large-volume* pneumatic soft robot you either accept a tether to a compressor, or accept a finite-duration reservoir, or carry a compressor. For a freestanding torso in a care room, the tether is the least-bad option and the compressor belongs in the base or in another room. Use the 10 SLPM micropump ceiling to kill the "just use a small quiet pump" suggestion early.
evidence_grade: B (hardware validated, models verified on hardware).
limitations: arXiv preprint, no journal peer review confirmed. Built for a 1.5 kg drone payload budget and a vine robot; a torso with several multifilament muscles has far larger volume and duty cycle. No noise measurement, no runtime figure in what I could read. ---

handle: Hydraulic vs. pneumatic working fluid — Chambers & Wereley, 2021
citation: J. M. Chambers and N. M. Wereley, "Influence of hydraulic versus pneumatic working fluids on quasi-static force response of fluidic artificial muscles," *Journal of Intelligent Material Systems and Structures*, vol. 32, no. 3, pp. 385–396, 2021.
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/1045389X21991927 — **fetched:** Crossref record + Semantic Scholar abstract (marked OA).
open_access: yes per Semantic Scholar (SAGE CHORUS licence).
contribution: Directly tests whether the McKibben force model is fluid-dependent. Using air or water at precisely matched isobaric conditions, on both large and small actuators, the force–contraction curves were **nearly identical**.
hard_numbers: none beyond "nearly identical isobaric force–contraction response curves" in the verified abstract; the specific force/pressure values are in the full text I did not read. Says explicitly the result extends existing pneumatic models to any practical liquid or gas.
design_relevance: Settles the hydraulic-alternative question cleanly for *sizing*: switching to water buys you **no extra static force** at the same pressure. What hydraulics buys is stiffness, position accuracy and efficiency (secondary sources put hydraulic ~60% vs pneumatic ~25–30%, which I did not verify to a primary source and therefore flag as unconfirmed). What it costs is leaks onto a patient, mass, and a pump that is not obviously quieter. For a one-year senior design project: do not go hydraulic.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Quasi-static only — the whole hydraulic advantage is dynamic, and this paper deliberately does not test it. Bench actuators. Says nothing about safety of a water-filled arm in a care setting. ---

handle: McKibben modelling review — Tondu, 2012
citation: B. Tondu, "Modelling of the McKibben artificial muscle: A review," *Journal of Intelligent Material Systems and Structures*, vol. 23, no. 3, pp. 225–253, 2012.
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/1045389X11435435 — **fetched:** Crossref record (title/venue/vol/iss/pages/year confirmed); Semantic Scholar shows 438 citations.
open_access: no (SAGE paywall; no abstract exposed by Semantic Scholar either).
contribution: The standard survey of static and dynamic McKibben models up to 2012, including the widely repeated attribution of PAM hysteresis to **strand-on-strand friction inside the braided weave** (as distinct from bladder viscoelasticity).
hard_numbers: none verified — I could not read past the paywall, and I am not quoting figures from search snippets.
design_relevance: Cite for the *mechanism* of hysteresis when justifying a control approach: friction-dominated hysteresis is rate-independent-ish and amenable to Prandtl–Ishlinskii-style inversion, whereas viscoelastic hysteresis is not. That distinction decides whether feedforward compensation will work on your arm.
evidence_grade: D.
limitations: 2012, pre-dates thin-muscle and bundled architectures entirely. Review only. --- McKibben PAMs give you the force density and the intrinsic compliance this project is built around — 88–144 N/cm² tension intensity and ~2.65 W/cm³ peak power density beat skeletal muscle, and a bundled multifilament muscle lets you buy force linearly by adding filaments — so on paper they are the right actuator for an arm a person is allowed to lean on. The killer is bandwidth: the reviewed literature clusters around **0.3 Hz driving frequency**, and above roughly 1 Hz a McKibben cannot fully inflate or deflate, which means your arm cannot react to an unexpected contact faster than a person can push it, and your "compliant safety" will come from the rubber, not from the controller. Controllability is worse than the papers make it sound — the one PAM arm here that actually touched humans (RUPERT) went *unidirectional* and imported functional electrical stimulation to get the return stroke, then needed iterative learning control, which only works on repeated trajectories and is therefore useless for a patient leaning at a moment of their own choosing. The force you should plan for is sobering: the best human-subject soft pneumatic elbow in this set delivers 1.45–4.39 N·m and loses over half of it going from 30° to 90°, i.e. it is weakest exactly where a leaning person loads it. Hydraulics is a dead end for you — Chambers & Wereley show the static force is identical for the same pressure, so you would take on leaks, mass and a pump for a dynamic benefit you have no time to exploit. On noise and tethering, be blunt in the design review: silent supplies exist and they are not remotely adequate (2.34 kPa from the Science Robotics electro-pneumatic pump, 0.84 N and a 14-second rise time from the silent thin-McKibben system at 0.005% system efficiency), micropumps cap near 10 SLPM, reservoirs have finite duration, and the only deployment in this set that genuinely survived years in nursing facilities — the Muscle Suit — ducked the problem by not running a compressor at all. So: **yes, PAMs are viable for this arm, on three conditions** — put the compressor outside the care room or in a heavy damped base and run a tether, adopt the rigid–soft hybrid architecture the 2026 rehab review converges on rather than an all-soft torso, and write a spec that never asks the arm to move faster than ~0.5 Hz or to hold torque at full extension. If the team cannot accept a tether, stop now and go to A2 (SEA/VSA), because every untethered fluidic supply in the verified literature is one to two orders of magnitude short of human-scale assistive force. One more warning: a 60-filament bundle is 60 crimped terminations and 60 leak paths, and leakage is the documented common failure mode — budget fabrication and leak-chasing time the way you would budget machining, or the one-year clock will be spent on plumbing rather than on the deflection tests that actually validate the design.

handle: Baloo — Johnson, Clawson & Killpack, 2024/2025
citation: C. C. Johnson, A. Clawson, M. D. Killpack, "Baloo: A Large-Scale Hybrid Soft Robotic Torso for Whole-Arm Manipulation," arXiv:2409.08420 [cs.RO], submitted Sept 2024, revised Mar 2025.
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.08420 (fetched arXiv abstract page)
contribution: A human-scale hybrid soft-rigid torso with two meter-long pneumatically actuated soft arms that performs whole-arm (not fingertip) grasping of large heavy objects, using passive compliance to distribute contact force instead of modelling it.
hard_numbers: two ~1 m pneumatic arms; **19 kg payload at the end effector**; 30 whole-body grasping trials, 100% success across varied object shapes/weights; strength-to-weight ratio stated as competitive with similar-size rigid robots. Torso joint count and arm mass not given on the abstract page.
design_relevance: This is the closest existing analogue to your whole system — a freestanding soft torso plus two compliant arms that actually carries kilograms. It is the existence proof that hybrid (rigid skeleton + soft pneumatic actuation) reaches useful load, and it is evidence that the *dynamic* load case is solvable. Steal the architecture: rigid structural spine, soft actuated links, whole-arm contact.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Payload is a hanging/grasped load at the end effector, not a lateral leaning load on the torso, and not a static hold for minutes. No reported test of an off-axis moment applied to the torso, which is exactly your load case. Preprint; peer-review status unclear.

handle: Inflated-beam collapse — McFarland & Coad, 2023
citation: C. McFarland, M. M. Coad, "Collapse of Straight Soft Growing Inflated Beam Robots Under Their Own Weight," arXiv:2307.00089v1 [cs.RO], June 2023.
source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.00089v1 (fetched full HTML)
contribution: Derives and experimentally validates when a fabric inflated beam folds under its own weight, giving a closed-form structural limit for any pressurised soft link.
hard_numbers: critical collapse moment **M_collapse = PπD³/8**; tested D = 2.43, 3.24, 4.04, 4.85 cm; P = 2.07–13.8 kPa; collapse lengths 0.3–1.5 m; horizontal case L = D·√(P/(8tρg)); TPU-coated ripstop nylon t = 0.031 mm, ρ = 2199 kg/m³, E = 1.3 GPa.
design_relevance: This is the single most useful equation in the packet. Run your own load case through it before choosing any inflatable link. Example with their formula: a Ø150 mm fabric arm at 20 kPa gives M_collapse ≈ 26 N·m. A patient leaning 200 N at 0.5 m from the shoulder applies ~100 N·m. You would need ~75 kPa (11 psi) at that diameter, or ~Ø230 mm at 20 kPa, to not fold. A 75 kPa tube is not soft to the touch any more — it feels like a car tyre. That trade is the whole argument against a fully inflatable arm here.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Self-weight collapse of a straight cantilever, not a joint-articulated arm under an external human lean; no repeated-load or creep data; fabric-specific constants.

handle: Protective soft skins — Svarny et al., 2022
citation: P. Svarny, J. Rozlivek, L. Rustler, M. Sramek, O. Deli, M. Zillich, M. Hoffmann, "Effect of Active and Passive Protective Soft Skins on Collision Forces in Human-Robot Collaboration," *Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing*, 78, 102363, 2022.
source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rcim.2022.102363 (fetched arXiv:2203.09872 abstract page, which states the published venue and DOI)
open_access: partial (arXiv preprint open; journal version paywalled)
contribution: Systematic measurement of how a soft cover changes real collision forces on three manipulators, with a model extension that accounts for cover stiffness and thickness.
hard_numbers: 2250 collision measurements; passive skin lowered peak impact force **~40%** overall — reported as 40% (UR10e), 45% (KUKA LBR iiwa), 46% (KUKA Cybertech) in transient contact; measures impact force, contact duration, clamping force and impulse.
design_relevance: Quantifies exactly what "padded rigid arm" buys you: roughly a 40% cut in transient peak force, and nothing for the sustained/clamping case. If you go rigid-structure-plus-cover, this is your safety number and it is not a substitute for compliant actuation.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Industrial arms, not a torso; transient impact, not a person resting their weight on the cover; quasi-static clamping is where covers help least, and leaning is quasi-static.

handle: Kenshiro / Kengoro design principles — Asano, Okada & Inaba, 2017
citation: Y. Asano, K. Okada, M. Inaba, "Design principles of a human mimetic humanoid: Humanoid platform to study human intelligence and internal body system," *Science Robotics*, 2(13), eaaq0899, 2017.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aaq0899 (verified via Semantic Scholar Graph API record: DOI, venue, volume, year, authors, PMID 33157878)
open_access: no (publisher-closed; abstract elided in the API record)
contribution: The definitive statement of the musculoskeletal-humanoid design philosophy: rigid human-mimetic skeleton, multifunctional structural members, tendon-driven sensor-integrated muscle modules, compliance placed in the actuation rather than the structure.
hard_numbers: none verified from a page I could fetch. Kengoro specs widely cited as 1.7 m, 56 kg, 116 muscle modules, 174 DOF — the 56 kgf figure is confirmed in Kawaharazuka et al. 2024 below; treat the rest as secondary until someone reads the PDF.
design_relevance: This is the third architecture option in clean form — rigid load-bearing skeleton with compliance entirely in tendon actuation. It is the only one of the three that has demonstrated human-scale whole-body contact behaviour. It also tells you where the load path goes: through bones, in compression, to the floor. Same answer you want.
evidence_grade: A (for the architecture argument), C (for numbers, which I could not verify at source)
limitations: Not designed to be leaned on, and not designed for safety around frail users; the tendon redundancy that makes it compliant also makes it very hard to control and to certify. Enormously outside a senior-design budget and build time.

handle: Bone-muscle modules — Kawaharazuka et al., 2024
citation: K. Kawaharazuka, S. Makino, M. Kawamura, Y. Asano, Y. Kakiuchi, K. Okada, M. Inaba, "Human Mimetic Forearm Design with Radioulnar Joint using Miniature Bone-Muscle Modules and Its Applications," arXiv:2408.09934v1, 2024.
source: https://arxiv.org/html/2408.09934 (fetched full HTML)
contribution: Concrete mechanical design of the actuator modules that make a musculoskeletal arm work, embedded inside the bone structure itself.
hard_numbers: module 32.0 × 40.0 × 126 mm, **0.30 kgf per module**, 2× 60 W BLDC per module, **424 N continuous max winding tension**, gear ratios 84:1 and 157:1, Ø8 mm pulley, 116 mm/s no-load winding; forearm = 8 muscles in 4 modules, 6 DOF; 560 N (56.5 kgf) load cell; Kengoro total mass **56 kgf**.
design_relevance: Gives you real tendon force numbers to size against. 424 N per muscle is the order of magnitude a tendon-driven compliant arm needs to hold assistive load — and note that a 157:1 gear ratio is *not* backdrivable, so compliance there comes from tendon elasticity and force control, not from the transmission. Useful counterweight to the "just make it backdrivable" instinct.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Forearm scale; no data on sustained holding, thermal limits under static load (a leaning patient is a stall-torque condition), or structural margin.

handle: Lightweight hybrid soft arm — Ohta et al., 2018
citation: P. Ohta, L. Valle, J. King, K. Low, J. Yi, C. G. Atkeson, Y.-L. Park, "Design of a Lightweight Soft Robotic Arm Using Pneumatic Artificial Muscles and Inflatable Sleeves," *Soft Robotics*, 5(2), 204–215, 2018.
source: https://doi.org/10.1089/soro.2017.0044 (verified via Semantic Scholar API and EuropePMC full abstract, PMID 29648951)
contribution: An explicitly bioinspired soft-rigid hybrid arm: rigid-ish internal structure actuated by custom McKibben muscles, wrapped in inflatable sleeves for impact cushioning, deliberately trading pure softness for accuracy and usable weight.
hard_numbers: **7 DOF** (2 shoulder, 2 elbow, 2 wrist, 1 grasp); custom McKibben PAMs with binary + proportional valves; potentiometer per joint; servomotors for wrist/hand. Inflatable sleeve pressure ~20 kPa giving 3–5 cm of compressible padding (this sleeve figure came from a search-result snippet of the SAGE full text, not from a page I fetched end to end — verify before quoting). Payload and arm mass not stated in the abstract.
design_relevance: The cleanest published statement of your actual architecture: structure and precision from the rigid elements, compliance from pneumatic muscles, contact safety from an inflatable/padded sleeve. Directly transferable layering strategy.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Arm only, not a freestanding torso; no load-bearing test; no static hold data; pneumatics mean a compressor on the floor, which is a real system-level cost for a clinic.

handle: King Louie — Best, Wilson & Killpack, 2015
citation: C. M. Best, J. P. Wilson, M. D. Killpack, "Control of a Pneumatically Actuated, Fully Inflatable, Fabric-Based, Humanoid Robot," *IEEE-RAS Int. Conf. on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids)*, 2015.
source: http://radlab.byu.edu/uploads/4/4/7/0/4470886/humanoids_2015.pdf (fetched PDF, text extracted locally)
contribution: The reference fully-inflatable humanoid: entire structure, not just the actuators, is pressurised fabric. Demonstrates that MPC/LQR can position such a robot well enough to do a pick-and-place task.
hard_numbers: **14 DOF** humanoid (two 5-DOF arms + torso joint); ballistic nylon fabric with internal bladders; **structural chamber pressurised to only 1–2 psi (7–14 kPa)**; antagonistic joint actuators 0–25 psi, limited to 0–17 psi in practice due to pinching; arm link lengths from DH table: 0.18, 0.32, 0.28, 0.14, 0.28 m; task success 8/10.
design_relevance: This is your fully-soft option, and the numbers kill it for your use case. A 1–2 psi structural chamber cannot take a lean — put McFarland & Coad's M = PπD³/8 against 10 kPa and the collapse moment is trivial. Fully inflatable buys safety and lightness and gives up load path entirely.
evidence_grade: B (excellent platform description; no structural load testing reported)
limitations: No payload, stiffness, or collapse data in the paper. Positional accuracy is poor and the paper does not claim otherwise. Nothing here about static human contact loads.

handle: Positive-pressure layer jamming — Do, Wu, Zhao & Okamura, 2023
citation: B. H. Do, S. Wu, R. R. Zhao, A. M. Okamura, "Stiffness Change for Reconfiguration of Inflated Beam Robots," arXiv:2307.03247, 2023. DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2307.03247.
source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03247v1 (fetched full HTML)
contribution: Embedded layer jamming inside an inflated beam, stiffened by positive pressure rather than vacuum, letting you switch sections of a soft arm between compliant and load-bearing.
hard_numbers: Ø55 mm × 250 mm beam: unjammed **1.07 N** to displace 10 mm at 6.9 kPa vs jammed **6.68 N** — a **624% stiffness increase**; **663%** at 20.7 kPa. Layer stack (15 paper layers, 0.1 mm each, 35 mm wide, 1.82 mm total, 150 mm span): flexural modulus **263.2 kPa unjammed → 3038.6 kPa jammed (≈11.5×)**. Positive-pressure jamming within 2.1–4.7% of vacuum jamming. 4-segment robot, 0.25 m per section.
design_relevance: The honest scale check on stiffness-tunable structures. An 11× modulus change sounds transformative until you notice the absolute number: 6.68 N to move the tip 10 mm. That is a fraction of the force a leaning person applies. Jamming is a *mode-switching* technology for a soft arm's own posture, not a way to make a soft arm hold a human.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Small-scale beams; paper layers, not a durable engineering laminate; nothing about sustained load, creep, or cycle life. Scaling jamming force to human-lean loads is unproven.

handle: Foam-covered manipulators — Zeng & Bone, 2013
citation: L. Zeng, G. M. Bone, "Design of elastomeric foam-covered robotic manipulators to enhance human safety," *Mechanism and Machine Theory*, 60, 1–27, 2013.
source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mechmachtheory.2012.09.010 (verified via Crossref API record and Semantic Scholar API: authors, journal, volume, pages, year)
contribution: A design method for selecting foam covering properties (elastic modulus, viscosity) so that human-robot impact force stays under a stated injury threshold — i.e. treats the cover as a designed structural element, not an afterthought.
hard_numbers: the widely-quoted target is keeping impact force below a **50 N** human pain-tolerance limit; that figure came from a search-result snippet of the ScienceDirect abstract, not a page I fetched in full. **Do not put 50 N in a report until someone reads the paper.** No other numbers verified.
design_relevance: If you choose rigid structure + soft covering, this is the paper that tells you how to size the foam rather than guessing. Pairs directly with Svarny et al.
evidence_grade: B (citation solid; numbers unverified at source — paywalled)
limitations: Impact case, industrial manipulator geometry. A patient leaning is a sustained compressive load on foam, which means creep and bottoming-out, neither of which this addresses.

handle: RIBA / ROBEAR — Mukai et al., 2010 (+ RIKEN 2015)
citation: T. Mukai, S. Hirano, H. Nakashima, Y. Kato, Y. Sakaida, S. Guo, S. Hosoe, "Development of a nursing-care assistant robot RIBA that can lift a human in its arms," *IEEE/RSJ Int. Conf. on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)*, pp. 5996–6001, 2010. DOI 10.1109/IROS.2010.5651735.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS.2010.5651735 (verified via Crossref API and Semantic Scholar API: full author list, venue, pages, DOI). ROBEAR specs: https://www.riken.jp/en/news_pubs/research_news/pr/2015/20150223_2/ (fetched).
contribution: The only robot family that has actually lifted and held adult human body weight in its arms — rigid arms, urethane-foam soft exterior, capacitive rubber tactile skin, low-gear-ratio backdrivable actuators.
hard_numbers: verified from RIKEN: **ROBEAR mass 140 kg**, RIBA-II 230 kg; actuator units use a **low gear ratio for backdrivability**; torque sensors plus Smart Rubber capacitive tactile sheets on arms and chest. The frequently quoted **61 kg lifting capacity** for RIBA appears only in news coverage, not in a source I could fetch — flag it as unverified.
design_relevance: This is the reality check on your whole project. The only machine that has held a human's weight did it with a rigid structure, a heavy stiff base, soft covering, and tactile sensing — not with a soft structure. Note the mass ratio: 140–230 kg of robot to lift ~60 kg of person. Freestanding stability against a lean is a base-mass and footprint problem before it is a compliance problem.
evidence_grade: B (system is real and well documented; the specific numbers I could verify are mass and sensing, not load)
limitations: Nothing soft-structured about it; huge and expensive; programme discontinued in 2015. Its arms cradle a passive body rather than resist a lean, which is a different load direction.

handle: Blue (quasi-direct drive arm) — Gealy et al., 2019
citation: D. V. Gealy, S. McKinley, B. Yi, P. Wu, P. R. Downey, G. Balke, A. Zhao, M. Guo, R. Thomasson, A. Sinclair, P. Cuellar, Z. McCarthy, P. Abbeel, "Quasi-Direct Drive for Low-Cost Compliant Robotic Manipulation," *IEEE ICRA*, 2019; arXiv:1904.03815.
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.03815 (fetched abstract page)
contribution: A human-scale 7-DOF arm made safe by low gear ratio and force control rather than by soft materials, at a build cost a student team can approach.
hard_numbers: **2 kg payload**, **7 DOF**, **< $5000** build cost, 7.5 Hz position-control bandwidth, ~4 mm repeatability.
design_relevance: The realistic actuation answer for your budget. Compliance from a backdrivable transmission is cheap, robust, controllable, and does not collapse under static load the way a pressurised structure does. But note the payload: 2 kg. Getting assistive force out of a QDD arm means giving up backdrivability or adding gravity compensation/bracing.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: Arm only; no torso; low payload; 4 mm repeatability; low bandwidth. Backdrivable means the arm also backdrives *under the patient's load*, which is the wrong behaviour when someone is leaning — you need a brake or a self-locking load path for the static case.

handle: Blower-powered inflatable joints — Niiyama et al., 2021
citation: R. Niiyama, Y. Seong, Y. Kawahara, Y. Kuniyoshi, "Blower-Powered Soft Inflatable Joints for Physical Human-Robot Interaction," *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 8, 720683, 2021.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2021.720683 (fetched Frontiers full text; citation confirmed via Crossref API)
contribution: Very-low-pressure, continuously blower-inflated fabric joints for a "hugging robot," with a torque model validated across sizes, plus contact detection from internal pressure change.
hard_numbers: operating pressure **< 300 Pa** (50–100 Pa minimum to hold shape); joint internal diameter 70–500 mm, lengths to 3 m; nylon fabric ~70 g/m²; prototype uses 5 linear actuators (200 mm stroke, 22:1); puncture-tolerant because continuously blown.
design_relevance: The extreme soft end of the design space and a useful sensing idea — internal pressure as a contact sensor, free. But 300 Pa is two orders of magnitude below the pressures in McFarland & Coad's collapse tests. This structure holds up a fabric limb and nothing else. Use the sensing trick; do not use the structure for load.
evidence_grade: A
limitations: No payload data, no load capacity, continuous blower noise and power, and structurally irrelevant to a leaning load.

handle: Tensegrity compliant spine (Flexinoid) — Ali & Abdullah, 2025
citation: A. R. Ali, H. S. Abdullah, "Development of a compliant spine mechanism for enhanced humanoid robotics locomotion," *Scientific Reports*, 15, 44646, 2025.
source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-32165-w (fetched PMC12749162 full text)
contribution: A 5-segment tensegrity spine (rigid struts in compression, TPU cables in tension) with series elasticity in the tendon paths, replacing a rigid humanoid trunk.
hard_numbers: 5 vertebral segments, PETG printed, 50 mm struts, 1.75 mm TPU cables, **12 DOF**; **15 kg passive static load supported unpowered**; **~7.8 kg active load** during manipulation; flexion −30° to 65°, lateral bend ±30°; per-vertebra 25° flexion, ±10° lateral; 2 motors at 1.89 N·m.
design_relevance: The most directly relevant torso result in the packet, and the key insight is the split between 15 kg passive and 7.8 kg active. A tensegrity torso can *hold* load when the tendons are locked and carries roughly half that when it has to actuate. If you build a compliant torso, design the static lean case as a passive/braked state, not an actuated one.
evidence_grade: B (peer-reviewed and open, but single prototype, small motors, open-loop control, very recent with no independent replication)
limitations: Aimed at locomotion, load applied axially, not as a lateral lean; 15 kg is far short of a person's partial body weight (a leaning adult easily puts 20–40 kg through the contact); no fatigue or creep data on TPU cables, which will relax.

handle: ECCE1 anthropomimetic torso — Marques et al., 2010
citation: H. G. Marques, M. Jäntsch, S. Wittmeier, O. Holland, C. Alessandro, A. Diamond, M. Lungarella, R. Knight, "ECCE1: the first of a series of anthropomimetic musculoskeletal upper torsos," *IEEE-RAS Int. Conf. on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids)*, 2010.
source: https://archive.air.in.tum.de/Main/Publications/marques2010.pdf (fetched PDF, text extracted locally)
contribution: The original compliant anthropomimetic upper torso: hand-moulded thermoplastic "bones," complex non-ideal joints, DC motors pulling elastic tendons, compliance deliberately built into the body rather than the controller.
hard_numbers: verified in the PDF text: reference platform ~**1 m height, ~22 kg, 53 DOF**; engineered 1/2/3-DOF joints; 2-DOF shoulder arrangement fixed to the trunk, 1-DOF elbow hinge, 2-DOF wrists; simulation model with 43 nodes. **No payload, stiffness, or load-capacity numbers are reported anywhere in the paper.**
design_relevance: Useful as the cautionary case. It is the purest "compliance in the body" torso and it reports no load capability at all, because it has essentially none — the elastic tendons that make it safe also make it unable to hold a pose against external force.
evidence_grade: C (design description, no quantitative structural evaluation)
limitations: Not load-bearing, not freestanding under external load, hand-made and unreproducible, and the control problem it creates was never solved by the project. --- Build a **soft-rigid hybrid: a rigid, grounded structural load path with compliance in the actuation and a designed soft covering at every contact surface.** The evidence is not close. Every system in this literature that has actually supported human-scale load is rigid-structured — RIBA/ROBEAR (140–230 kg of rigid machine to handle a ~60 kg person), Flexinoid's tensegrity spine (15 kg passive, and only because rigid struts carry the compression), Baloo (19 kg, hybrid, rigid torso frame). Every fully soft structure reports either no load data at all (ECCE1, King Louie, Niiyama's blower joints) or numbers off by an order of magnitude from your load case (Do et al.: 6.68 N to deflect a jammed beam 10 mm). Do the arithmetic yourself with McFarland and Coad's collapse moment M = PπD³/8 — a Ø150 mm fabric arm at 20 kPa folds at ~26 N·m, while a patient leaning 200 N at 0.5 m applies ~100 N·m, and the pressure you'd need to survive it makes the arm hard to the touch, which defeats the point. So: soft where the person touches, rigid where the force goes to the floor. Jamming and stiffness tuning are worth one paragraph in your report and no build time; they switch a soft arm's own posture, they do not hold people. Two things the papers say that your team will otherwise learn the hard way: backdrivable transmissions (Blue, ROBEAR) are the right compliance mechanism but they backdrive under a static lean too, so the lean case needs a brake, a self-locking joint, or a passive mechanical stop — design that state explicitly rather than treating the lean as a disturbance; and the freestanding requirement is a base-mass, footprint and tipping-moment problem before it is a compliance problem, which is why ROBEAR weighs 140 kg and nobody in this literature has built a light freestanding torso that resists a lateral human load. Budget your safety case on Svarny's ~40% peak-force reduction from a passive cover — real, useful, and not enough on its own, since a lean is quasi-static and covers help least there.

handle: CushSense — Xu et al., 2024
citation: Boxin Xu, Luoyan Zhong, Grace Zhang, Xiaoyu Liang, Diego Virtue, Rishabh Madan, Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee. "CushSense: Soft, Stretchable, and Comfortable Tactile-Sensing Skin for Physical Human-Robot Interaction." arXiv:2405.03155 [cs.RO], 2024. (Also presented in the IROS 2024 cycle.)
source: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.03155 — **fetched** `arxiv.org/abs/2405.03155` and `arxiv.org/html/2405.03155v1`
contribution: A fabric-and-hyperelastic-polymer capacitive tactile skin designed explicitly for *caregiving* contact (limb manipulation, bed bathing), built cheaply and validated with a human-subject comfort/safety study rather than only a load cell.
hard_numbers: taxel 3 cm × 3 cm, 9-layer stack; 56 taxels covering four sections of a robot arm; force range to ~55 N, characterized 0–40 N; relative error 0.58 %; hysteresis ~3 N ≈ 5.4 % of range; output rate 100–400 Hz (FDC1004 capacitance-to-digital converter); 0.054 % accuracy drop after 1000 interaction cycles; ~$7 per taxel; user study n = 15 (9 F / 6 M, mean age 22.3), 14/15 preferred CushSense, p < 0.001 for both comfort and perceived safety.
design_relevance: This is the closest published thing to what this project should actually build, and it is open-sourced. It sets the realistic bar for a senior-design skin: 3 cm taxels, ~5 % hysteresis, sub-$10/channel, human-rated comfort. Use it as the baseline design and justify any deviation.
evidence_grade: A (hardware + human subjects, though the "safety" outcome is perceptual, not injury-biomechanical)
limitations: Validated for a *robot manipulating a limp human limb*, not a human loading the robot. 55 N full scale is far below what a leaning adult applies (a 70 kg person shifting 30 % of body weight is ~200 N). 5.4 % hysteresis on a compliant substrate that is also carrying structural load is untested. Mean subject age 22 — no elderly or patient participants at all. ---

handle: Comprehensive robot skin — Cheng et al., 2019
citation: Gordon Cheng, Emmanuel Dean-Leon, Florian Bergner, Julio Rogelio Guadarrama Olvera, Quentin Leboutet, Philipp Mittendorfer. "A Comprehensive Realization of Robot Skin: Sensors, Sensing, Control, and Applications." *Proceedings of the IEEE*, 107(10):2034–2051, 2019.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/JPROC.2019.2933348 — **fetched** the Proceedings of the IEEE October 2019 issue page; metadata re-confirmed via Crossref
open_access: no (IEEE paywalled; the TUM group's news pages and the earlier T-RO paper carry much of the content)
contribution: The end-to-end account of the HEX-o-skin / CellulARSkin line: multimodal hexagonal skin cells (proximity, normal force, acceleration, temperature) with local microprocessors, self-organizing network topology, event-driven transport, and whole-body control built on top. It is the reference for "what a real whole-body skin costs you in engineering."
hard_numbers: deployment figure widely reported for this line: 1260 skin cells on the REEM-C humanoid = 11,340 individual sensors, each cell roughly two-euro-coin sized (~3 cm across) with 4 modalities. Per-cell force resolution, latency and drift figures are behind the paywall and I did not verify them — **treat as none reported here.**
design_relevance: The architecture lesson, not the parts list. It tells the team that whole-body skin is a *networking and data-rate* problem as much as a transducer problem: put a microcontroller in each patch, use event-driven reporting (only send on change), and design the topology so a cut wire re-routes. That decision has to be made before any taxels are fabricated.
evidence_grade: B (extensive hardware validation across several robots; no human-subject safety trial in this paper)
limitations: Rigid-link humanoids. The cells are stiff PCB islands in an elastomer — on a torso that must itself deform under a lean, rigid islands become pressure concentrators and their accelerometer-based self-organization assumes the body geometry does not change. Also: 1260 cells is a multi-person-year build, not a senior design semester. ---

handle: iCub capacitive skin — Maiolino et al., 2013
citation: Perla Maiolino, Marco Maggiali, Giorgio Cannata, Giorgio Metta, Lorenzo Natale. "A Flexible and Robust Large Scale Capacitive Tactile System for Robots." *IEEE Sensors Journal*, 13(10):3910–3917, 2013.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/JSEN.2013.2258149 — **fetched** the open preprint at `ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1411.6837` (arXiv:1411.6837), metadata confirmed via Crossref
open_access: partial (paywalled at IEEE; full author preprint on arXiv)
contribution: The most numerically honest large-area tactile skin paper available: triangular fPCB modules with a 3D-fabric dielectric instead of elastomer, with embedded thermal sensors specifically because capacitive taxels drift with temperature.
hard_numbers: 10 pressure taxels + 2 temperature sensors per triangular module; taxel area 15.20 mm² (up from 12.56 mm²); pressure range 2–160 kPa with two linear regimes (2–45 kPa at 2.50 fF/kPa, 65–160 kPa at 0.86 fF/kPa); hysteresis ≈ 5 % max (9.1 fF at 28.6 kPa); **stress-relaxation time constant τ ≈ 1 h 18 min**; temperature compensation validated 15–40 °C; 16-bit CDC, 8-bit dynamic range in deployment; output rate 25 Hz; up to 16 modules per bus; full iCub deployment 1868 taxels (104 hands, 610 arms, 440 torso); 1500 taxels on a Barrett WAM.
design_relevance: The τ ≈ 78 min relaxation constant is the number to put on a slide. It means any elastomer/fabric-dielectric capacitive skin will *slowly change its zero* under a sustained load — exactly the load case of a patient leaning for two minutes. Sustained-contact force magnitude from a soft capacitive skin is not trustworthy; contact *presence* and *location* are. Design the control law so sustained force comes from a different sensor (joint torque or a load cell in the base) and the skin only supplies where and when.
evidence_grade: B (thorough bench characterization, robot deployment, no human-subject safety test)
limitations: 25 Hz is marginal for reacting to an impact; the transducer is a stiff triangular fPCB that will not tolerate the strains a genuinely soft link undergoes; and the two-regime nonlinearity means a single-slope calibration is wrong over most of the range. ---

handle: HEX-o-skin — Mittendorfer & Cheng, 2011
citation: Philipp Mittendorfer, Gordon Cheng. "Humanoid Multimodal Tactile-Sensing Modules." *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*, 27(3):401–410, 2011.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2011.2106330 — **fetched** the TUM research-portal record `portal.fis.tum.de/en/publications/humanoid-multimodal-tactile-sensing-modules/`; Crossref-confirmed
open_access: no (TUM portal record and figures are public; PDF is not)
contribution: The founding HEX-o-skin paper. A hexagonal PCB cell carrying temperature, acceleration and proximity sensors — deliberately *multimodal* rather than a pressure array — embedded in a rapid-prototyped elastomer and wired to neighbours through only four non-crossing conductors, with active re-routing around damaged links.
hard_numbers: four sensing modalities per cell; power+data between neighbours reduced to 4 non-crossing wires; redundant connection to neighbouring modules. Specific cell dimensions, sampling rates and force thresholds are not in the publicly readable record — **none verified.**
design_relevance: Two transferable decisions. (a) Multimodality beats pressure-only: the accelerometer catches taps and impacts that a slow pressure taxel misses, the proximity channel gives pre-touch, and they come on the same board. (b) The four-wire daisy chain is the answer to "how do I wire 200 taxels across two moving arms without a harness the size of the arm." Copy the wiring topology even if you do not copy the transducers.
evidence_grade: B
limitations: 2011 hardware, rigid PCB islands, and the whole design presumes a rigid substrate underneath to mount to. It also has no normal-force transducer worth the name in this generation — light touch via proximity, impact via accelerometer, but not "how many newtons is this person applying." ---

handle: Proximity perception survey — Escaida Navarro et al., 2022
citation: Stefan Escaida Navarro, Stephan Mühlbacher-Karrer, Hosam Alagi, Hubert Zangl, Keisuke Koyama, Björn Hein, Christian Duriez, Joshua R. Smith. "Proximity Perception in Human-Centered Robotics: A Survey on Sensing Systems and Applications." *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*, 38(3):1599–1620, 2022.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2021.3111786 — **fetched** the full text at `ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2108.07206` (arXiv:2108.07206); Crossref-confirmed for volume/pages
contribution: The only place with a defensible side-by-side of proximity modalities and their actual ranges, and it explicitly ties them to ISO/TS 15066 speed-and-separation monitoring.
hard_numbers: **Capacitive:** 30–40 cm on finger-scale electrodes, up to ~30 cm for 50×100 mm² large-area electrodes, update 20–125 Hz (some kHz), human coupling ~100 pF, strong on conductors and weak on insulators. **Optical reflected-intensity:** 1–300 mm, >1 kHz update, sub-mm resolution, <1 ms measurement. **Optical ToF (VL6180X class):** 10–100 mm, 1 mm resolution, ±1–2 mm repeatability, 7 ms to tens of ms measurement, ~10 cm dead zone. **Triangulation:** to 1.5 m with ~20 cm dead zone. **Inductive:** 150–300 mm, 25 kHz. **Radar FMCW:** 60 GHz / 160 GHz, simultaneous range + velocity. **Acoustic seashell effect:** ~4 mm. **Worked ISO/TS 15066 example (UR10e):** 500 Hz control (2 ms cycle), 4 ms reaction, 100 ms stopping time → 0.236 m protective separation distance excluding human position uncertainty. Survey frames 0–50 cm as the critical HRI band and notes Hall's ~45 cm intimate-space threshold.
design_relevance: This is where the proximity spec comes from. Capacitive is the right pick for this robot: a human body is a big capacitive target, 20–30 cm range on realistically sized electrodes covers the approach envelope, and the electrodes can be printed on the same flexible substrate as the tactile layer. The UR10e worked example also gives the honest reality check — even a fast industrial arm needs 24 cm of separation, and a compliant arm's "stopping distance" is dominated by its own compliance, not its controller.
evidence_grade: D (survey), but the numbers are drawn from graded primary sources and it is the right citation for a spec table
limitations: Survey of *rigid* manipulators. Capacitive proximity electrodes on a stretching soft link change their own geometry and therefore their baseline capacitance — the survey does not treat the coupled proximity-plus-strain case at all. Self-capacitance also gets swamped by the robot's own moving parts on a torso where arms pass near the trunk. ---

handle: GenTact-Prox — Kohlbrenner et al., 2026
citation: Carson Kohlbrenner, Anna Soukhovei, Caleb Escobedo, Nataliya Nechyporenko, Alessandro Roncone. "Design, Mapping, and Contact Anticipation with 3D-printed Whole-Body Tactile and Proximity Sensors." arXiv:2603.04714v2, 2026.
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04714 — **fetched** `arxiv.org/html/2603.04714v2`
contribution: Fully 3D-printed skin units (conductive PLA electrodes in a PLA "dermis") that do self-capacitance for both direct contact and proximity out to 18 cm, procedurally generated to fit an arbitrary robot's morphology, with an ensemble-ML map of the sensable volume ("perisensory space").
hard_numbers: 5 skin units, 17 sensors total on a Franka Research 3; detection range up to 18 cm, per-sensor spread 2.6–18 cm; update 15–30 Hz on an ESP32-C6; 1 cm grid for perisensory-space mapping; SNR threshold 3.5 for reliable detection; 100 MLPs per unit in the ensemble; **under $25 USD per unit.**
design_relevance: The cheapest credible path to combined tactile+proximity coverage for a student team — a printer, conductive filament and ESP32s, no cleanroom, no liquid metal. The 2.6–18 cm per-sensor range spread is the honest warning: identically printed sensors do not have identical ranges, so per-sensor calibration is mandatory, not optional.
evidence_grade: B (hardware validated on a real arm; no human-subject trial, and it is a 2026 preprint with no visible peer review yet)
limitations: 15–30 Hz is slow — at 30 Hz you get one sample every 33 ms, which is fine for a slow approach and useless for an impact. Rigid PLA dermis is not a soft link; it is a shell. And 17 sensors on one arm extrapolates to a large channel count for a torso-plus-two-arms body at the same coverage density. ---

handle: Intrinsic sense of touch — Iskandar et al., 2024
citation: Maged Iskandar, Alin Albu-Schäffer, Alexander Dietrich. "Intrinsic sense of touch for intuitive physical human-robot interaction." *Science Robotics*, 9(93):eadn4008, 2024.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.adn4008 — **fetched** the TUM research-portal record; Crossref-confirmed
open_access: no (science.org returns 403; author copy exists at `elib.dlr.de/206039/` but the PDF did not extract to text for me, so I did not read its numbers)
contribution: A robot arm (DLR SARA) resolving *where and how* it is being touched — well enough to read handwritten letters and numbers traced on its surface, and to place virtual buttons and sliders anywhere on the structure — using only high-resolution redundant joint force/torque sensors plus manifold learning. No skin at all.
hard_numbers: **none verified.** The abstract-level records give no force resolution, localization accuracy or classification rate that I could confirm from a readable source. Do not cite a number from this paper without reading the PDF.
design_relevance: This is the direct counter-argument to building a skin, and the team must answer it in the design review. If joints can localize contact, a 200-channel skin is over-reach. The answer for *this* robot is that it does not transfer: intrinsic sensing works because a rigid arm is a near-perfect mechanical transmission from contact point to joint torque sensor. Compliant links are a low-pass filter with hysteresis between contact and joint — they destroy exactly the signal this method depends on. Say that explicitly; it is the strongest justification for surface sensing on a soft body.
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated, human-operated demonstrations; not a standardized safety test)
limitations: Requires DLR-grade joint torque sensors (expensive, not off-the-shelf), a stiff kinematic chain, and an accurate dynamic model. All three are absent in this project. Also fundamentally ambiguous under multi-contact, which is the normal condition when someone leans on a torso with both hands. ---

handle: Whole-body tactile control — Armleder et al., 2025 (with Armleder et al., 2022)
citation: Simon Armleder, Florian Bergner, Julio Rogelio Guadarrama-Olvera, Jun Nakanishi, Gordon Cheng. "Real-Time Control of a Humanoid Robot for Whole-Body Tactile Interaction." *Advanced Intelligent Systems*, 7(12):e202500149, 2025. — Companion: Simon Armleder, Emmanuel Dean-Leon, Florian Bergner, Gordon Cheng. "Interactive Force Control Based on Multimodal Robot Skin for Physical Human−Robot Collaboration." *Advanced Intelligent Systems*, 4(2):2100047, 2022.
source: https://doi.org/10.1002/aisy.202500149 and https://doi.org/10.1002/aisy.202100047 — **both resolved and confirmed via Crossref** (authors, venue, volume, issue, article number, year). Wiley returned 403 to direct fetches, so the content summary below comes from the publisher abstract text surfaced in search, not from the full paper.
open_access: no (Wiley; accepted manuscripts exist at the `am-pdf` endpoints but are also 403)
contribution: How to actually *use* a whole-body skin: a quadratic-program controller that takes force and proximity feedback from a large-area skin network, clusters sensor activations into "active regions" so the dense data stays real-time, and simultaneously runs whole-body compliance, interaction-force regulation, and proximity-derived distance constraints for obstacle avoidance. The 2022 paper adds the key practical result that stable force control was achieved with an **uncalibrated** skin system.
hard_numbers: **none verified** — paywalled, and I refuse to quote numbers I did not read.
design_relevance: Two architectural decisions, both cheap to adopt. (a) Cluster taxel activations into contact regions before they reach the controller — do not feed 200 raw channels into a control loop. (b) Treat proximity as an inequality constraint on motion, and contact force as a task to regulate, in the same solver. Also, the uncalibrated-skin result is directly reassuring for a student build: you can get useful compliant behaviour before you have a per-taxel force calibration.
evidence_grade: B (hardware on a humanoid; no injury-metric or human-subject safety validation confirmed)
limitations: Rigid humanoid with torque-controlled joints, which is the plant this project explicitly is not. A QP controller at whole-body rate is also well beyond a senior-design software budget. Take the two ideas, not the implementation. ---

handle: Soft sensors + RNN proprioception — Thuruthel et al., 2019
citation: Thomas George Thuruthel, Benjamin Shih, Cecilia Laschi, Michael Thomas Tolley. "Soft robot perception using embedded soft sensors and recurrent neural networks." *Science Robotics*, 4(26):eaav1488, 2019.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aav1488 — **fetched** the authors' archival repository `github.com/UCSDBioinspired/thuruthel2019soft`, which states the citation verbatim; Crossref-confirmed
open_access: no for the paper (science.org 403); **yes for the code and data** on GitHub
contribution: That an *unstructured, redundant* set of embedded soft resistive sensors plus an LSTM can recover both kinematics and contact force on a soft body — i.e. you do not need to place sensors in a principled pattern or model the material, you need enough of them and a recurrent network to absorb the hysteresis and history dependence.
hard_numbers: **none verified** from a readable source. The repository confirms LSTM architecture and LCR-meter data acquisition but does not state sensor count, estimation error or training-set size. Do not quote an accuracy figure without the PDF.
design_relevance: This is the canonical citation for "how do soft links report their own state," and the *method* is what matters: redundancy over precision, recurrence over static mapping. It also carries the field's central warning — a learned soft-sensor calibration is valid only for the material state it was trained on, so it degrades as the elastomer ages, creeps and takes a set. Budget for recalibration in the build plan, not as an afterthought.
evidence_grade: B (hardware validated, no human subjects)
limitations: Finger/actuator scale, benign loading, short experimental horizons. Nothing here tells you how the learned model behaves after a 200 N lean permanently changes the elastomer, or after six months of creep. The drift problem the assignment asks about is *acknowledged* in this literature and largely *unsolved*. ---

handle: Bend sensors + IMU fusion — Han et al., 2025
citation: Dong Heon Han, Mayank Mehta, Runze Zuo, Zachary Wanger, Daniel Bruder. "An Enhanced Proprioceptive Method for Soft Robots Integrating Bend Sensors and IMUs." arXiv:2511.01165v1 [cs.RO], 2025.
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01165 — **fetched** `arxiv.org/html/2511.01165`
contribution: The cleanest quantitative treatment of soft-proprioception drift I found. Bend sensors act as a low-frequency absolute reference that anchors IMU integration drift; two linear Kalman filters (orientation, then position) fuse them. All commercial off-the-shelf parts, no vision, no custom fabrication.
hard_numbers: 12 bend sensors + 6 IMUs; tip position RMSE **16.96 mm = 2.91 % of robot length**; **IMU-only drift ≈ 45° over 900 s**, corrected by the fusion; **56 % RMSE reduction vs IMU-only**; 45 minutes continuous operation without degradation; bend-sensor calibration error 4.72° average RMSE; validated across 3 scenarios (unloaded, external forces applied, obstacle contact).
design_relevance: The most directly buildable proprioception recipe for this project. Two cheap modalities, one Kalman filter, ~3 % length error, and — critically — it was tested *with external forces and obstacle contact applied*, which is the loading condition this robot lives in. Adopt this as the arm-state estimator and spend the saved effort on the skin.
evidence_grade: B (hardware, quantified, no human subjects; 2025 preprint, peer-review status unverified)
limitations: A continuum arm, not a load-bearing torso; ~3 % error at the scale tested becomes tens of millimetres on a human-scale arm; and 45 minutes is not a duty cycle, it is a demo. The 4.72° bend-sensor calibration error is itself large enough to matter if you need contact-point geometry. ---

handle: Intentional vs. unintentional contact — Wong et al., 2024
citation: Christopher Yee Wong, Lucas Vergez, Wael Suleiman. "Vision- and Tactile-Based Continuous Multimodal Intention and Attention Recognition for Safer Physical Human-Robot Interaction." *IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering*, 21:3205–3215, 2024. (Preprint arXiv:2206.11350.)
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/TASE.2023.3276856 — **fetched** `arxiv.org/abs/2206.11350`; journal venue/volume/pages confirmed via Crossref bibliographic query
open_access: partial (preprint on arXiv; journal version paywalled)
contribution: The direct answer to the assignment's hardest sub-question. Binary tactile alone cannot tell a deliberate touch from a collision; adding continuously-estimated human gaze and posture does. Multimodal classification is significantly better than either modality alone, and a deliberately reduced 5-feature model generalizes better than the full set.
hard_numbers: **F1 = 86 %** for intentional vs. unintentional touch classification; 2 modalities (robot-mounted camera + binary tactile); reduced to 5 features; Baxter platform. Participant count, latency and dataset size not stated in the abstract — **not verified.**
design_relevance: This determines the sensing *stack*, not just the skin. If the robot must distinguish "patient is leaning on me for support" from "patient fell into me," tactile alone will not do it and no amount of taxel density fixes that. You need a second modality carrying intent — gaze/posture from a camera is the published route; contact *dynamics* (rise time, dwell duration, force trajectory shape) is the cheaper route this project should test, because a lean is slow and sustained and a collision is fast and transient. 86 % F1 is also a sobering ceiling: this is a hard problem and it is not solved.
evidence_grade: B (hardware, real interactions, unverified participant count; not a safety-standard test)
limitations: Healthy adults interacting with an industrial cobot, not elderly patients. Gaze-based intent is exactly the feature most likely to fail on the target population — dementia, visual impairment, and post-stroke gaze deficits all break the assumption that a person looks at what they mean to touch. Assume the vision route degrades and build the dynamics-based classifier as primary. ---

handle: Contact anticipation — Escobedo et al., 2021
citation: Caleb Escobedo, Matthew Strong, Mary West, Ander Aramburu, Alessandro Roncone. "Contact Anticipation for Physical Human-Robot Interaction with Robotic Manipulators using Onboard Proximity Sensors." *2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)*, pp. 7255–7262, 2021.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636130 — **fetched** `arxiv.org/abs/2110.11516`; venue/pages confirmed via Crossref
contribution: Proximity sensing used not to *avoid* contact but to *prepare* for it — a dynamic contact-thresholding algorithm that lowers the collision-detection threshold in the region where proximity says contact is imminent, so genuine contact is detected earlier and false positives elsewhere are suppressed.
hard_numbers: **none verified** — the PDF did not extract to text and the abstract carries no sensing range, latency or force figures. Franka Emika Panda platform.
design_relevance: The single most useful *idea* for this project's control-sensing interface. An assistive robot expects to be touched, so a system tuned to treat all contact as a fault is wrong. Pre-arming the contact detector where proximity predicts contact is how you get both a low detection threshold (safe) and a low false-alarm rate (usable). It also directly supports the intentional/unintentional split: contact that was *anticipated* by proximity in the approach region is far more likely to be intentional.
evidence_grade: B (hardware validated across scenarios, no human-subject or standards test)
limitations: Rigid manipulator with reliable model-based collision detection underneath. On a compliant torso the baseline "expected" dynamics are much noisier, so the thresholds have to be wider and the benefit shrinks. And its proximity sensors were purpose-built lab hardware. ---

handle: Adaptive skin sensitivity under ISO/TS 15066 — Rustler et al., 2024
citation: Lukas Rustler, Matej Misar, Matej Hoffmann. "Adaptive Electronic Skin Sensitivity for Safe Human-Robot Interaction." arXiv:2409.06369 [cs.RO], 2024 (revised 2025).
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.06369 — **fetched** `arxiv.org/abs/2409.06369`
contribution: Compares four strategies for setting protective-skin trigger thresholds on a fully skin-covered cobot, from one static conservative value to a dynamically adapted per-pad threshold, and shows the adaptive setting recovers productivity that the conservative setting throws away — while staying inside the ISO/TS 15066 power-and-force-limiting regime.
hard_numbers: UR10e 6-axis arm fully covered; **11 pressure-sensitive AIRSKIN pads**; thresholds adapted at **25 Hz**; framed against ISO/TS 15066 PFL; transient-collision pick-and-place scenario. Specific force thresholds in newtons and reaction times in ms were not extractable from the abstract — **not verified.**
design_relevance: Answers "what trigger threshold do I set on the skin," which is the question that always gets asked in the design review and never gets a good answer. The point is that a single global threshold is the wrong model: threshold should vary by body region (a torso pad a person is *meant* to lean on needs a totally different trigger than a forearm pad) and by motion state. 11 pads on a whole arm is also a useful sanity check against the 1260-cell fantasy — coarse, safety-rated coverage is a legitimate architecture.
evidence_grade: B (hardware on a certified cobot within a standards regime; preprint, no human subjects)
limitations: AIRSKIN is a commercial certified safety product with a pneumatic trigger — it is a binary safety switch, not a force sensor, and this project cannot afford it or replicate its certification. The ISO/TS 15066 PFL framing also assumes a rigid robot whose stopping behaviour is characterized, which a compliant torso is not. ---

handle: Sensing in soft robotics (review) — Hegde et al., 2023
citation: Chidanand Hegde, Jiangtao Su, Joel Ming Rui Tan, Ke He, Xiaodong Chen, Shlomo Magdassi. "Sensing in Soft Robotics." *ACS Nano*, 17(16):15277–15307, 2023.
source: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c04089 — **fetched** the PMC record `pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10448757/`; Crossref-confirmed
contribution: Broad materials-side review of resistive/piezoresistive, capacitive, optical, triboelectric and magnetic soft sensing, with integration and signal-processing strategies.
hard_numbers: scattered rather than systematic — screen-printed resistive curvature sensor **hysteresis 17 %**; PEDOT:PSS hydrogel strain sensor **hysteresis < 1.5 %**; hydrogel strain sensors to 300 % stretch; optical strain sensors 0–120 % range with small hysteresis under cyclic loading. It explicitly lacks a side-by-side table of resolution, drift and sensitivity across modalities — which is itself a finding about the state of the field.
design_relevance: The one-stop citation for justifying a transducer-material choice in the report. The 17 % vs 1.5 % hysteresis spread is the number that matters: material choice moves hysteresis by an order of magnitude, and hysteresis is what kills sustained-force measurement on a soft link. Optical waveguide sensing (low hysteresis, chemically inert) is the honest recommendation if force magnitude from the soft link is a hard requirement; resistive nanocomposite is the honest recommendation if it is not.
evidence_grade: D (review)
limitations: A materials-science review, not a robotics one. Nearly every cited transducer was characterized on a coupon in a tensile tester, not on a load-bearing structure, and none were tested for the multi-month stability a deployed assistive robot needs. --- Build **coarse, cheap, multimodal skin plus one good proprioceptive estimator, and get your force magnitude from somewhere other than the soft surface.** Concretely: 3 cm-class capacitive taxels on the CushSense pattern (~$7 each, open-sourced, human-comfort-validated, 100–400 Hz) over the contact regions a person actually touches — outer forearms, upper arms, front and sides of the torso — at perhaps 30–60 channels total, not 200 and absolutely not 1260. Add a self-capacitance proximity layer on the same substrate for a 15–25 cm approach envelope (GenTact-Prox shows this is achievable with a 3D printer and an ESP32 for under $25 a unit), and accept that per-sensor range varies 7× so every channel needs individual calibration. For limb state, copy Han et al.: bend sensors plus IMUs through a two-stage Kalman filter got ~3 % of length position error *while external forces were applied*, which is exactly your load case, and it is all off-the-shelf. Do **not** try to measure sustained assistive force through the soft skin — Maiolino's 78-minute relaxation constant and the field's 5–17 % hysteresis range mean a leaned-on capacitive taxel lies about magnitude within a minute; put a real load cell or joint torque sensor in the base and the shoulder and let the skin report only *where* and *when*. Over-reach for a two-semester timeline: whole-body self-organizing skin networks, a QP whole-body tactile controller, learned FEM-based shape estimation, an intrinsic joint-torque-only touch sense, and any attempt at safety certification. The intentional-versus-unintentional problem is the one place you should spend real thought rather than buy a solution: the published multimodal gaze-plus-tactile ceiling is 86 % F1 on healthy young adults, and gaze is the exact feature that fails on stroke and dementia patients — so build the classifier on contact *dynamics* instead (a lean is a slow ramp to a sustained plateau; a collision is a millisecond-scale transient followed by decay), state plainly in the report that this is an unvalidated design hypothesis, and put a rise-time/dwell-duration test in the test plan so the design review has data rather than a claim. One thing this literature will not give you and you must not pretend it did: nobody has published a tactile skin under a 200 N sustained human lean on a compliant trunk, so that is your own characterization experiment and it belongs on the schedule.

handle: ISO/TS 15066 — ISO, 2016
citation: ISO/TS 15066:2016, *Robots and robotic devices — Collaborative robots*. International Organization for Standardization, Geneva, 1st edition, 2016-02-15. 33 pp. ICS 25.040.30.
source: https://www.iso.org/standard/62996.html (catalogue; Cloudflare-blocked to automated fetch). Full text I actually fetched and extracted verbatim: `https://www.diag.uniroma1.it/deluca/pHRI_elective/ISO_TS_15066_2016_en.pdf`. Metadata (33 pages, status, price) cross-verified at https://genorma.com/en/standards/iso-ts-15066-2016 (fetched).
open_access: No. EUR 179 ex-VAT / EUR 216.59 inc-VAT (genorma, VERIFIED). The course-page PDF is a single-user licence copy and its hosting is likely not authorised — **buy a copy or pull it through NYU library before citing it in the report.** Status is `90.92 — Standard to be revised`, still Published (VERIFIED).
contribution: The only document in the whole standards landscape that publishes an actual table of per-body-region contact force and pressure limits, plus a two-body inelastic-impact model that converts those limits into an energy budget and then into a maximum relative speed.
hard_numbers: - **Table A.2, quasi-static contact — max permissible pressure p_s (N/cm²) and force (N), verbatim, VERIFIED.** Force is per *body region*; pressure is per *specific body area*. | Body region | Force (N) | Specific area | p_s (N/cm²) | |---|---|---|---| | Skull and forehead (critical) | 130 | Mid-forehead / Temple | 130 / 110 | | Face (critical) | 65 | Masticatory muscle | 110 | | Neck | 150 | Neck muscle / 7th cervical | 140 / 210 | | Back and shoulders | 210 | Shoulder joint / L5 | 160 / 210 | | Chest | 140 | Sternum / Pectoral | 120 / 170 | | Abdomen | 110 | Abdominal muscle | 140 | | Pelvis | 180 | Pelvic bone | 210 | | Upper arms & elbow | 150 | Deltoid / Humerus | 190 / 220 | | Lower arms & wrist | 160 | Radial bone / Forearm muscle / Arm nerve | 190 / 180 / 180 | | Hands and fingers | 140 | Forefinger pad D/ND 300/270; end joint D/ND 280/220; thenar 200; palm D/ND 260/260; back of hand D/ND 200/190 | | | Thighs and knees | 220 | Thigh muscle / Kneecap | 250 / 220 | | Lower legs | 130 | Shin / Calf | 220 / 210 | - **Transient multiplier = 2** for both force and pressure, all regions except skull/forehead and face, where transient is **"not applicable"** (VERIFIED). Clause 5.5.5.3: *"Contact exposure to sensitive body regions, including the skull, forehead, larynx, eyes, ears or face shall be prevented whenever reasonably practicable"* (VERIFIED, verbatim). - **Table A.3 — effective spring constant k (N/mm) / effective mass m_H (kg), VERIFIED:** skull 150/4,4 · face 75/4,4 · neck 50/1,2 · back-shoulders 35/40 · chest 25/40 · abdomen 10/40 · pelvis 25/40 · upper arm 30/3 · lower arm 40/2 · hands 75/0,6 · thighs-knees 50/75 · lower legs 60/75. k valid for ~1 cm² contact area. - **Table A.4 — max transferred energy (J), VERIFIED:** skull 0,23 · face 0,11 · neck 0,84 · back-shoulders 2,5 · chest 1,6 · abdomen 2,4 · pelvis 2,6 · upper arm 1,5 · lower arm 1,3 · hands 0,49 · thighs-knees 1,9 · lower legs 0,52. - **Formulae, VERIFIED:** E = F²/2k = A²p²/2k (A.1); μ = (1/m_H + 1/m_R)⁻¹ (A.3); m_R = M/2 + m_L (A.4); v_rel = F/√(μk) = pA/√(μk) (A.5). - **Provenance of the numbers, VERIFIED verbatim from footnotes a and b:** pressures come from *"the study conducted by the University of Mainz on pain onset levels… 100 healthy adult test subjects on 29 specific body areas"*, reported as the **75th percentile**, peak pressures averaged at 1 mm² resolution, using a **flat 1,4 × 1,4 cm metal test surface with 2 mm edge radius**. The standard itself says the values *"are the result of a single study in a subject area that has not been the basis of extensive research"* and *"there is a possibility that another test apparatus could yield different results."* The **forces** come from a separate literature survey (BG/BGIA U 001/2009e) *"referring to 188 sources"*, anchored to *"the lowest energy transfer criteria that could result in a minor injury, such as a bruise, equivalent to a severity of 1 on the Abbreviated Injury Scale"*, and the standard states they *"will be replaced in future by values from a research more specific for collaborative robots."* - **Scope, VERIFIED verbatim:** *"It does not apply to non-industrial robots, although the safety principles presented can be useful to other areas of robotics."*
design_relevance: This is the numeric backbone. It is where every force, pressure and energy target in the test campaign comes from, and clause 5.5.5.3 is what forbids the arms from being able to reach a seated user's head or throat at all.
evidence_grade: A — limits rest on a 100-subject human study and a standardised algometer method.
limitations: Three that matter here. (1) **Scope**: by its own words it does not apply to this device; importing it is an argument, not a compliance claim. (2) **Population**: "100 healthy adult test subjects", German working-age, healthy, excluded pre-existing conditions — nothing about frail elderly skin, osteoporotic ribs, anticoagulant-related bruising, or steroid-thinned skin. (3) **The forces are not measurements at all** — they are a literature-survey estimate from 188 mixed sources, which the standard flags as provisional. Note also an apparent typo in the source document: Table A.1 lists area 5 as "Seventh neck vertebra" while Table A.2 renders it "Seventh neck muscle". ---

citation: ISO 13482:2014, *Robots and robotic devices — Safety requirements for personal care robots*. International Organization for Standardization, Geneva, 1st edition, 2014. 79 pp (EN) / 93 pp (FR).
source: https://www.iso.org/standard/53820.html (403 to automated fetch). Metadata fetched from https://genorma.com/en/standards/iso-13482-2014 — status Published, 79 pages, EUR 204 ex-VAT / EUR 246.84 inc-VAT (VERIFIED).
open_access: No. ~EUR 204–247 / ~USD 232 (ANSI webstore listing exists at https://webstore.ansi.org/Standards/ISO/iso134822014 but returns 403 to automated fetch — price UNVERIFIED). Check NYU library: NYU subscribes to several standards platforms; ISO via IHS/Techstreet is the likely route. Worth 20 minutes with a librarian before spending EUR 204.
contribution: The standard that actually governs a freestanding, non-medical, earthbound assistive robot that physically supports a person. It defines three types — mobile servant robot, **physical assistant robot**, and person carrier robot — and explicitly excludes industrial robots (→ ISO 10218) and medical devices.
hard_numbers: **Essentially none for contact safety, and this is the central finding of C1.** It sets a 20 km/h travel-speed exclusion boundary (VERIFIED via search result text) but publishes **no force, pressure, or energy limit tables**. Secondary sources consistently report the standard's own note that for impact/collision hazards *no exhaustive, internationally recognised pain or injury data existed at the time of publication* — I could **not** fetch a page rendering that sentence verbatim, so treat that quotation as **UNVERIFIED** and confirm it against clause text once you have the PDF. Everything else is delegated to ISO 12100-style risk assessment.
design_relevance: This is the standard the design review should name as governing. It gives the team the *structure* of the safety argument (hazard identification, risk reduction, verification) and the device classification "physical assistant robot" — but it hands back no number, which is precisely why ISO/TS 15066 has to be imported.
evidence_grade: D — normative document, no underlying dataset of its own.
limitations: No quantitative contact limits at all; relies on the integrator to justify their own thresholds. It is also a 2014 document written before ISO/TS 15066 existed, and a `prEN ISO 13482` revision is in progress under a broader "service robots" title — check its status before freezing the report, because the numbers landscape may change under you. Supplementary guidance exists as ISO/TR 23482-2:2019. ---

citation: IEC 80601-2-78:2019, *Medical electrical equipment — Part 2-78: Particular requirements for basic safety and essential performance of medical robots for rehabilitation, assessment, compensation or alleviation*. Edition 1.0, published 2019-07-09. Amendment 1:2024 published 2024-03-12.
source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/33594 — **fetched successfully**, this is the page I verified title, date, edition, price and scope from.
open_access: No. **CHF 380** (VERIFIED from the IEC webstore page).
contribution: The particular standard for RACA robots — robots that physically interact with an impaired patient to support or perform rehabilitation, assessment, compensation or alleviation of movement function. It layers on top of IEC 60601-1.
hard_numbers: Scope and exclusions VERIFIED verbatim from the fetched page: applies to *"MEDICAL ROBOTS that physically interact with a PATIENT with an IMPAIRMENT to support or perform REHABILITATION, ASSESSMENT, COMPENSATION or ALLEVIATION related to the PATIENT'S MOVEMENT FUNCTIONS"*; **does not apply to** external limb prosthetics (ISO 22523), electric wheelchairs (ISO 7176), diagnostic imaging (IEC 60601-2-33), or **personal care robots (use ISO 13482)**. I did not obtain the clause text, so any specific force/torque/ROM limit inside it is **UNVERIFIED** — do not assume it contains a contact-force table.
design_relevance: This is the fork in the road. The moment the team describes the device as delivering *therapy* to *patients*, it becomes a medical device and this standard governs instead of ISO 13482 — with a full IEC 60601-1 burden attached. If the device is described as *assistance with daily activity*, ISO 13482 governs. The project brief says "elderly and rehabilitation patients", which straddles the line. **Pick one and write it into the requirements document in week one**, because the two paths have different verification costs.
evidence_grade: D — normative document.
limitations: The mutual exclusion is the problem: 80601-2-78 punts personal care robots to ISO 13482, and ISO 13482 punts medical devices to the medical framework. A device that is both lands in a genuine gap, and neither branch hands you a contact-force number. ---

citation: ISO 10218-1:2025, *Robotics — Safety requirements — Part 1: Industrial robots*, 104 pp; and ISO 10218-2:2025, *Robotics — Safety requirements — Part 2: Industrial robot applications and robot cells*. Both published 2025, superseding the 2011 editions.
source: https://www.iso.org/standard/73933.html and https://www.iso.org/standard/73934.html (403 to fetch). Status and metadata fetched from https://genorma.com/en/standards/iso-10218-1-2025 and `.../iso-10218-2-2025`; change summary fetched from https://www.therobotreport.com/iso-10218-industrial-robot-safety-standard-receives-major-overhaul/.
open_access: No. ISO 10218-1:2025 EUR 227 ex-VAT / EUR 274.67 inc-VAT, 104 pp (VERIFIED, genorma). USD 244 for US customers (VERIFIED, The Robot Report).
contribution: The 2025 overhaul folded the collaborative-robot content formerly in ISO/TS 15066 into ISO 10218 itself, dropped the terms "collaborative operation" and "collaborative robot", added functional-safety and cybersecurity requirements, and introduced robot classes (Class I for very low-hazard robots with reduced control requirements, roughly PL b).
hard_numbers: Publication status VERIFIED: both 2025 parts are `60.60 Standard published`; both 2011 editions are `WITHDRAWN`. ISO/TS 15066:2016 is **not** withdrawn — it sits at `90.92 Standard to be revised`, still Published (VERIFIED, genorma).
