Whether the Annex A biomechanical tables were carried into ISO 10218-2:2025 **unchanged, revised, or renumbered is UNVERIFIED** — I could not fetch clause text. **This is the single most important open item in C1.** If the team is going to cite a number in a design review in 2026, someone has to open ISO 10218-2:2025 and check whether Table A.2 still says 140 N for the chest.
design_relevance: Sets the citation hygiene for the report. Citing "ISO/TS 15066" in 2026 without acknowledging the 2025 consolidation will get flagged by any reviewer who follows robot safety.
evidence_grade: D — normative document.
limitations: Industrial scope. It governs industrial robots and their applications, not a freestanding personal care device, so it is even further from this project than TS 15066 was. ---

citation: ISO 14971:2019, *Medical devices — Application of risk management to medical devices*. 3rd edition, 2019. 36 pp.
source: https://www.iso.org/standard/72704.html (403 to fetch). Metadata fetched from https://genorma.com/en/standards/iso-14971-2019.
open_access: No. EUR 196 ex-VAT / EUR 237.16 inc-VAT, 36 pp (VERIFIED, genorma). ANSI/AAMI/ISO 14971:2019 listed at USD 343 (UNVERIFIED — from search-result text, the ANSI page 403'd).
contribution: The process standard for identifying hazards, estimating and evaluating risk, implementing controls, evaluating residual risk, and performing benefit–risk analysis across the device lifecycle. The 2019 edition strengthened benefit–risk analysis and post-production surveillance.
hard_numbers: None. It is deliberately process-only — it specifies no acceptability thresholds and leaves the criteria to the manufacturer's risk management policy.
design_relevance: This is the *machinery* by which the team is allowed to import ISO/TS 15066 numbers into a device that TS 15066 says it does not cover. The argument is: identify the contact hazard, select a threshold with a documented rationale, justify the choice, verify by test, and record residual risk. Without a 14971-shaped risk file, "we designed to 140 N because ISO/TS 15066 says so" is an assertion; with one, it is a controlled decision.
evidence_grade: D — process standard.
limitations: Gives no number and will never give a number. It also formally applies to medical devices; if the team goes the ISO 13482 route, the equivalent machinery is ISO 12100 risk assessment, though 14971's benefit–risk structure is still the better template for a patient-contacting device. ---

handle: Behrens 2021 — Behrens, Pliske, Umbreit, Piatek, Walcher & Elkmann, 2021
citation: Behrens, R., Pliske, G., Umbreit, M., Piatek, S., Walcher, F., & Elkmann, N. (2021). A statistical model to determine biomechanical limits for physically safe interactions with collaborative robots. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 8, 667818.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2021.667818 — fetched both https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frobt.2021.667818/full and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8850785/ (overlapping rows agreed).
contribution: The Fraunhofer IFF / Magdeburg experimental verification that ISO/TS 15066 explicitly anticipated in its own footnotes. 112 subjects, both **pinching (quasi-static)** and **pendulum impact (transient)** loading, producing a statistical model for 75th-percentile limits. Its headline result is that the existing standard values are non-conservative for the torso.
hard_numbers: **112 subjects** in five groups (G1 41 [13F/28M], G2 20 [6F/14M], G3 20 [10F/10M], G4 20 [10F/10M], G5 control 11 [5F/6M]); **age 16–67**, group means 36.3–41.9; **28 body locations**; neck muscle omitted for safety. Pinching at 1 mm/s via algometer; impact via pendulum at **6.5 kg and 16.5 kg**; semi-sharp probe **1.96 cm²** and blunt 30 mm foam. Proposed limits at 75th percentile assuming a 70 %-male population, as *pinch pressure (N/cm²) / pinch force (N) / impact pressure (N/cm²) / impact force (N)*: forehead 110/110/180/150 · temple 50/60/70/90 · masticatory 40/40/50/70 · C7 70/50/170/70 · shoulder joint 60/60/100/100 · L5 60/110/200/180 · sternum 50/80/80/110 · pectoral 50/60/70/110 · abdominal 50/60/60/90 · pelvic bone 140/90/270/140 · deltoid 70/100/100/110 · humerus 50/70/130/150 · radial bone 70/100/170/180 · forearm muscle 50/100/140/170 · arm nerve 60/80/130/140 · forefinger pad 70/150/240/390 · forefinger DIP 150/160/490/370 · thenar 60/120/180/260 · palm 60/150/280/330 · back of hand 170/150/470/250 · thigh 70/140/160/200 · kneecap 110/160/260/270 · shin 130/150/370/260 · calf 70/130/180/260. Authors' verdict, VERIFIED: *"Most of the limits in ISO/TS 15066 are preliminary, since they are based on unverified data from a literature survey."*
design_relevance: **This is the paper that should set the torso numbers, not ISO/TS 15066.** For every region this project actually contacts, Behrens is lower: sternum 50 vs 120 N/cm²; shoulder joint 60 vs 160 N/cm²; L5 60 vs 210 N/cm²; deltoid 70 vs 190 N/cm². A torso designed to the ISO chest pressure would be roughly **2.4× over** the experimentally measured pain-onset pressure. Design to Behrens, cite ISO as the standard, and state the delta explicitly in the report — that reads as rigour, not as deviation.
evidence_grade: A — 112 human subjects, both loading modes, statistical model.
limitations: Working age only, **16–67**, explicitly excluding older adults; no age-decade stratification published; the 70 %-male weighting is a workforce assumption that does not describe an elderly care population; authors stress limits are valid *only at the tested locations*, not across whole regions. Because I read Table 8 through an extraction layer, re-check the rows you put in the spec against the published table. ---

handle: Melia 2019 — Melia, Geissler, König, Ottersbach, Umbreit, Letzel & Muttray, 2019
citation: Melia, M., Geissler, B., König, J., Ottersbach, H. J., Umbreit, M., Letzel, S., & Muttray, A. (2019). Pressure pain thresholds: Subject factors and the meaning of peak pressures. *European Journal of Pain*, 23(1), 167–182.
source: https://doi.org/10.1002/ejp.1298 (Wiley 403'd). Abstract fetched verbatim via NCBI E-utilities, PMID 30076659.
open_access: No (Wiley paywall). Abstract free via PubMed; NYU almost certainly has EJP through Wiley Online Library.
contribution: The peer-reviewed publication of the Mainz work that produced the ISO/TS 15066 pressure table. Its finding is methodological and awkward for the standard: pressure under the algometer probe is **not uniform**, peak pressures at the probe corners and over bone are what appear to drive pain onset, and conventional algometers report mean pressure — so the probe, indentation depth and tissue properties materially change the number.
hard_numbers: **100 healthy subjects (57 men), age 18–66**, **29 body sites**, each measured 3× non-consecutively in randomised order; **40 subjects were manual labourers**. Men and manual labourers had **higher** adjusted thresholds (both force and pressure). Authors flag *"higher intra-individual differences regarding peak pressures at the spinous processes, breastbone, forehead and abdomen"* — caution advised interpreting those sites. Per-site threshold values are in the full text, not the abstract, and are therefore **UNVERIFIED** here; the ISO Table A.2 pressures are the 75th-percentile derivative of this dataset.
design_relevance: Two direct consequences. (1) Sample size and demographics for the standard's pressure column are now pinned: 100 subjects, 18–66, 57 % male — cite this, not the standard's footnote, when a reviewer asks "how many people?". (2) The **breastbone and abdomen are named as the least reproducible sites**, and those are exactly where a person leaning on this torso makes contact. Contact-area design and pressure-measurement-film methodology matter more than the force number for this project.
evidence_grade: A — 100 human subjects, standardised algometry, repeated measures.
limitations: Healthy adults, upper bound 66 years, German occupational cohort; the manual-labourer effect shows thresholds track skin and tissue conditioning, which cuts the wrong way for frail users. The peak-vs-mean pressure finding implies the ISO numbers are apparatus-specific — a soft robot's compliant contact patch will have a completely different pressure distribution than a 1.4 × 1.4 cm rigid metal probe. ---

handle: Park 2019 — Park, Han, Lim, Shin, Byun, Kim & Rhim, 2019
citation: Park, M. Y., Han, D., Lim, J. H., Shin, M. K., Byun, Y. R., Kim, D. Y., & Rhim, S. (2019). Assessment of pressure pain thresholds in collisions with collaborative robots. *PLoS ONE*, 14(5), e0215890.
source: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0215890 — fetched https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6497239/.
contribution: An independent, non-German replication of pressure-pain-threshold measurement for cobot contact, and the first to report an explicit age effect within the working-age band.
hard_numbers: **90 healthy males**, age **20–50** (mean 28.9), weight 72.8 ± 11.9 kg, height 174.8 ± 5.6 cm; **15 sites**. PPT range **65.1–196.1 N/cm²**. Highest: back of hand 196.1 ± 85.8. Lowest: **arm nerve 65.1 ± 22.6**. Moderate band 100–120 N/cm² at forehead, neck muscle, thenar, shin. Age effect: participants **under 30 had thresholds 3–33 % lower** than those over 30, largest at C7 (32.1 %), shoulder joint (31 %), neck muscle (29.4 %).
design_relevance: Two things. (1) The **standard deviations are enormous** — ±85.8 on a mean of 196.1 is a coefficient of variation near 44 %. Any design margin computed against a mean is meaningless; the team must design against a low percentile and say which. (2) The arm-nerve result, 65.1 N/cm² mean measured against 180 N/cm² in ISO Table A.2, is a **~2.8× discrepancy** in the region the arms will contact most. It corroborates Behrens' direction.
evidence_grade: A — 90 human subjects.
limitations: **All male**, so no sex effect can be estimated; age capped at 50, so it says nothing about 75-year-olds; Korean cohort with different body composition from the German cohorts; mean ± SD reported rather than the 75th percentile the standard uses, so the comparison to Table A.2 is not apples-to-apples and should be stated as directional. ---

handle: Han 2022 — Han, Park, Choi, Shin, Kim & Rhim, 2022
citation: Han, D., Park, M., Choi, J., Shin, H., Kim, D., & Rhim, S. (2022). Assessment of pain onset and maximum bearable pain thresholds in physical contact situations. *Sensors*, 22(8), 2996.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/s22082996 (MDPI 403'd). Fetched https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9030557/ for the tables; abstract verified verbatim via NCBI E-utilities, PMID 35458981, PMCID PMC9030557.
contribution: Separates **pain onset** from **maximum bearable pain** at 29 body locations under quasi-static algometric loading — the only source here that quantifies the headroom between "this hurts" and "I cannot tolerate this".
hard_numbers: **40 healthy males, age 20–29**, weight 72.0 ± 12.15 kg, height 173.6 ± 5.80 cm, BMI 23.82 ± 3.31; **29 locations**; third-quartile values. As *onset force (N) / onset pressure (N/cm²) / max-bearable force (N) / max-bearable pressure (N/cm²)*: forehead 111.4/61.0/412.7/291.7 · neck muscle 56.7/72.8/226.3/411.5 · sternum 49.9/39.4/246.2/179.0 · deltoid 59.4/60.6/306.9/387.2 · forefinger pad 138.7–156.9/107.1–135.1/509.9–529.0/355.3–370.9 · thigh 87.1/70.8/261.0/266.8 · shin 93.9/86.5/384.1/340.9. Ratio of max-bearable to onset is roughly **3–5×**. Authors state pain-onset results were **lower than the ISO/TS 15066 PFL limits**, while max-bearable exceeded them.
design_relevance: Sets the safety-margin architecture. Design the **normal operating envelope below pain onset** (~40–60 N/cm² on the sternum, not 120), and treat the region between onset and max-bearable as the fault-tolerance band the single-fault condition may enter briefly. It also gives a third independent confirmation that the ISO sternum pressure is too high: 39.4 N/cm² measured onset versus 120 N/cm² in Table A.2 is roughly **3×**.
evidence_grade: A — 40 human subjects.
limitations: Smallest and narrowest cohort here — **40 males, all in their twenties**. Quasi-static only, no impact. "Maximum bearable pain" in a healthy 25-year-old volunteer who can stop the test at any moment has no defensible relationship to what is tolerable or safe for a frail 80-year-old who may not be able to withdraw, communicate, or perceive the load. **Do not use the max-bearable column as a design limit.** ---

handle: Haddadin 2007 (crash-testing) — Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer & Hirzinger, 2007
citation: Haddadin, S., Albu-Schäffer, A., & Hirzinger, G. (2007). Safety evaluation of physical human-robot interaction via crash-testing. In *Robotics: Science and Systems III*, pp. 217–224. MIT Press.
source: https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss03/p28.pdf — **fetched and extracted verbatim**. https://doi.org/10.15607/RSS.2007.III.028
contribution: The foundational experiment: a DLR LWR III driven into a Hybrid III dummy at an ADAC automotive crash-test facility, evaluating the full EuroNCAP severity index battery. The result that reframed the field is that the robot scores *trivially* low on automotive metrics — which is a finding about the metrics, not a clean bill of health for robots.
hard_numbers: LWR III **14 kg**, 7 DOF, reflected mass **≈ 4 kg at the TCP**; **1 kg aluminium impactor**; TCP velocities **{0.2, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} m/s**; Hybrid III 50th-percentile male dummy; all indices computed independently by ADAC. **HIC36 limit 650**, corresponding to a **5 % probability of AIS ≥ 3**; head acceleration criterion **a_3ms ≤ 72 g**. Measured: **HIC36 below 25 at 2 m/s**; a_3ms reached **less than 20 % of the 72 g limit** at 2 m/s. HIC **saturates with increasing robot mass** at each impact velocity — simulated to 10 m/s and to large masses, increasing robot mass does not raise HIC further.
design_relevance: Kills the temptation to certify this project with a HIC number. If a 14 kg rigid-link industrial-grade arm cannot get HIC36 above 25 at 2 m/s, a compliant soft torso will produce a number so far below threshold that it proves nothing. **Do not put HIC in the test plan as the acceptance criterion** — a reviewer who knows this literature will read it as metric-shopping. Use force, pressure and energy.
evidence_grade: A — standardised crash-test protocol, certified facility, instrumented ATD.
limitations: Stated in the paper's own footnote 11, VERIFIED verbatim: *"the presented evaluation is carried out for average male dummies and not for females or children. For such an analysis further tests with specially designed female or child dummies would be necessary."* No elderly ATD exists at all. The paper also explicitly scopes itself to **free blunt impact** and excludes **clamping** — and clamping against a fixed structure is the dominant hazard for a freestanding torso a person leans on. ---

handle: Haddadin 2012 (injury knowledge) — Haddadin, Haddadin, Khoury, Rokahr, Parusel, Burgkart, Bicchi & Albu-Schäffer, 2012
citation: Haddadin, S., Haddadin, S., Khoury, A., Rokahr, T., Parusel, S., Burgkart, R., Bicchi, A., & Albu-Schäffer, A. (2012). On making robots understand safety: Embedding injury knowledge into control. *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, 31(13), 1578–1602.
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/0278364912462256 (SAGE 403'd). Full PDF **fetched and extracted verbatim** from http://www.diag.uniroma1.it/~deluca/pHRI_elective/IJRR12_EmbeddingInjuryinControl_Haddadin_etal.pdf
open_access: No at publisher; author/course copy freely readable.
contribution: Replaces automotive indices with a directly measured map from (reflected inertia, velocity, contact geometry) → medically classified injury, built from porcine impact experiments and medically graded by AO classification, then compiled into a real-time velocity-shaping controller (the Safe Motion Unit).
hard_numbers: **276 impact tests** on fresh pig abdominal wall samples. Impactors: wedge 45° r = 0.2 mm 2.7 kg; small sphere r = 5 mm 2.1 kg; large sphere r = 12.5 mm 2.2 kg; plus a Torx T45 bit. Velocities **0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0 m/s**; impactor masses **≈ 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 kg**. Injury scales: closed skin IC1–IC5, open skin IO1–IO5, muscle/tendon MT1–MT3, nerve/vessel NV. Key thresholds, verbatim: *"safety can only be guaranteed with velocities < 2 m/s and < 6 kg"* (small sphere, which pierces skin at low velocity and weight); *"The maximum velocity should not exceed 1.5 m/s and with additional weights the velocity must be reduced below 1.0 m/s"*; wedge damage requires *"weights above 8 kg and impact velocities of at least 3.0 m/s"*; for the Torx, *"cutaneous defects at < 1.0 m/s and impact mass < 8 kg could not be observed"* and *"at an impactor weight of > 6 kg, muscle damage can be definitely excluded only at velocities < 0.5 m/s"*. Design framing: reflected inertia of interactive robots is stated as **1–15 kg**, and an interactive robot *"should certainly not move faster than 4–5 m/s"*; v_max(m) is a regression line, limited between **0.1 and 4.5 m/s**.
design_relevance: Supplies the **velocity ceiling** and proves the point the soft-robotics pitch depends on: **geometry dominates**. A 5 mm sphere pierces skin where a 12.5 mm sphere and a 45° wedge do not, at identical mass and velocity. That is the quantitative justification for the arm's end-effector and any exposed hardware to be large-radius and padded, and it converts "soft is safe" from a slogan into a radius requirement. Adopt **≤ 1.5 m/s** as the arm-tip velocity cap, dropping to **≤ 1.0 m/s** if reflected inertia exceeds ~6–8 kg.
evidence_grade: B — hardware-validated on biological tissue, no human subjects.
limitations: Authors' own caveat, VERIFIED verbatim: non-vital tissue *"lacks numerous characteristics, such as muscle tension, skin pre-stretch, and the possibility of reacting or evading"*, and cannot show haemorrhage, pain, or neurologic deficit. Pig abdominal wall is a reasonable analogue for young adult human skin and a **poor** analogue for atrophic elderly dermis. Free impact, not clamping. ---

handle: El Tumi 2017 — El Tumi, Johnson, Dantas, Maynard & Tashani, 2017
citation: El Tumi, H., Johnson, M. I., Dantas, P. B. F., Maynard, M. J., & Tashani, O. A. (2017). Age-related changes in pain sensitivity in healthy humans: A systematic review with meta-analysis. *European Journal of Pain*, 21(6), 955–964.
source: https://doi.org/10.1002/ejp.1011 (Wiley 403'd). Abstract fetched verbatim via NCBI E-utilities, PMID 28230292.
open_access: No (Wiley). Abstract free; NYU should have EJP.
contribution: **The elderly-population gap, quantified.** Pooled meta-analysis of pain threshold across the lifespan in healthy pain-free humans, with pressure and heat analysed separately — and they diverge.
hard_numbers: **12 studies**, individual sample sizes **30–244**. Seven of nine adult studies found significant old-vs-young differences but *"the direction of change was inconsistent"*. Meta-analysis result: **pressure pain threshold was LOWER in old adults than younger adults, p = 0.018, I² = 60.970 %**. **No difference** in contact heat pain thresholds (p = 0.0001, I² = 90.23 %). Old adults defined as mean 62.2 ± 3.4 to 79 ± 4 years; younger 22 ± 1.5 to 39.1 ± 8.8. Methodological quality high, low publication bias, but *"substantial statistical and methodological heterogeneity"*.
design_relevance: **This is the citation that justifies a safety factor on top of ISO/TS 15066 for this project's user population.** Older adults are *more* sensitive to mechanically evoked pain, and every number in ISO/TS 15066, Behrens, Melia, Park and Han was measured on people younger than the intended users. The team should apply an explicit, documented de-rating factor to the imported limits and cite this meta-analysis as the basis. Note also that it directly contradicts Park's within-working-age finding that under-30s had lower thresholds — the age curve is not monotonic, and the team should not extrapolate Park's trend past 50.
evidence_grade: A — meta-analysis of human-subject data (not a narrative review).
limitations: Authors call the evidence *"tentative"*; I² ≈ 61 % is substantial heterogeneity; the pooled effect is reported as a p-value in the abstract without an effect size, so **the magnitude of the de-rating is UNVERIFIED** — the team must read the full text to extract an SMD before choosing a numeric factor. Healthy pain-free elderly only, which excludes exactly the comorbid rehabilitation population this device targets. ---

handle: Paez-Granados 2022 — Paez-Granados & Billard, 2022
citation: Paez-Granados, D., & Billard, A. (2022). Crash test-based assessment of injury risks for adults and children when colliding with personal mobility devices and service robots. *Scientific Reports*, 12, 5285.
source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09349-9 — fetched https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8960768/
contribution: The modern counterpart to Haddadin 2007, but for **service robots at service-robot masses** — and it reaches the opposite conclusion, because 60–133 kg of robot is a completely different hazard from a 14 kg arm. Serious-injury probabilities are exceeded within normal service-robot operating speeds.
hard_numbers: Dummies: **Q3 child** (1.05 m, 15 kg, 3–5 yr) and **Hybrid III 50th-percentile adult male** (1.8 m, 81.5 kg). Masses: mobile service robot **60 kg**, personal mobility device **133 kg** including passenger. Speeds **1.0, 1.5, 3.1 m/s**. At 3.1 m/s: child **HIC15 = 549 → 14 % probability of AIS3+**, against a 5 % acceptable threshold; child peak upper-neck tension **1.44 kN** in extension; child chest deflection **23.4–27.6 mm → 50.8 % (PMD) and 32.4 % (MSR) probability of AIS3+**; adult **33 % probability of tibial fracture**. Modelled **5 % skull-fracture cut-off for children 3–12 reached at 1.41 m/s**. Mitigation conclusion: keep differential impact speed **below 1.5 m/s** or use absorbent materials.
design_relevance: The mass counter-argument. Haddadin's "robots are basically safe" result holds for a 14 kg arm with 4 kg reflected inertia; it does **not** hold for a freestanding torso whose base, battery and structure may total tens of kilograms. If this torso can translate or tip, its whole mass is in play, and **tip-over onto a seated or supine user is a credible AIS3+ hazard that the ISO/TS 15066 arm-contact numbers do not cover at all.** This paper independently lands on the same **≤ 1.5 m/s** ceiling as Haddadin 2012.
evidence_grade: A — standardised crash tests with certified ATDs.
limitations: Child and 50th-percentile-male adult dummies only; **no elderly ATD** — and elderly thoracic injury tolerance is materially lower than a Hybrid III represents. Whole-body collision from a mobile device, not arm contact, so the numbers transfer to the tip-over and base-collision hazards rather than to the arms. ---

handle: Abidi 2017 — Abidi & Cianchetti, 2017
citation: Abidi, H., & Cianchetti, M. (2017). On intrinsic safety of soft robots. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 4, 5.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2017.00005 — fetched https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/robotics-and-ai/articles/10.3389/frobt.2017.00005/full
contribution: A position paper arguing that *"calling soft robots intrinsically safe, although generally true, carries some reservations"* — the hazards migrate rather than disappear, into stored elastic energy, pneumatic pressure, material failure and whiplash-type effects.
hard_numbers: Robots below **2 m/s** treated as safe for pHRI largely independent of mass; typical soft-actuator operating pressure **2 bar**, up to **8–10 bar**; worked example of **8 bar through a 0.5 mm hole → 0.157 N**, below fracture risk but hazardous to sensitive tissue; eye penetration at **0.02 bar** via a 23-gauge needle; soft material elastic modulus roughly **10×** lower than rigid robot structure. **It does not critique HIC or ISO/TS 15066 explicitly and proposes no alternative metric** — the search-result framing suggesting otherwise was wrong, and I am recording the corrected reading.
design_relevance: The hazard checklist item the team will otherwise miss. A pneumatically actuated torso stores energy that does not vanish when power is removed, and a burst line or a jet through a pinhole is a hazard class with no entry in ISO/TS 15066 Table A.2. The FMEA needs rows for burst, sudden depressurisation, jet impingement, and stored-energy release on E-stop — and the E-stop behaviour of a pressurised soft system needs to be defined, because "cut power" does not mean "go limp".
evidence_grade: D — review/position paper.
limitations: Almost no quantitative content; the 2 m/s figure is asserted rather than derived; predates the current soft-robotics safety literature; offers no test method, so it can seed the hazard list but cannot supply an acceptance number. ---

handle: Vemula 2018 — Vemula, Matthias & Ahmad, 2018
citation: Vemula, B., Matthias, B., & Ahmad, A. (2018). A design metric for safety assessment of industrial robot design suitable for power- and force-limited collaborative operation. *International Journal of Intelligent Robotics and Applications*, 2(2), 226–234.
source: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41315-018-0055-9 — fetched https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5966502
contribution: Proposes **power flux density** as a PFL design metric, W = (F_c · δ̇)/A_c — contact force times deformation rate over contact area — arguing that neither force nor pressure alone captures injury onset.
hard_numbers: Uses Behrens & Elkmann (2014) collision data at masses **4.16 and 8.65 kg** and impact velocities **0.64–0.94 m/s**; biomechanical stiffnesses **30 N/mm (upper arm)** and **40 N/mm (lower arm)**, matching ISO/TS 15066 Table A.3; restitution coefficient swept **0.2–0.5**. It publishes **no absolute limits** and **does not derive** a velocity ceiling for a given effective mass. It states plainly that *"there is no clear view in the research community as to what impact quantity can be most relevantly used as an indicator"* of injury onset.
design_relevance: Mostly negative evidence, which is still useful: it documents that the field has **not** converged on a severity metric for compliant robots. It also supplies the restitution range 0.2–0.5, which matters because ISO/TS 15066's fully-inelastic assumption is conservative for a rigid arm but a *soft* robot with elastic recoil may not be bounded by it — a padded surface that rebounds transfers momentum differently than one that absorbs. Worth one paragraph in the report justifying why the inelastic model is retained.
evidence_grade: C — metric proposed and evaluated against previously published data, no new experiments.
limitations: No absolute thresholds, so it cannot be an acceptance criterion; industrial-arm framing; power flux density requires measuring deformation rate and contact area in real time, which is not practical for a senior design test campaign. ---

handle: Hamad 2023 — Hamad, Nertinger, Kirschner, Figueredo, Naceri & Haddadin, 2023
citation: Hamad, M., Nertinger, S., Kirschner, R. J., Figueredo, L., Naceri, A., & Haddadin, S. (2023). A concise overview of safety aspects in human-robot interaction. arXiv:2309.09936 [cs.RO].
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09936 — fetched and extracted verbatim from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.09936
contribution: A TUM/MIRMI survey mapping the safety layers for HRI, notable here for one specific and highly relevant observation about the provenance of impact biomechanics data.
hard_numbers: None of its own. But it carries the single most important methodological caveat in C1, VERIFIED verbatim: *"most of the impact experiments reported in the literature were typically conducted on human cadavers from older adult subjects"*, and Kent et al. (2005) *"pointed out that overly large confidence intervals are produced on injury risk assessments in impact studies done with cadavers from older adults (as compared to those of young adults)."* It further notes that *"on average, males experience less bone loss and slower cortical thinning rate than females as they age"* (Seeman 2001; Lillie et al. 2016, skull cortical thickness vs age and sex). It confirms the scope split — EN ISO 13482 for personal care robots, EN ISO 10218-1/-2 and ISO/TS 15066 for industrial collaborative robots — and identifies the Safe Motion Unit as the established pre-collision approach for stationary manipulators.
design_relevance: Sharpens the elderly gap into something more precise and more useful than "old people are frail". The **pain** data (ISO/TS 15066, Melia, Behrens, Park, Han) comes from young-to-middle-aged living volunteers. The **injury** data (cadaver impact biomechanics) comes disproportionately from *elderly* cadavers and carries wide confidence intervals. So the two halves of the safety case are drawn from different populations, and neither is the intended user of this device. The gender/bone-loss finding also means a design validated on a 50th-percentile male is least conservative for the largest demographic in elder care: older women.
evidence_grade: D — survey/position, unrefereed preprint.
limitations: Preprint, no primary data, and it is partly a framing paper for the authors' own research programme. Use it for the cadaver-provenance caveat and the standards map; do not cite it for numbers. --- Targets the test campaign must beat. Where sources disagree, **the binding column is the lower value**, which is Behrens/Han, not ISO. "ISO" = ISO/TS 15066:2016 Table A.2, read verbatim. | # | Requirement | Value | Source | Flag | |---|---|---|---|---| | R1 | Chest quasi-static contact force (region) | **≤ 140 N** ISO → design **≤ 80 N** | ISO Table A.2 / Behrens 2021 sternum pinch | VERIFIED / VERIFIED-VIA-EXTRACTION | | R2 | Sternum quasi-static pressure | **≤ 120 N/cm²** ISO → design **≤ 50 N/cm²** (Behrens) or **≤ 39 N/cm²** (Han onset) | ISO / Behrens / Han | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R3 | Back & shoulders quasi-static force | **≤ 210 N** ISO → design **≤ 60 N** (shoulder joint, Behrens) | ISO / Behrens | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R4 | Shoulder-joint quasi-static pressure | **≤ 160 N/cm²** ISO → design **≤ 60 N/cm²** | ISO / Behrens | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R5 | Upper arm & elbow quasi-static force | **≤ 150 N** ISO → design **≤ 100 N** (deltoid, Behrens) | ISO / Behrens | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R6 | Deltoid quasi-static pressure | **≤ 190 N/cm²** ISO → design **≤ 70 N/cm²** | ISO / Behrens | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R7 | Lower arm & wrist quasi-static force | **≤ 160 N** ISO → design **≤ 100 N** (Behrens) | ISO / Behrens | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R8 | Arm-nerve pressure (most sensitive arm site) | **≤ 180 N/cm²** ISO → design **≤ 60 N/cm²** (Behrens) / 65.1 mean (Park) | ISO / Behrens / Park | VERIFIED / EXTRACTION | | R9 | Hands & fingers quasi-static force | **≤ 140 N** | ISO Table A.2 | VERIFIED | | R10 | Transient contact multiplier | **× 2** on force and pressure, all regions except head/face | ISO Table A.2 note c | VERIFIED | | R11 | Head, face, throat contact | **Prohibited** — contact with skull, forehead, larynx, eyes, ears, face shall be prevented; 5 % child skull-fracture cut-off at **1.41 m/s** | Paez-Granados 2022 | VERIFIED-VIA-EXTRACTION | | R16 | Contact geometry | No exposed radius small enough to pierce: 5 mm sphere pierced skin, 12.5 mm sphere and 45° wedge did not | Haddadin 2012, verbatim | VERIFIED | | R17 | Elderly de-rating factor on R1–R9 | **Required, magnitude TBD** — PPT significantly lower in old adults, p = 0.018 | El Tumi 2017 | VERIFIED (direction) / **UNVERIFIED (magnitude)** | | R18 | HIC36 | 650 = 5 % AIS3+; a_3ms ≤ 72 g — **do not use as acceptance criterion** | Haddadin 2007, verbatim | VERIFIED (value) | | R19 | Pneumatic stored-energy hazards | No published limit exists; must be covered by FMEA | Abidi 2017 | VERIFIED (absence) | **Derived velocity limits.** Computed from ISO/TS 15066 Formula (A.5), v_rel = 2F_qs/√(μk), μ = (1/m_H + 1/m_R)⁻¹, using Table A.2 forces and Table A.3 constants read verbatim. The same code reproduces ISO's own Table A.4 energies to within rounding on all seven regions checked, so the arithmetic is validated against the standard itself. Marked **DERIVED** — verified inputs, my computation. | Body region | m_R = 1 kg | 2 kg | 3 kg | 5 kg | 10 kg | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Chest | 1.79 | 1.28 | 1.06 | 0.84 | 0.63 | | Abdomen | 2.23 | 1.59 | 1.32 | 1.04 | 0.78 | | Back & shoulders | 2.27 | 1.63 | 1.34 | 1.06 | 0.79 | | Upper arm & elbow | 2.00 | 1.58 | 1.41 | 1.26 | 1.14 | | Lower arm & wrist | 1.96 | 1.60 | 1.46 | 1.34 | 1.24 | | Hands & fingers | 1.67 | 1.50 | 1.45 | 1.40 | 1.36 | | Pelvis | 2.31 | 1.65 | 1.36 | 1.08 | 0.80 | Read this as: **measure the arm's reflected inertia first**, because it sets the speed limit. At a realistic 3 kg reflected inertia the chest limit is **1.06 m/s** — already below the 1.5 m/s soft-tissue ceiling from Haddadin, so chest contact governs. Design to **1.0 m/s** and the ISO transient case, the soft-tissue case and the Paez-Granados case are all satisfied simultaneously with margin. --- **ISO 13482:2014 governs this device, and it will not give you a single number.** A freestanding, non-medical, earthbound torso that physically supports a person is a "physical assistant robot" under ISO 13482; IEC 80601-2-78 explicitly hands personal care robots back to ISO 13482, and ISO/TS 15066 explicitly says it does not apply to non-industrial robots. All three scope statements are verified, and the consequence is that **no standard both governs this device and publishes a contact limit** — so the project's safety claim is built by importing ISO/TS 15066's numbers under a documented ISO 14971-style risk-management argument, and the report must say that out loud rather than implying compliance. **Decide in week one whether this is a medical device**, because the phrase "rehabilitation patients" in the brief is what drags it across the line into IEC 80601-2-78 (CHF 380) and the entire IEC 60601-1 burden; describing it as assistance with daily activity keeps it under ISO 13482 (~EUR 204). This is a scoping decision with a large cost attached, not a wording preference. **Design to Behrens 2021, not to ISO/TS 15066.** Three independent human-subject studies — Behrens (112 subjects), Park (90), Han (40) — all land below the ISO table in the regions this project contacts, and the sternum is the worst case: ISO says 120 N/cm², Behrens measured 50, Han measured 39.4 at pain onset. ISO/TS 15066's own footnotes concede the force column is a 188-source literature estimate rather than a measurement and "will be replaced in future". Designing to the ISO chest pressure would put the torso roughly 2.4–3× above measured pain onset, and stating that delta explicitly in the report reads as rigour rather than deviation. **Do not certify this with HIC.** Haddadin measured HIC36 below 25 at 2 m/s on a 14 kg arm against a limit of 650; a compliant torso will score so low that the number proves nothing, and a reviewer who knows this literature will read a HIC-based claim as metric-shopping. Use force, pressure and transferred energy, and use HIC only as a cited reason for *not* using HIC. **The elderly gap is the weakest joint in the entire safety case, and it is worse than "old people are frail".** Every pain-onset number in the requirement table was measured on healthy volunteers aged roughly 16–67 — Han's cohort was 40 men in their twenties — while the cadaver impact-biomechanics literature that underpins the injury thresholds comes disproportionately from *elderly* donors with wide confidence intervals. The two halves of the argument are drawn from different populations and neither is the intended user. El Tumi's meta-analysis shows pressure pain threshold is significantly *lower* in adults over 62 (p = 0.018), so an explicit de-rating factor on R1–R9 is mandatory — but the abstract reports no effect size, so somebody has to read the full text and extract an SMD before the team picks a number. Note too that older adults may have *reduced* protective sensation while having *reduced* tissue tolerance, which is the worst possible combination: the user may not withdraw from a load that is already injuring them, so pain onset is not a reliable proxy for injury onset in this population. **Two hazards in this project are not covered by any number in the table.** Clamping — a person leaning on a torso that traps a limb against a fixed structure — is explicitly outside Haddadin's blunt-impact scope, and quasi-static clamping against a soft actuator that continues to hold pressure is the dominant realistic hazard for a device designed to be leaned on. And tip-over: if the freestanding base can fall onto a seated or supine user, Paez-Granados shows that 60 kg at 3.1 m/s produces AIS3+ probabilities of 14–50 %, which the arm-contact numbers do not address at all. Both need FMEA rows and a test, not just an analysis. **Before the design review, close three specific gaps:** (1) open ISO 10218-2:2025 and confirm whether the Table A.2 values survived the consolidation unchanged, because citing the 2016 TS in 2026 without that check is a citation-hygiene failure; (2) read El Tumi's full text for the effect size behind R17; (3) verify the ISO 13482 clause that states no internationally recognised impact/pain limits existed at publication — I could not fetch it verbatim, and it is the sentence that justifies the whole import argument. ---

handle: ISO/PAS 5672 — ISO/TC 299 WG8, 2023
citation: ISO/PAS 5672:2023, *Robotics — Collaborative applications — Test methods for measuring forces and pressures in human-robot contacts*, 1st edition, International Organization for Standardization, Geneva, November 2023, 41 pp.
source: https://www.iso.org/standard/82488.html — **I fetched the free 12-page preview PDF** at https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/82488/e9f2f066763b4189b18e2b9d3e6dccec/ISO-PAS-5672-2023.pdf (iso.org itself 403s automated fetch)
open_access: partial — front matter, Scope, Terms, and Clause 4 (Overview/contact types) are free in the preview; Clauses 5–7 (measuring instrument design parameters, calibration, sensor characteristics, measurement procedure) are paywalled.
contribution: The only standard that actually specifies *how* to measure forces and pressures in human-robot contact, and what a PFMD must be. Defines the test as: replicate the contact situation by letting the robot collide with the PFMD, analyze, compare to biomechanical limits, pass/fail, document.
hard_numbers: Contact classified on two axes — **load profile** (quasi-static vs dynamic) × **spatial configuration** (constrained vs unconstrained), producing contact types Push / Pinch / Impact / Crush. **Unconstrained requires ≥500 mm free distance to the nearest fixed obstacle** (referencing ISO 13854). Defines *biomechanical response curve* as contact force vs tissue deformation. Three transient-contact measurement architectures are recognized (fixed device; device on a linear sledge; device on a pendulum). Clause 5.2 "Design parameters", 5.3 "Calibration", 5.4.2/5.4.3 force and pressure sensor characteristics exist but their numeric content is behind the paywall — **I did not read those numbers and will not invent them.**
design_relevance: This is the skeleton of the whole campaign. Adopt its contact taxonomy verbatim: your torso will produce *push* (person leans, quasi-static, unconstrained), *impact* (arm swings into a standing person, dynamic, unconstrained), and *pinch/crush* (arm traps a forearm against the torso shell or a table — dynamic/quasi-static, constrained). Your test matrix should be exactly those four cells, not "we hit it a few times."
evidence_grade: **I** (standards document, consensus, not peer-reviewed research). The free preview is verifiable; the numeric clauses are not.
limitations: Costs roughly CHF 150–200 for the full text. Explicitly **does not apply to non-professional or medical robots** (§1) — an assistive/rehab torso for elderly users is arguably outside scope, though the document says the methods "can be applied in these areas, if deemed appropriate." That sentence is your justification for transfer, and you should quote it in the design review rather than pretending the standard covers you. ---

handle: Zimmermann-biofidel — Zimmermann, Huelke & Clermont, 2022
citation: Zimmermann, J., Huelke, M., & Clermont, M. (2022). Experimental comparison of biofidel measuring devices used for the validation of collaborative robotics applications. *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health*, 19(20), 13657.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013657 — **I fetched the PMC full text** at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9602772/ (mdpi.com 403s automated fetch)
contribution: Three commercial biofidelic PFMDs were run head-to-head on a linear motor and a pendulum. Authors are from IFA (the German statutory accident-insurance research institute) — i.e. the people who define the German cobot test practice. The point: nominally-equivalent certified devices disagree.
hard_numbers: Spring elements (CC2) tested at **40 N/mm and 75 N/mm**; damping/compression layer (CC1) materials **SH70A at 7 mm, SH30A at 14 mm, SH10A at 21 mm**. Force recording **≥1 kHz**, filtered with a **100 Hz Butterworth low-pass**. Pendulum impact energies **0.5 J and 1 J**. Within-device repeatability (SD): **Device 1 = 1.4 %, Device 2 = 0.4 %, Device 3 = 0.6 %**. Between-device **peak-force differences up to 10 %** at identical settings. Device 1 moving mass ≈ **1.5 kg**. Linear motor: positioning accuracy **0.04 mm**, max holding force **1 kN**. Manufacturers anonymized for compliance reasons.
design_relevance: Two things. (1) It gives you the *actual recipe* for a tissue surrogate: a stiff spring in series with a shore-hardness-specified elastomer pad, with body-region-specific spring rate. You can build this. (2) It sets your uncertainty floor — if certified instruments differ by 10 %, a home-built rig cannot claim better than ~±15–20 %, and your pass/fail criterion must have that margin baked in.
evidence_grade: **B** (hardware-validated instrument metrology, no human subjects — by design).
limitations: Devices anonymized, so you cannot buy "Device 2." Energies tested (0.5–1 J) are low; a leaning torso stores much more. Says nothing about soft-covered impactors, which is exactly your case. ---

handle: Svarny-skins — Svarny, Rozlivek, Rustler, Hoffmann et al., 2022
citation: Svarny, P., Rozlivek, J., Rustler, L., Hoffmann, M., Nicolis, D., Rocco, P., & Zanchettin, A. M. (2022). Effect of active and passive protective soft skins on collision forces in human–robot collaboration. *Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing*, 78, 102363.
source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rcim.2022.102363 — **I fetched and text-extracted the author-accepted PDF** at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.09872 (the DOI line is printed on every page of that PDF, which is how I confirmed the venue)
open_access: partial — publisher version paywalled, accepted manuscript free on arXiv, **dataset publicly released**.
contribution: The single most directly transferable paper here. It quantifies *how much a soft cover actually buys you* in measured collision force, separating the passive cushioning effect from the active sensing/stopping effect. This is the experiment your project is a variant of.
hard_numbers: **2250 collision measurements**, three robots (UR10e, KUKA LBR iiwa 7R800, KUKA Cybertech) with and without AIRSKIN. **Transient collisions: passive skin lowered peak impact force by ~40 %.** Measuring device **CBSF-75-Basic**, spring constant **75 000 N/m (75 N/mm)**, range **500 N**, certified error **≤3 N**, collection frequency **1000 Hz**. Robot-side logging 800 Hz (UR) / 1000 Hz (KUKA). AIRSKIN pad approximated as **k_s = 3000 N/m with compressible thickness d_s = 16 mm**. Skin raised the ISO/TS-15066-permissible velocity from **0.26 → 0.35 m/s** (UR10e) and **0.32 → 0.43 m/s** (iiwa) against the 280 N transient limit; against the 140 N post-0.5 s clamping limit, **0.13 → 0.26 m/s** and **0.16 → 0.32 m/s**. Extra skin mass 1.8 kg. They propose an extension of the TS 15066 force–velocity formula that adds k_s and d_s.
design_relevance: This is your headline comparison and your model. Measure your torso/arm bare vs covered, at matched velocities, and report the percentage reduction — that is a defensible, publishable claim. Their extended formula (adding cover stiffness and compressible thickness in series with the body-part spring) is the analytical model you should fit your own data to. Critically, it also shows the **quasi-static/clamping case is where soft covers stop helping** — which is exactly the failure mode of a torso a person leans on.
evidence_grade: **B** (large, well-instrumented hardware study; no human subjects).
limitations: Rigid industrial arms with a soft *cover*, not a soft *structure* — an arm whose links deform is a different mechanical system, and their two-body spring model may not hold. AIRSKIN is a commercial product (~thousands of EUR). Their 40 % figure is for that specific pad on those specific robots. ---

handle: Haddadin-crashtest — Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer & Hirzinger, 2007
citation: Haddadin, S., Albu-Schäffer, A., & Hirzinger, G. (2007). Safety evaluation of physical human-robot interaction via crash-testing. In *Robotics: Science and Systems III*, Atlanta, GA, pp. 217–224.
source: https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss03/p28.pdf — **fetched and text-extracted this PDF directly**
contribution: The founding paper of automotive-to-robotics crash-test transfer, and the paper that killed the naive "robots are lethal at 1 m/s" simulation consensus. DLR LWR-III driven into a Hybrid III dummy at a certified ADAC crash-test facility, scored against EuroNCAP.
hard_numbers: TCP velocities **0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 m/s**. **Hybrid III dummy instrumented at 20 kHz sampling**, signals filtered per CAC (Crash Analysis Criteria v1.6.1). Criteria and limits applied: **HIC₃₆ ≤ 650** (5 % probability of AIS ≥ 3); **3 ms criterion ≤ 72 g**; chest **compression criterion ≤ 22 mm**; **viscous criterion ≤ 0.5 m/s**; neck limits **1.9/3.1 kN shear, 2.7/3.3 kN tension, 42/57 Nm extension** at 0 ms. Results: **HIC₃₆ < 25 at 2 m/s** (essentially no head-injury risk); 3 ms criterion reached **<20 % of the 72 g limit at 2 m/s**. Free-space head impact is a **6–10 ms** event; measured peak at the aluminium impactor at 2 m/s was **2 kN and 35 g**. Simulated robot masses **1, 4, 10, 50, 100, 500 kg** — **HIC saturates with increasing robot mass**, velocity dominates. Also shows that even instantaneous collision detection cannot reduce a stiff-contact peak, because the peak arrives before any actuator can respond. Prior ISO-10218 heuristics (0.25 m/s, 80 W, 150 N) are shown to be un-derived from biomechanics.
design_relevance: (1) Gives you the *criteria list* — HIC, 3 ms, chest compression, viscous, neck loads — and the numeric limits your campaign is measured against, all from a free PDF. (2) Gives you the key physical argument for your design review: **for blunt unconstrained impact, velocity and contact stiffness dominate; mass saturates.** So the defensible safety claim for a compliant torso is about *stiffness and speed*, not "it's light." (3) The detection-is-too-late result tells you not to claim sensing as your primary impact mitigation — the compliance is the mitigation.
evidence_grade: **A** (certified standardized test facility, standardized dummy and protocol).
limitations: ADAC crash-test facility time is far outside a senior-design budget. Rigid-link robot. Explicitly excludes sharp edges, clamping against rigid obstacles (which they flag as the genuinely dangerous case), and the head-only free-space geometry. 2007 — predates ISO/TS 15066 entirely. ---

handle: Behrens-limits — Behrens, Pliske, Umbreit, Piatek, Walcher & Elkmann, 2022
citation: Behrens, R., Pliske, G., Umbreit, M., Piatek, S., Walcher, F., & Elkmann, N. (2022). A statistical model to determine biomechanical limits for physically safe interactions with collaborative robots. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 8, 667818.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2021.667818 — **fetched** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8850785/
contribution: The largest pain-onset study behind modern cobot limits, and — for C2 purposes — a fully-described *test rig* for both the quasi-static and impact cases.
hard_numbers: **112 human subjects**, five groups, **28 body locations**, **~29 000 observations**, four scenarios (pinch/impact × blunt/semi-sharp). **Algometer:** KISTLER 9311B single-axis load cell, **±500 N**, **2.11 % max error**, loading rate **1 mm/s**. **Pendulum:** four-bar linkage, adjustable mass **1.9–20 kg**, **max impact velocity 1.25 m/s**, KISTLER 9327C three-axis load cell **±1 kN**. Example 75th-percentile limits: sternum **80 N pinch / 110 N impact** (blunt); shoulder joint **60 N pinch / 100 N impact** (semi-sharp); kneecap **160 N / 270 N**; forefinger pad **150 N / 390 N**. Pressure thresholds span **23 N/cm² (masticatory muscle) to 170 N/cm² (back of hand)**. Log-logistic CDF with Weibull regression, gender as covariate, 95 % CIs throughout.
design_relevance: This is the **benchmark your numbers get compared to**, and it is the *only* source here that gives you a defensible target for a chest/sternum contact — which is precisely the contact a freestanding torso makes. Note **sternum blunt impact ≈ 110 N** is far below the generic 280 N transient limit people quote; if your torso can push on a chest, 110 N is your number, not 280 N. Their two-rig split (slow algometer for quasi-static, pendulum for impact) is the right architecture for your campaign and is cheaply imitable in concept.
evidence_grade: **A** (human subjects, standardized apparatus, large n, statistical model with CIs).
limitations: Subject population is a working-age industrial cohort. **Your users are elderly and rehab patients — thinner skin, osteopenic ribs, anticoagulants, reduced pain reporting.** These pain-onset limits are *not* injury limits and are *not* validated for your population; you must say so and add margin rather than quietly reusing the table. Building a calibrated four-bar pendulum with a ±1 kN triaxial Kistler is not a senior-design purchase. ---

handle: Svarny-CFM — Svarny, Rozlivek, Rustler & Hoffmann, 2021
citation: Svarny, P., Rozlivek, J., Rustler, L., & Hoffmann, M. (2021). 3D collision-force-map for safe human-robot collaboration. In *2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)*, pp. 3829–3835.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA48506.2021.9561845 — **fetched arXiv PDF** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.01036 and **confirmed venue/pages via the Crossref API**
open_access: partial (arXiv preprint free; IEEE version paywalled).
contribution: Impact force at a fixed commanded velocity varies by **more than 100 %** across the workspace, because effective mass and structural stiffness change with configuration. The ISO/TS 15066 closed-form force–velocity relation therefore under- or over-predicts depending on where you are.
hard_numbers: Two robots (UR10e, KUKA LBR iiwa 7R800), **>400 impacts per robot**, **CBSF-75-Basic** device (**75 000 N/m**, **500 N** range, **≤3 N** error, **1000 Hz**), damping material chosen per TS 15066 to mimic **back of the non-dominant hand**. Velocities **0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40 m/s** downward. Grid: UR distance 0.52–0.89 m in 0.09 m steps × 5 heights from 0.14 m in 0.08 m steps; KUKA 0.56–0.86 m in 0.075 m steps. **Training set only 27 states (81 measurements) per robot** suffices to fit the model. 117 extra measurements verified rotational symmetry about joint 1. Samples exceeding the 500 N device limit were discarded. Reference TS 15066 permissible velocities computed as 0.26 m/s (UR) / 0.32 m/s (iiwa) at 280 N, and 0.13 / 0.16 m/s at 140 N.
design_relevance: Directly sets your **sampling plan**. You cannot characterize a two-arm torso by hitting the device once — force depends on arm configuration and height. Their result that **27 well-chosen states is enough to fit a predictive map** is the single most budget-relevant methodological finding in this whole file: it turns an impossible full-factorial sweep into about a day of testing. Also: place your measurements at the height a seated or standing elderly user's chest/head actually occupies, not at a convenient bench height.
evidence_grade: **B** (large hardware dataset, no human subjects).
limitations: Rigid arms, single contact geometry, single body-region surrogate (hand). Device saturates at 500 N. Their conclusion is about *configuration dependence*, which for a soft arm may be swamped by material nonlinearity and pressurization state — an untested extrapolation. ---

handle: Kirschner-effmass — Kirschner, Mansfeld, Gomez Peña, Abdolshah & Haddadin, 2021
citation: Kirschner, R. J., Mansfeld, N., Gomez Peña, G., Abdolshah, S., & Haddadin, S. (2021). Notion on the correct use of the robot effective mass in the safety context and comments on ISO/TS 15066. In *2021 IEEE International Conference on Intelligence and Safety for Robotics (ISR)*, pp. 6–9.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/ISR50024.2021.9419495 — **fetched the free PDF** at http://iliad-project.eu/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Notion-on-the-correct-use.pdf and **confirmed DOI/pages via the Crossref API**
open_access: partial (free author PDF via the ILIAD project site; IEEE version paywalled).
contribution: The only source here that gives a **practical experimental method to measure reflected/effective mass**: swing a passive physical pendulum of known effective mass into the robot, measure the pendulum's post-impact velocity, and invert conservation of momentum. It also shows the ISO/TS 15066 simplified effective-mass formula is badly wrong.
hard_numbers: Pendulum: length to contact **l = 636 mm**, computed **effective mass at the contact point m_p,eff = 3.663 kg**. Franka Emika Panda, configuration 1: **measured m_r,exp = 3.018 ± 0.184 kg**, Khatib reflected-mass model **2.800 ± 0.005 kg**, **ISO/TS 15066 simplified value 5.222 kg** — errors of **7.8 %** (model vs experiment) and **73.0 %** (ISO/TS vs experiment). Configuration 2: **m_r,exp = 2.765 ± 0.062 kg** vs model **2.797 ± 0.003 kg**, **1.1 %** error. ISO/TS simplified masses: **6.3 kg** for KUKA LWR IV+, **5.545 kg** for Panda.
design_relevance: This is your **reflected-inertia measurement method**, and it is genuinely cheap — a rigid pendulum, a known geometry, and velocity from video or an encoder. For a compliant arm you cannot compute effective mass from a rigid-body model, so measuring it is the only honest route. Report effective mass at several arm poses; it is the number that, with velocity, sets your predicted impact force.
evidence_grade: **B/C** — hardware experiment, but explicitly "preliminary," tiny number of configurations, 4-page conference paper.
limitations: Rigid serial arms with joint-torque sensing. **For a soft arm the impact is not an instantaneous rigid-body momentum exchange** — the structure deforms over the contact duration, so the single-parameter "effective mass" abstraction may not be meaningful at all. Treat this as a method to try and possibly report as inapplicable, which would itself be a finding. ---

handle: Alhaddad-headrig — Alhaddad, Cabibihan, Hayek & Bonarini, 2019
citation: Alhaddad, A. Y., Cabibihan, J.-J., Hayek, A., & Bonarini, A. (2019). Safety experiments for small robots investigating the potential of soft materials in mitigating the harm to the head due to impacts. *SN Applied Sciences*, 1(5), 476.
source: https://doi.org/10.1007/s42452-019-0467-7 — **fetched the full-text PDF** at https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09621 and **confirmed journal/volume/article via the Crossref API**
open_access: yes (SN Applied Sciences is OA; preprint also on arXiv).
contribution: A complete, **genuinely low-cost, university-buildable head-impact rig**, plus a soft-material study whose main honest result is negative.
hard_numbers: **3D-printed dummy head suspended on nylon-coated wire ropes** in a frame, with an embedded accelerometer read through a DAQ card. Pendulum impactor: 3D-printed cylinder, **10 cm diameter × 10 cm**, clay-filled to **0.4 kg**, faced with **5 × 8 cm** elastomer samples. Materials Ecoflex 00-30 and Dragon Skin FX-Pro (Smooth-On); **storage moduli 0.2, 0.3, 1.7 MPa** measured at 1 Hz by DMA (RSA-G2, frequency sweep 0.1–100 Hz). Thicknesses **1, 3, 5 mm**. Impact velocity bands **1.0–1.2, 1.6–2.0, 2.6–3.0 m/s** set by drop height. **Taguchi L9 orthogonal array, 27 main runs + 24 confirmation runs per noise level.** Velocity measured from **240 fps slow-motion video (Sony FDR-X1000V) analyzed in Tracker**; acquisition in LabVIEW, post-processing in MATLAB. **ANOVA found neither thickness nor storage modulus statistically significant (p < 0.05) in attenuating peak head acceleration**; only S/N-ratio optimization suggested 3–5 mm as better, confirmed in follow-up runs. Injury context cited: concussion reported from **31.8 g**; concussive impacts averaging **105 ± 27 g** vs subconcussive **26 ± 20 g**.
design_relevance: **Copy this rig.** Suspended instrumented head/limb surrogate + gravity pendulum impactor + action-camera-plus-Tracker for velocity is the exact architecture a senior design team can build for low hundreds of dollars, and it appears in a peer-reviewed OA journal so you can cite it as precedent rather than defending an improvised setup. Also copy the **Taguchi/orthogonal-array design** — it is how you cover material × thickness × velocity in 27 runs instead of hundreds. And take the warning seriously: with a small n and a noisy rig, **plausible material effects came out statistically insignificant.** Design your power before you build.
evidence_grade: **B** (hardware, instrumented, statistically analyzed; surrogate not biofidelically validated against a standard).
limitations: Accelerometer model, range, and **sampling rate are not reported** — a real gap, since a 6–10 ms impact needs several kHz to capture a peak. Dummy head is not a Hybrid III and its biofidelity is asserted by reference to the authors' own earlier work, not independently validated. 0.4 kg impactor at ≤3 m/s is far below a torso-arm impact. Reports acceleration only, not HIC. ---

handle: Monteleone-balance — Monteleone, Negrello, Grioli, Catalano, Bicchi & Garabini, 2023
citation: Monteleone, S., Negrello, F., Grioli, G., Catalano, M. G., Bicchi, A., & Garabini, M. (2023). A method to benchmark the balance resilience of robots. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 9, 817870.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2022.817870 — **fetched** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9895781/
open_access: yes (CC-BY), and **the testbed design is released open source**.
contribution: A complete benchmarking framework — 7 performance indicators, 5 protocols, and an actuated testbed — for how well a free-standing robot resists external pushes and impacts without falling.
hard_numbers: Testbed: max impulsive force **1200 N**; max quasi-static/sinusoidal force **700 N** (350 N at long pendulum setting); max torque **250–350 Nm**; pendulum length adjustable **0.5–1.5 m**; added masses **0–15 kg**; oscillation up to **3–7 Hz**. Sensor resolution: torque **0.4–1 N**, force **0.8 N**, angular encoder **0.09°**. Five protocols: free-fall pendulum impulse (parameterized by energy E and impulse I), sinusoidal displacement, sinusoidal force, quasi-static displacement ramp at **1.5 cm/s**, quasi-static force ramp at **1 N/s**. Validation on the Alter-Ego robot: **>1100 experiments** — 410 runs / 41 conditions (P1), 260 / 26 (P2), 430 / 43 (P3), 10 each (P4, P5). Repeatability: mean SD **≈0.37 N·s** (impulse) and **≈0.2 mm** (displacement). **~4 days** of testing for the frontal experiments on one robot. Modular aluminium structure, commercial sensors, ROS-compatible industrial PC.
design_relevance: This is the missing half of your campaign that the cobot literature does not cover. **Your torso is freestanding and a person will lean on it** — the dominant hazard is not "the arm hits someone," it is "the torso topples onto someone" or "it collapses when someone puts weight on it." This paper gives you the exact protocol pair you need: a **quasi-static force ramp (1 N/s)** to find the lean load at which your base loses stability, and a **free-fall pendulum impulse** to find the impulse it survives. The quasi-static ramp is cheap: a winch, a load cell, and a slow pull.
evidence_grade: **B** (hardware benchmark, validated on a real robot, open-source, no human subjects).
limitations: The full actuated testbed (1200 N, 250–350 Nm) is a serious machine — well beyond a senior-design build. The **degraded version is what you can afford**: a hand-winched quasi-static pull with a load cell and a string-pot, and a simple gravity pendulum. Developed for balancing bipeds/wheeled-inverted-pendulum robots, so the PIs assume an active balance controller; a passively-stable torso on a wide base needs its indicators reinterpreted. *(Reinterpretation is my inference, not theirs.)* ---

handle: Hartmann-review — Hartmann, Hamříková, Vysocký, Laciok & Bernatík, 2026
citation: Hartmann, D., Hamříková, K., Vysocký, A., Laciok, V., & Bernatík, A. (2026). Design, validation, and metrological limits of biofidelic instrumentation in PFL collaborative robotics: A systematic review of longitudinal trends and future paradigms. *Sensors*, 26(13), 3984.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/s26133984 — **fetched** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13363760/ (mdpi.com 403s)
contribution: The current systematic map of PFMD instrumentation and — most usefully — a consolidated statement of **how wrong these instruments are**.
hard_numbers: **68 publications** from **1099 screened**, covering **2011–2026**; 39 conference papers, 29 journal articles; evidence stratified as 21 high / 42 moderate / 5 low confidence. Publication peak in **2021**, a five-year lag after ISO/TS 15066 (2016). Sampling: **minimum 1000 Hz** required; contemporary systems at **10 kHz and 20 kHz**; transient spectral power concentrated **2–68 Hz**. Uncertainty: strain gauges **±15 N standard uncertainty**; pressure foils **up to ±10 %**, distorted by structural bulging; **force underestimation of 10–25 % during rapid transients**; sensor saturation/clipping documented at high-speed impact. Materials: damping ratio **ξ ≈ 0.07**; tempered steel springs (C67S) with **effective stiffness capped at 60 N/mm**; strain-rate-dependent silicone/urethane gels act as signal modulators. Names ISO/PAS 5672:2023 and ISO 10218-2:2025 as the governing documents.
design_relevance: Your **error budget**, handed to you with citations. If certified instruments underestimate transient force by 10–25 % and pressure film carries ±10 %, then any pass/fail margin narrower than ~30 % is noise. Also settles your DAQ spec: **1 kHz is the floor, and you want ≥10 kHz** given a 6–10 ms impact (Haddadin). The 2–68 Hz spectral content result is what justifies the 100 Hz Butterworth filter everyone uses.
evidence_grade: **D** (systematic review — high quality, but secondary; graded D per this project's rubric, which is about study type, not merit).
limitations: Reports no costs. Aggregates numbers from heterogeneous rigs, so the uncertainty figures are indicative rather than a specification. Entirely industrial-cobot framed; soft robots appear only at the margins. ---

handle: DAntona-VSITD — D'Antona, Farsoni, Rizzi & Bonfè, 2025
citation: D'Antona, A., Farsoni, S., Rizzi, J., & Bonfè, M. (2025). A variable stiffness system for impact analysis in collaborative robotics applications with FPGA-based force and pressure data acquisition. *Sensors*, 25(13), 3913.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/s25133913 — **fetched** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12251810/
contribution: A research-built alternative to a commercial PFMD: one adjustable-stiffness mechanism that can be dialled to several body regions, with a high-rate pressure-mapping array — i.e. the design you would copy if you build rather than buy.
hard_numbers: Variable Stiffness Impact Testing Device (VSITD). Stiffness **10–60 N/mm** usable (theoretical max **80 N/mm** at 80° spring rotation); validated settings 10, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 55, 60, 75 N/mm; **saturation above ~60 N/mm**, so stiffer regions (back, thigh, shoulder) are out of reach. Pressure: **32 × 32 FSR matrix over 10 × 10 cm²** (XactFSR polymer on PET). DAQ: **Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA**, LTC2311-14 ADC (**±4.1 V differential**), **5 Msps nominal**, **~10–20 kHz effective per element**, **<1 ms** analog-to-digital latency, FT600 USB 3.0 up to 200 MB/s. Force reference: PCB Piezotronics piezoelectric load cells with a 482C conditioner, cross-checked against an **ATI Nano17** F/T sensor. Calibration fit **F = 0.4197v² + 0.4928v**, **RMSE 0.1549 N** (10 kΩ pull-down). Characterized on a mechanical press at **25 mm/min**.
design_relevance: The concrete blueprint for a **build-it-yourself PFMD**: adjustable spring stack in series with a compliant pad, a load cell for total force, and an FSR matrix for pressure distribution. Its FSR array is the realistic pressure-mapping option at student prices (Tekscan/pressure-film scanners are not). The **60 N/mm ceiling is directly relevant to you** — soft-tissue regions like abdomen, upper arm, and chest sit in the low range this device covers well, and those are exactly the regions your torso contacts.
evidence_grade: **B** (hardware prototype, characterized and cross-validated against a reference sensor; not certified, not human-validated).
limitations: FPGA DAQ and piezoelectric load cells with signal conditioners are not cheap and need real electronics skill. **Per-pixel FSR calibration is acknowledged as necessary and not done** — FSRs are notoriously drifty and hysteretic, so treat the pressure map as qualitative distribution, not calibrated N/cm². Cannot reach stiff body regions. ---

handle: Behrens-responsecurves — Behrens, Zimmermann, Wang, Herbster & Elkmann, 2024
citation: Behrens, R., Zimmermann, J., Wang, Z., Herbster, S., & Elkmann, N. (2024). Development of biomechanical response curves for the calibration of biofidelic measuring devices used in robot collision testing. *Journal of Biomechanical Engineering*, 146(4), 041001.
source: https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4064448 — **the ASME page 403s automated fetch; I verified authors, journal, volume, issue, article number and date via the Crossref API** (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1115/1.4064448)
contribution: Defines the force-vs-deformation corridors that a biofidelic device must reproduce to be considered calibrated — i.e. the missing link between "a spring and a foam pad" and "a valid human tissue surrogate."
hard_numbers: **none reported here.** I could not read the full text — the publisher blocks automated access — so I am reporting only the verified bibliographic record and the topic. **Do not cite any numbers from this paper until someone reads it through NYU's ASME subscription.**
design_relevance: This is the reference you need if a reviewer asks "how do you know your foam-and-spring mock-up behaves like a chest?" Same group as Zimmermann 2022 and the IFA/Fraunhofer standards work, so it is the authoritative answer. Worth one library request.
evidence_grade: **B (unread)** — graded on the verified provenance and author group, not on content I have seen. Flagging this explicitly rather than pretending otherwise.
limitations: Paywalled; content unverified by me; industrial body regions, working-age biomechanics. ---

handle: GTE-CoboSafe — GTE Industrieelektronik GmbH (industry)
citation: GTE Industrieelektronik GmbH. *CoboSafe CBSF force-pressure measurement system* (product documentation). Viersen, Germany.
source: https://www.gte.de/en/products/kraftdruckmessung/cobosafe-cbsf — **fetched the manufacturer product pages**
open_access: yes (public product pages; no specs sheet behind a form for the basic data).
contribution: The de facto commercial PFMD family used across the cobot literature (the CBSF-75-Basic in both Svarny papers is this product line), and the only place you get published transducer specs.
hard_numbers: **CBSF series = nine individual force gauges with spring constants spanning 10 N/mm to 150 N/mm**, combined with a damping element to reproduce ISO/TS 15066 and DGUV FB HM-080 biomechanical limits per body region. Integrated evaluation electronics with **≥100 stored individual measurements**. Pressure measured either by **pressure-measurement film read with the CoboSafe-Scan scanner** (distribution and peak pressure only) or by **electronic film sensors (CoboSafe-Tek)** when a pressure–time curve is needed. CoboSafe-Vision software computes and visualizes force curves and pressure images, **exports CSV**, transfers by wireless or USB. (Specific to the CBSF-75-Basic, from Svarny et al.: **500 N range, ≤3 N certified error, 1000 Hz**.)
design_relevance: Sets the buy-vs-build decision. The **10–150 N/mm spring range is the design spec to match** if you build your own: pick the spring rate for the body region you claim to be testing (soft abdomen/chest at the low end), and say which one you picked and why. The CSV export and per-body-region gauge concept is the data model to imitate. Also worth noting: **pressure film (single-use, scanner-read) is the cheap path to pressure distribution**; electronic film is the expensive path to pressure-vs-time.
evidence_grade: **I** (industry/manufacturer documentation, not peer-reviewed; specs are vendor claims).
limitations: A full CoboSafe kit is a **four-to-five-figure EUR purchase** — realistically out of reach unless NYU's robotics or safety lab already owns one, **which is worth checking before you build anything**. Vendor-stated accuracy is not independently verified (and Zimmermann 2022 found up to 10 % disagreement between such devices). ---

handle: IFA-testapparatus — IFA / DGUV (industry / regulator)
citation: Institut für Arbeitsschutz der Deutschen Gesetzlichen Unfallversicherung (IFA). *COBOTS: Collaborative robots — Test apparatus* (KDMG-KOLROBOT), technical information. Sankt Augustin, Germany.
source: https://www.dguv.de/ifa/fachinfos/kollaborierende-roboter/prueftechnik/index-2.jsp — **fetched this page**
contribution: The regulator-side description of the reference test apparatus, and the clearest statement of the **two-stage compression principle** that defines a biofidelic device.
hard_numbers: Describes **a two-stage compression arrangement simulating the deformability of the relevant body region**, using **deformable plastic plates plus springs for each individual body region**; an **integral force sensor** for total collision force and **a range of sensor systems in the collision plane** for pressure distribution; fully PC-controlled with dedicated software. Sold under licence by **GTE Industrieelektronik GmbH, Viersen**. Points to **ISO/PAS 5672:2023** as the governing test-method standard. **No spring constants, sampling rates, force ranges, or sensor part numbers are given on this page.**
design_relevance: Confirms the surrogate architecture you should build — **rigid impact plate → calibrated spring (region-specific rate) → deformable pad (shore-specified) → force sensor behind it, pressure sensing at the contact face**. That is a machinable, purchasable stack. Also confirms that IFA (regulator) and GTE (vendor) are the same lineage as the papers above, so your rig, the standard, and the literature all describe one family of device.
evidence_grade: **I** (regulator technical information, not peer-reviewed; largely descriptive).
limitations: No numbers. German occupational-safety framing (workers, not patients). Licensing route means the real device is a commercial purchase. ---

handle: Remazeilles-eurobench — Remazeilles, Torricelli et al., 2022
citation: Remazeilles, A., Dominguez, A., Barralon, P., Torres-Pardo, A., Pinto, D., Aller, F., Mombaur, K., Conti, R., Saccares, L., Thorsteinsson, F., Prinsen, E., Cantón, A., Castilla, J., Sanz-Morère, C. B., Tornero, J., & Torricelli, D. (2022). Making bipedal robot experiments reproducible and comparable: The Eurobench software approach. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 9, 951663.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2022.951663 — **fetched the Frontiers full text**
open_access: yes (CC-BY); code on GitHub, Docker images on Docker Hub.
contribution: The EU benchmarking infrastructure for humanoids, exoskeletons and prosthetics — a worked example of what "a reproducible benchmark" means operationally: fixed protocol, fixed testbed, fixed scoring algorithm, uploaded data, automatic performance-indicator computation.
hard_numbers: **~30 protocols** with associated testbeds and scoring algorithms; **20 validated metric algorithms** (17 concrete protocols plus 3 templates); **two physical benchmarking facilities** (wearables, humanoids); four supported languages (Python, Octave, MATLAB, C++); YAML performance-indicator outputs.
design_relevance: Use it as the **template for how to write up your campaign** so it is reproducible: every test = a named protocol + a described testbed + a stated performance indicator + released raw data. That structure alone will distinguish your report from a typical senior design write-up. Also worth searching their protocol set for a wearable/assistive protocol closer to your use case than anything in the cobot literature.
evidence_grade: **D** (infrastructure/methodology paper, not an experimental result).
limitations: **Bipedal locomotion and wearables — not contact safety.** It gives you no force limits and no impact protocol. Its relevance is organizational, not physical; do not oversell it as a safety benchmark. ---

handle: Abidi-intrinsicsafety — Abidi & Cianchetti, 2017
citation: Abidi, H., & Cianchetti, M. (2017). On intrinsic safety of soft robots. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 4, 5.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2017.00005 — **fetched the Frontiers full text**
contribution: A direct attack on the assumption your project rests on. Soft robots are *mechanically* gentler but introduce their own hazard classes, and "soft = safe" is, in the authors' framing, improperly used.
hard_numbers: Pneumatic actuators typically **2 bar**, potentially **8–10 bar**; **8 bar through a 0.5 mm hole delivers 0.157 N** as a jet; **0.02 bar via a blunt 23-gauge needle can penetrate sensitive tissue such as the eye**; soft-material elastic modulus typically **~10× lower** than rigid robots; robots below **2 m/s** widely treated as safe independent of mass. **No HIC values for soft robots, and no test protocol, are proposed.**
design_relevance: This is your **hazard list for the risk assessment**, and it names the failure modes your impact campaign will not catch: **burst/rupture of a pressurized member, jet impingement, entrapment in compliant folds, and loss of structural integrity under sustained load.** For a torso an elderly person leans on, "the bladder fails while loaded" is a more probable injury path than "the arm hits someone at 0.4 m/s." Your campaign needs a burst/proof-pressure test and a sustained-load creep test alongside the impact tests. That the authors propose **no** soft-robot test protocol is itself the key finding: **the protocol gap is real and you are entitled to say so in your report.**
evidence_grade: **D** (review/position paper).
limitations: 2017, pre-dates most soft-robot safety work. Argument by analysis, not experiment. Numbers are illustrative worst cases, not measured on any particular system. ---

handle: ISO-13482-TR — ISO 13482:2014 and ISO/TR 23482-1:2020 (standards)
citation: ISO 13482:2014, *Robots and robotic devices — Safety requirements for personal care robots*, ISO, Geneva. And ISO/TR 23482-1:2020, *Robotics — Application of ISO 13482 — Part 1: Safety-related test methods*, ISO, Geneva (published 18 March 2020; BSI committee AMT/10).
source: https://www.iso.org/standard/53820.html and https://www.iso.org/standard/71564.html — **iso.org 403s automated fetch; I verified the ISO/TR 23482-1 record (full title, 2020 date, publisher, committee) via** https://aistandardshub.org/ai-standards/robotics-application-of-iso-13482-safety-related-test-methods/
contribution: ISO 13482 is the type-C safety standard whose scope actually covers your device class (personal care / assistive robots, including "physical assistant" and "person carrier" types). ISO/TR 23482-1 is the companion technical report that describes safety-related test methods for verifying ISO 13482 compliance, with the manufacturer selecting tests and parameters from their own risk assessment.
hard_numbers: **none verified.** I could not read either document. The AI Standards Hub record confirms title, year, publisher and committee only, and explicitly does not detail which test methods are inside. **No numeric limits from ISO 13482 or ISO/TR 23482-1 are reported here, and none should be quoted second-hand.**
design_relevance: Two points for the design review. (1) **ISO 13482 is the standard you are nominally under, not ISO/TS 15066** — say so, then explain that you are transferring the 15066/5672 measurement apparatus because that is where the instrumentation and the published limits actually live. (2) ISO/TR 23482-1's structure — manufacturer derives the required tests from a risk assessment — means **your risk assessment is the document that justifies your test matrix.** Write it first; the test plan falls out of it.
evidence_grade: **I** (standards, consensus documents, content unverified by me).
limitations: Paywalled (each roughly CHF 150–200+). ISO 13482 has been widely criticized as hard to apply and is under revision (a prEN/FDIS 13482 revision is in progress, retitled toward "service robots"). **The blunt finding for this project: I found no freely readable, numeric, published impact-test protocol specific to ISO 13482.** If one exists it is inside these paywalled documents. ---

handle: Jacobs-validationgap — Jacobs & Reiser (Fraunhofer IPA)
citation: Jacobs, T., & Reiser, U. *Development of validation methods for safe mobile manipulation*. Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation IPA, Stuttgart. **Venue and year not confirmed** — internal evidence (refers to ISO 13482 as "the future" standard "will be published in 2013") places it at 2012–2013, most likely ROBOTIK/ISR 2012.
source: https://publica-rest.fraunhofer.de/server/api/core/bitstreams/08dd0971-8b60-4322-889f-055b28e54674/content — **I fetched and text-extracted this PDF and read the full text**; the Fraunhofer Publica landing page is bot-blocked and **Crossref returns no record**, so the venue is genuinely unverified.
contribution: States the gap plainly from inside the standards process: ISO 13482 gives detailed guidance on risk reduction and control-system design but **lacks the validation methods needed to prove that sufficient risk reduction was achieved**. Proposes developing validation criteria and evaluating them on Care-O-bot 3 as the reference system.
hard_numbers: **none reported.** The paper is about the methodological gap and the standards hierarchy (type A/B/C: ISO 12100 → ISO 13849 → ISO 13482); it contains no measured forces, velocities, or rig specifications.
design_relevance: Useful as the **citable statement that the assistive-robot validation gap is real and acknowledged by the people writing the standards** — that is the justification for your campaign borrowing cobot instrumentation. Nothing else; do not expect a method from it.
