evidence_grade: **D** (position/concept paper, and with an unverified venue I would treat it as grey literature).
limitations: ~13 years old, so its claim that the gap is unfilled is partly superseded by ISO/TR 23482-1 (2020) and ISO/PAS 5672 (2023). Mobile manipulator, not a compliant torso. **Cite with the venue caveat or not at all.** ---

handle: Bonsignorio-benchmarking — Bonsignorio & del Pobil, 2015
citation: Bonsignorio, F., & del Pobil, A. P. (2015). Toward replicable and measurable robotics research [From the Guest Editors]. *IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine*, 22(3), 32–35.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/MRA.2015.2452073 — **the IEEE page returns no content to automated fetch; I verified authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and date via the Crossref API** (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/MRA.2015.2452073), and the DOI resolves to IEEE document 7254310
contribution: The guest editorial introducing RAM's first Special Issue on Reproducible Robotics Research — the origin of the R-Article format (papers published with datasets, code, and hardware descriptions sufficient to replicate).
hard_numbers: **none reported** (editorial; and I have not read the text).
design_relevance: The citation to use when you justify releasing your raw impact data, CAD of the rig, and analysis scripts alongside the report. That is what distinguishes a measurement from an anecdote, and it costs you nothing. Note that Svarny 2022 released its dataset — follow that example.
evidence_grade: **D** (editorial, and unread by me — bibliographic record verified only).
limitations: Not about safety or contact at all. General methodology framing. Weak evidence for anything physical. --- Everything marked **[cited]** comes from a source above. Everything marked **[inferred]** is my engineering judgement and must be defended on its own, not by citation. **Rig 1 — Biofidelic contact surrogate (the core instrument).** Build the two-stage stack that IFA describes and Zimmermann characterizes **[cited]**: rigid impact plate → calibrated compression spring → shore-specified elastomer pad → uniaxial load cell → rigid backing. Spring rate selected per body region from the CoboSafe CBSF range, **10–150 N/mm** **[cited, industry]**; for chest/abdomen/upper-arm contacts use the low end, and note that D'Antona's research device saturates above **~60 N/mm** **[cited]**, which is fine because your target regions are soft. Pad per Zimmermann: **SH10A at 21 mm, SH30A at 14 mm, or SH70A at 7 mm** **[cited]**. Sample force at **≥1 kHz**, filter with a **100 Hz Butterworth low-pass** **[cited]** — and prefer **10 kHz** if your DAQ allows, since transients are **6–10 ms** events **[cited, Haddadin]** and the review documents **10–25 % force underestimation during rapid transients** **[cited, Hartmann]**. Add pressure-measurement film at the contact face for distribution **[cited, GTE]**; an FSR matrix gives you pressure-vs-time but needs per-pixel calibration you probably will not do **[cited, D'Antona]** — report it as qualitative distribution only **[inferred]**. **Rig 2 — Gravity pendulum impactor.** Copy Alhaddad: suspended instrumented surrogate in a frame, pendulum impactor of known mass, drop height sets velocity, **240 fps video analyzed in Tracker** to measure the actual impact velocity **[cited]**. Use the same pendulum, run in reverse, to measure your arm's **effective mass** by Kirschner's momentum-inversion method **[cited]** — note the pendulum's own effective mass at the contact point must be computed from its inertia and contact radius (Kirschner: **l = 636 mm, m_p,eff = 3.663 kg**) **[cited]**. Whether "effective mass" is even a meaningful parameter for a deforming soft arm is an open question and a legitimate finding either way **[inferred]**. **Rig 3 — Quasi-static lean/push rig.** Take Monteleone's quasi-static protocols: **force ramp at 1 N/s** and **displacement ramp at 1.5 cm/s** **[cited]**, applied at chest height to the torso, measuring applied force, torso displacement, and the tipping/collapse point. A hand winch, an inline load cell, and a string potentiometer will do it **[inferred]**. This is the test that addresses "an elderly person puts their weight on it," which is the hazard the cobot literature does not cover **[inferred]**. **Rig 4 — Pressurized-system integrity (if the design is fluidic).** Abidi & Cianchetti's hazard list — burst, jet impingement, entrapment **[cited]** — implies a proof-pressure test and a sustained-load hold. Neither has a published protocol in the sources I found; you would be writing it yourself **[inferred]**. **Measurement matrix.** Use the ISO/PAS 5672 taxonomy: **push (quasi-static, unconstrained), impact (dynamic, unconstrained), pinch (quasi-static, constrained), crush (dynamic, constrained)** **[cited]**, with **≥500 mm clearance** to qualify as unconstrained **[cited]**. Sample arm configuration and height, not just velocity — Svarny showed force varies **>100 %** across a workspace, and that **27 well-chosen states** are enough to fit a predictive map **[cited]**. Sweep velocity over roughly **0.1–0.5 m/s**, the band where the cobot limits bite **[cited, Svarny]**; add a **1–3 m/s** band on the pendulum rig if you want to characterize the worst-case runaway **[cited, Alhaddad]**. Use an orthogonal-array design (L9/L27) to keep the run count sane **[cited, Alhaddad]**. **Headline comparison.** Bare structure vs compliant-covered structure, matched velocities, same surrogate. Svarny's **~40 % transient force reduction** from passive skin is your benchmark to beat or fail to beat **[cited]**. Fit their extended force–velocity model that adds cover stiffness **k_s** and compressible thickness **d_s** in series with the body-part spring **[cited]**. **Pass/fail criteria.** Against the measured pain-onset limits, **not** the generic 280 N: for chest/sternum blunt impact the relevant figure is **~110 N impact / 80 N pinch**, and shoulder is **~100 N / 60 N** **[cited, Behrens]**. Quasi-static limits are the tighter case (ISO/TS 15066 applies **280 N for the first 0.5 s, 140 N after** **[cited, Svarny]**). For head impact, if you can generate one: **HIC₃₆ ≤ 650, 3 ms criterion ≤ 72 g** **[cited, Haddadin]** — though Haddadin's result that a light arm produces **HIC₃₆ < 25 at 2 m/s** **[cited]** means you will pass those trivially and should not present it as an achievement. **Apply a margin of at least 30 % below the limit** **[inferred]**, justified by the stacked uncertainties: **±10 % between certified devices** **[cited, Zimmermann]**, **10–25 % transient underestimation** and **±10 % on pressure film** **[cited, Hartmann]**, plus an uncharacterized home-built rig. Then state explicitly that pain-onset limits from a **working-age cohort of 112** **[cited, Behrens]** are **not** validated for elderly or rehab patients **[inferred]** — this is the most important caveat in your entire report and the reviewers will look for it. **Affordable vs needs a certified lab.** *Affordable (low hundreds to low thousands of USD):* spring-and-pad surrogate, uniaxial load cell + ≥1 kHz DAQ, gravity pendulum, 240 fps action camera + Tracker **[cited, Alhaddad]**, quasi-static winch pull with load cell, pressure-measurement film (single-use sheets), accelerometer-instrumented 3D-printed surrogate, orthogonal-array test design, open data release **[cited, Bonsignorio]**. *Needs a lab or a real budget:* certified CoboSafe/KDMG-KOLROBOT PFMD **[cited, GTE/IFA]**; Hybrid III dummy at 20 kHz in an ADAC-class facility **[cited, Haddadin]**; Kistler ±1 kN triaxial load cells and a calibrated four-bar pendulum **[cited, Behrens]**; Monteleone's 1200 N actuated balance testbed **[cited]**; FPGA/piezo pressure-mapping array **[cited, D'Antona]**; DMA for material storage modulus **[cited, Alhaddad]** — though a university materials lab likely has one. **Check first whether NYU already owns a PFMD or a Hybrid III component** before building anything **[inferred]** — that single email changes the whole plan. --- You can build a credible impact-safety rig for a few hundred dollars, and there is peer-reviewed precedent for every piece of it — the spring-and-elastomer surrogate, the gravity pendulum, the high-frame-rate-video velocity measurement, and the orthogonal-array test design are all published and all cheap. What you cannot do is claim compliance: you have no certified PFMD, no biofidelic calibration against published response corridors, and no accredited lab, so every number you produce is a *relative* comparison, not a *pass*. Lean into that — the strongest result available to you is bare-vs-covered at matched velocity, reported as a percentage force reduction against Svarny's ~40 % benchmark, with your raw data released. Your uncertainty will be worse than the ±10 % that certified devices disagree by and the 10–25 % underestimation those devices already suffer on transients, so do not report three significant figures and do not set a pass/fail margin tighter than about 30 %. The most important number in this file is not 280 N: it is Behrens's ~110 N for blunt impact on the sternum, because a torso contacts chests, and anyone quoting 280 N in your design review has read the wrong row of the wrong table. Two gaps will not be closed by the cobot literature at all, and they are the ones that will actually hurt someone — the quasi-static lean case, where Svarny showed soft covers stop helping, and the pressurized-structure failure modes Abidi and Cianchetti list, so budget for a lean-load ramp and a burst/proof-pressure test or accept that your campaign has a hole in it. Be equally blunt about the population: every limit you will cite comes from working-age subjects reporting pain onset, and your users are elderly and rehabilitation patients with thinner skin, weaker bone, and blunted pain reporting, which means the published numbers are an upper bound you should deliberately undercut, not a target you should hit. Finally, there is no published, freely readable impact-test protocol for ISO 13482 personal-care robots — I looked, and it is not there — so write your risk assessment first and derive your test matrix from it, because under ISO/TR 23482-1 that is what a manufacturer is expected to do anyway. ---

handle: CollisionSurvey — Haddadin, De Luca & Albu-Schäffer, 2017
citation: S. Haddadin, A. De Luca, A. Albu-Schäffer, "Robot Collisions: A Survey on Detection, Isolation, and Identification," *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*, 33(6), 1292–1312, 2017.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2017.2723903 — verified by fetching the TUM research-portal record (https://portal.fis.tum.de/en/publications/robot-collisions-a-survey-on-detection-isolation-and-identificati/), which shows authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, article number 8059840 and the DOI.
open_access: No (IEEE paywalled; the TUM record is metadata + abstract only).
contribution: The reference taxonomy for the collision *event pipeline* — detection → isolation → identification → classification → reaction — using **proprioceptive sensors only** (motor current / joint torque + position), with the generalized-momentum residual as the workhorse estimator. Covers both rigid and flexible-joint (elastic-transmission) arms.
hard_numbers: none reported in the record I fetched (metadata + abstract only). The abstract claims experimental comparison of the algorithms but the numeric results sit behind the paywall.
design_relevance: This is the architecture spine for the "provably gentle" half of the question. It tells you that a torso+arm robot does **not** need a skin, a camera, or a wrist F/T sensor to know it hit someone: a model-based residual on the actuator side is enough, and the same residual gives you a *direction* to retreat along. Build your safety layer as residual → threshold → reaction-strategy switch.
evidence_grade: A (definitive survey, top venue, by the people who invented the method; downgraded from A+ only because I could not read the experimental numbers).
limitations: Every method assumes you have a usable rigid/flexible-joint dynamic model `M(q)q̈ + C q̇ + g = τ`. A soft torso with a person leaning on it violates that: the "model error" from unmodeled body compliance, air-pressure dynamics and hysteresis will swamp the contact residual. On soft hardware the residual becomes a *change detector*, not a force estimator, and a sustained lean is exactly the signal it is worst at (see next entry's threshold discussion). ---

handle: DLR-Reaction — De Luca, Albu-Schäffer, Haddadin & Hirzinger, 2006
citation: A. De Luca, A. Albu-Schäffer, S. Haddadin, G. Hirzinger, "Collision Detection and Safe Reaction with the DLR-III Lightweight Manipulator Arm," *2006 IEEE/RSJ Int. Conf. on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)*, Beijing, pp. 1623–1630, 2006.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS.2006.282053 — verified by fetching the author-hosted green-OA PDF at http://www.diag.uniroma1.it/~labrob/pub/papers/IROS06_DLR.pdf (full text extracted locally) plus the Semantic Scholar record for the DOI.
open_access: Yes (green OA, author copy at DIAG Sapienza).
contribution: The concrete recipe: build a residual `r` from total energy or generalized momentum, threshold it component-wise, then switch the controller into one of four reaction strategies (0 = none, 1 = stop, 2 = zero-gravity float, 3 = reflex torque `τ = K_R · r`, 4 = admittance reaction on the motor side). Extends the whole thing to elastic joints, which is the closest rigid-robot analogue to a compliant arm.
hard_numbers: High-level control loop **1 ms**, local joint control **333 µs**. Detection observer gain `K_I = 25·I`; reflex gains `K_R = 1.4·I` (strategy 3) and `0.05·I` (strategy 4). Detection thresholds set at **10 % of each joint's max output torque**, giving "reliable detection without false alarms and with just a one-step delay (**1 ms**)", but the current-control communication path added **4–6 ms** more, i.e. real end-to-end latency ≈ **5–7 ms**. Hardware: 13.5 kg arm, joint stiffness **10–15 × 10³ Nm/rad**, max joint torques 180 / 80 / 30 Nm, end-effector speed > 4 m/s. Impacts at cruise speeds 10–100 °/s; human collisions at contact speeds **up to ~1.5 m/s**. With no detection (strategy 0) the arm pressed the target to **35 Nm** at joint 4; all reactive strategies drove contact torque to zero. Human trials were **qualitative only** — the paper explicitly says instrumented testing would be needed to quantify impact forces.
design_relevance: Gives you numbers you can design against: the threshold-as-%-of-max-torque heuristic, the fact that comms latency (4–6 ms) dominates the estimator latency (1 ms), and the observation that **strategy 3 (reflex torque, i.e. become an admittance the human can push) felt smoothest to humans** — which is exactly the behaviour a lean-on torso needs. Copy this structure; do not copy the gains.
evidence_grade: A (real hardware, explicit gains, explicit latency budget, honest about what was not measured).
limitations: Direct transfer risk is high. A person *leaning* on the torso is a slow, sustained, quasi-static contact — the worst case for a residual with a 10 %-of-max-torque threshold, because the lean load can look like model error or payload. The DLR arm is a stiff-link/elastic-joint machine; nothing here says the residual is well-conditioned when the *links themselves* deform. And the 1 ms loop assumes a hard-real-time joint bus; a hobby-grade servo bus at 50–100 Hz throws the whole latency argument away. ---

handle: HoganImpedance — Hogan, 1985
citation: N. Hogan, "Impedance Control: An Approach to Manipulation: Part I—Theory," *ASME Journal of Dynamic Systems, Measurement, and Control*, 107(1), 1–7, 1985. (Companion papers: Part II—Implementation, 107(1), 8–16; Part III—Applications, 107(1), 17–24.)
source: https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3140702 — verified by fetching the MIT-hosted PDF (https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.mit.edu/dist/5/1384/files/2025/02/1985-impedance-control-an-approach-to-manipulation-part-I-theory.pdf) and reading the title block and abstract directly; Part II/III page ranges cross-checked on the ASME Digital Collection listing.
open_access: Partial (author/institution-hosted copy of Part I is free; the ASME versions are paywalled).
contribution: The founding argument. "Control of position or force alone is inadequate; control of dynamic behavior is also required." Because manipulation is nonlinear, impedance and admittance are **not** interchangeable, and — the sentence that decides your architecture — *given the environment contains inertial objects, the manipulator must be an impedance.* Also defines the nonlinear Norton-equivalent that separates commanded motion from commanded impedance.
hard_numbers: none reported (theory paper).
design_relevance: A human leaning on your torso is an inertial, energy-storing environment. Hogan's result says the robot should present itself as an impedance (accept motion, produce force) rather than an admittance (accept force, produce motion) *at the contact*. For this project that argues for: command a virtual spring-damper about a reference posture, and let the assistive force fall out of the deflection — not a force-servo loop chasing a setpoint. The Norton separation also gives you the clean split your team wants: one module plans the equilibrium trajectory, another sets stiffness/damping.
evidence_grade: A (foundational; 40 years of downstream validation).
limitations: Assumes you can *render* the impedance you command — i.e. actuator torque authority and bandwidth exceed the impedance you're asking for. A pneumatic/tendon soft arm cannot render an arbitrary impedance; its physical impedance is largely fixed by its construction and pressure, so much of your "impedance design" happens in the mechanical design phase, not the control code. Treat Hogan as the specification language, not as an implementable controller. ---

handle: AdmittancePHRI — Keemink, van der Kooij & Stienen, 2018
citation: A. Q. L. Keemink, H. van der Kooij, A. H. A. Stienen, "Admittance control for physical human–robot interaction," *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, 37(11), 1421–1444, 2018.
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/0278364918768950 — verified two ways: the Semantic Scholar Graph API record for the DOI, and the full green-OA PDF from the University of Twente repository (https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/files/29087621/admittance.pdf), text extracted locally.
contribution: The most practically useful single document on the impedance/admittance trade-off. States the trade-off cleanly and then *engineers* it: "For admittance controlled devices it is easier to render stiff virtual surfaces and a challenge to render low inertia… Impedance control, on the other hand, is a better candidate to render low inertia but not to render stiff virtual surfaces." Produces **seven design guidelines** (feed-forward, avoid force filtering, compensate post-sensor inertia, add virtual damping, modify the velocity reference, raise velocity-loop bandwidth, optimise for robot stiffness) each tied to a positive-real / passivity condition for coupled stability.
hard_numbers: Worked baseline: making a **10 kg** device with damping feel like a **2 kg** pure inertia — a **factor-5** inertia reduction — is the stated performance target, and the guidelines exist because naive admittance loses passivity well before that. Example parameters used: `G_f = 5`, `µ_ff = 10 kg`, `β_ff = 2 Ns/m`, differential gain `k_d = 25 Ns²/m`. Notes industrial current-controller bandwidth is "commonly > 2 kHz". **No human subjects** — the paper is analysis + guidelines.
design_relevance: Decides the sensing question. Admittance control needs a real force sensor at the interaction port and a stiff, high-bandwidth inner velocity loop. Your torso has neither cheaply. Guideline 7 ("optimise for robot stiffness") and the internal-flexibility analysis are the direct warning: **structural compliance between the force sensor and the actuator destroys admittance-control passivity**, which is the defining condition of a soft arm. This paper is the strongest single argument in the pile for *not* doing admittance control on this robot.
evidence_grade: A (rigorous, open, immediately actionable, and it tells you when its own method fails).
limitations: Single-DOF, idealised-stiff analysis; the authors say so. It gives you conditions to *avoid*, not a controller for a soft multi-segment torso. Zero human-subject data, so nothing here speaks to comfort or perceived safety. ---

handle: ProiettiALS — Proietti et al., 2023
citation: T. Proietti, C. O'Neill, L. Gerez, T. Cole, S. Mendelowitz, K. Nuckols, C. Hohimer, D. Lin, S. Paganoni, C. J. Walsh, "Restoring arm function with a soft robotic wearable for individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis," *Science Translational Medicine*, 15(681), eadd1504, 2023.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.add1504 — verified by fetching the Europe PMC REST record (core result, PMID 36724237), which returned the full author list, journal, volume/issue, year and verbatim abstract. Crossref record fetched as a cross-check.
contribution: A textile inflatable shoulder-assist wearable evaluated on **10 people with ALS**, i.e. exactly the clinically fragile, variable-impairment population this project claims. Immediate improvement in active range of motion, improved ADL performance **with no training**, reduced shoulder EMG and perceived exertion, increased holding endurance, and — the important design property — the device is **mechanically transparent when unpowered**.
hard_numbers: **150 g added per arm**; **10 participants** with ALS at differing impairment levels; **2 participants followed for 6 months** showing compensation for continued deterioration. Force-tracking error, bandwidth and commanded-stiffness figures: not reported in the abstract, and the full text is paywalled — so **not verified**.
design_relevance: The single best evidence in this set that soft, low-authority, *non-force-servoed* assistance produces measurable clinical benefit in the target population. Two design rules fall out: (1) unpowered mechanical transparency is a safety feature and a usability feature — design your torso so a powered-off failure is a benign failure; (2) assistance can be delivered as a slowly-modulated pressure/torque profile rather than a closed-loop force setpoint and still be worth something to a patient.
evidence_grade: A (human subjects, clinical population, top translational venue).
limitations: A wearable is grounded on the user's own skeleton; your torso is grounded on the floor and must resist a lean without tipping. Nothing here addresses balance, tipping, or the reaction load path through a freestanding base. Also shoulder *elevation assist* is a single-DOF, mostly gravity-compensating task — far easier than a commanded assistive force in an arbitrary direction. n = 10, single-arm study, no control group. ---

handle: UFIC — Haddadin & Shahriari, 2024
citation: S. Haddadin, E. Shahriari, "Unified force-impedance control," *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, 43(14), 2112–2141, 2024. (Builds on C. Schindlbeck, S. Haddadin, "Unified passivity-based Cartesian force/impedance control for rigid and flexible joint robots via task-energy tanks," *ICRA 2015*, pp. 440–447, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA.2015.7139036.)
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/02783649241249194 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API record for the DOI (title, authors, journal, volume, pages, full abstract, CC-BY-NC hybrid status). The ICRA 2015 predecessor verified independently via the Crossref REST record (DOI, pages 440–447).
open_access: Partial (hybrid, CC-BY-NC per the S2 record; the SAGE PDF endpoint refused my fetch, so I could not read the body).
contribution: How to get *exact force regulation* and *compliance* out of one controller instead of switching between them, with passivity guaranteed by **energy tanks**, for both rigid and flexible-joint robots, and with either measured or model-estimated contact force. Explicitly attacks the failure mode that should scare this project: abrupt, dangerous motion on **contact loss** — the thing that happens when the person leaning on your torso suddenly stands up.
hard_numbers: none verified (abstract only; the experimental section is behind the SAGE paywall and my fetch returned HTTP 403). The abstract claims simulation plus "various experiments" and rigorous stability analysis for arbitrary passive environments.
design_relevance: This is the *right* answer to the assigned design question and almost certainly the wrong answer for a senior-design timeline. If you do implement force tracking on top of impedance, steal exactly two ideas: the energy tank (a scalar state that bounds how much energy the controller may inject) and the contact/non-contact stabilisation shaping function (ramp the force command in and out instead of switching).
evidence_grade: B (top journal, rigorous, but I could not verify a single experimental number, and it has no human-subject validation).
limitations: Assumes a serial rigid or flexible-joint robot with a trustworthy dynamic model and joint torque sensing or good contact-force estimation. Your soft torso has none of those. Implementing UFIC correctly is a graduate-thesis-scale task. ---

handle: TankVSC — Ferraguti, Secchi & Fantuzzi, 2013
citation: F. Ferraguti, C. Secchi, C. Fantuzzi, "A tank-based approach to impedance control with variable stiffness," *2013 IEEE Int. Conf. on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)*, pp. 4948–4953, 2013.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA.2013.6631284 — verified via the Crossref REST record (DOI, exact title, all three authors, container title, pages 4948–4953, year).
contribution: The canonical energy-tank construction: time-varying stiffness can inject energy and destabilise an interaction, so you attach a virtual tank fed by dissipated power and only permit stiffness changes the tank can pay for. Result: **passivity for any choice of stiffness matrix**, in free motion and in contact.
hard_numbers: none verified — I confirmed the bibliographic record and the method's claim via the Crossref record and the paper's widely-quoted abstract statement, but did not reach the full text, so I report no experimental figures.
design_relevance: If your team wants "gentle when the person is passive, firmer when they need a real assist," you are doing variable stiffness, and variable stiffness is where naive impedance control stops being provably safe. The tank is about **twenty lines of code**: one scalar energy state, integrate dissipated power in, subtract the cost of stiffness increases, clamp stiffness when the tank empties. This is the single highest value-per-line safety mechanism available to you.
evidence_grade: B (well-established, heavily cited, but numbers unverified here and the demonstration is a rigid manipulator).
limitations: Passivity guarantees the robot injects no unbounded energy. It does **not** guarantee the *forces* stay below an injury threshold, and it does not guarantee the robot stays upright. A perfectly passive torso can still be passively too stiff for a frail person. You need a force/torque cap on top of the tank, not instead of it. ---

handle: AR3n — Pareek, Nisar & Kesavadas, 2023
citation: S. Pareek, H. Nisar, T. Kesavadas, "AR3n: A Reinforcement Learning-Based Assist-as-Needed Controller for Robotic Rehabilitation," *IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine*, 2023. Preprint arXiv:2303.00085.
source: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.00085 (IEEE version: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10158787/) — verified by fetching the arXiv abstract page (authors, journal-ref "IEEE Robotics and Automation Magazine, 2023") **and** the accepted-version PDF, whose text I extracted locally to read the human-subject section.
contribution: Assist-as-needed assistance modulated by an RL policy against a *virtual patient model*, so the controller does not need per-patient tuning or a per-patient physical model — the standard objection to classical AAN. Benchmarked head-to-head against a conventional rule-based error-reduction (ER) controller.
hard_numbers: **8 healthy subjects** (5 M / 3 F, mean age 26, range 19–33), IRB #15990, single session, three trials each (baseline / training / post). Robot sampled at **1000 Hz**; the RL environment runs at **50 Hz** with a history window n = 25. Reward weights λ_T = 1, λ_N = 0.4 chosen experimentally. SAC beat PPO on training reward. The paper concedes the study was "conducted on a fairly small pool of healthy subjects." Force-tracking error in newtons: not reported in those terms.
design_relevance: Useful mainly as a *negative* result for your scope. It confirms the real problem in AAN is the patient model, and it solves that with an RL policy trained in simulation — which needs a simulator of your plant. You do not have a trustworthy simulator of a soft torso. The transferable idea is much cheaper: **penalise assistance magnitude and assistance rate-of-change in whatever rule you use**, which is what makes AR3n's profiles smooth versus ER's step-like bursts.
evidence_grade: B (real human subjects with numbers, open preprint; downgraded for n = 8 healthy, single session, magazine-tier venue, and a rigid planar device).
limitations: Healthy young subjects, a handwriting task on a stiff planar manipulandum, and an artificially induced "impairment" (non-dominant hand + mirrored axes). None of that is an elderly person leaning on a compliant torso. The 50 Hz policy rate is fine for assistance modulation but far too slow for a safety reflex — do not put the learned policy in the safety path. ---

handle: ShoulderExosuit — Zhou et al., 2024
citation: Y.-M. Zhou, C. J. Hohimer, H. T. Young, C. M. McCann, D. Pont-Esteban, U. S. Civici, Y. Jin, P. Murphy, D. Wagner, T. Cole, N. S. Phipps, H. Cho, F. Bertacchi, I. Pignataro, T. Proietti, C. J. Walsh, "A portable inflatable soft wearable robot to assist the shoulder during industrial work," *Science Robotics*, 9, 2024.
source: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.adi2377 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API record for the DOI (full author list, journal, volume, year, abstract). The Science site itself returned HTTP 403 to my fetch.
contribution: A shirt-form inflatable shoulder assist driven by a **kinematics-based controller** (IMU-driven, not force-servoed) reduced shoulder muscle activity by up to 40 % in simulated industrial tasks, with minimal change to joint angles, and the controller was robust to equipment malfunction. Piloted with real factory workers.
hard_numbers: up to **6.6 N·m** shoulder assist torque; **up to 40 %** reduction in agonist muscle activity (anterior/middle/posterior deltoid, biceps brachii); assistance cycled on/off **6 times per minute**. Exact participant count not stated in the record I fetched — the abstract says "human participant evaluations" plus factory-worker pilot testing, so I list it as **not verified**.
design_relevance: The blunt lesson for your team: a **kinematics-triggered, open-loop-in-force** assist delivered a 40 % measurable physiological benefit with no force feedback loop at all. If your success metric is "measurable assistive force," a well-characterised pressure→force map plus a posture-triggered state machine may hit your spec, and it is a tenth of the engineering of a closed-loop force controller.
evidence_grade: B (strong venue, real users, good numbers; downgraded because it is a wearable, closed-access, and the subject count is unverified).
limitations: Same grounding problem as ProiettiALS — the suit reacts against the wearer's skeleton. 6.6 N·m against your own shoulder is not the same problem as reacting a leaning adult's body weight through a freestanding base. Assistance cycling at 0.1 Hz says nothing about your reflex bandwidth needs. ---

handle: AAN-EMG — Arantes, Bressan, Borges & McGibbon, 2023
citation: A. P. Arantes, N. Bressan, L. R. Borges, C. A. McGibbon, "Evaluation of a novel real-time adaptive assist-as-needed controller for robot-assisted upper extremity rehabilitation following stroke," *PLOS ONE*, 18(10), e0292627, 2023.
source: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0292627 — verified by fetching the full open-access text at PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10566685/).
contribution: An EMG-driven adaptive AAN controller that assists when the user is *trying* (EMG present) but not moving, and progressively switches to **resistance** as performance improves — an explicit anti-slacking design. Tested on real stroke patients with EMG + EEG instrumentation.
hard_numbers: **5 chronic stroke participants** (mean age ~66, Fugl-Meyer 36–65). Assistance/resistance authority band **−6 N to +6 N**. EMG trigger threshold **20 %** of baseline maximum entropy amplitude; six upper-extremity muscles monitored; 9-channel EEG, beta band 16–24 Hz. Significant EMG increase during training (paired t = 3.73, p = 0.02); EEG changes non-significant.
design_relevance: Two directly usable facts. First, a **±6 N** authority band was clinically meaningful for stroke patients — that is a defensible order of magnitude for your assistive-force spec, and it is small enough to be safe. Second, intent detection does not require a force sensor at the contact: a crude EMG-or-effort gate plus a deadband is enough to distinguish "the user is trying" from "the user is slacking." A load-cell threshold in your torso can play the same role.
evidence_grade: C (real patients, fully open, honest reporting — but n = 5, pilot, no control group, and the primary outcome was an EMG surrogate, not function).
limitations: Planar horizontal arm task on a rigid haptic device. Says nothing about compliant plants, contact safety, or a person putting body weight into the robot. n = 5 cannot support any efficacy claim; cite it for the force magnitude and the controller logic, never as evidence that AAN works. ---

handle: SoftModelBased — Della Santina, Katzschmann, Bicchi & Rus, 2020
citation: C. Della Santina, R. K. Katzschmann, A. Bicchi, D. Rus, "Model-based dynamic feedback control of a planar soft robot: trajectory tracking and interaction with the environment," *The International Journal of Robotics Research*, 39(4), 490–513, 2020.
source: https://doi.org/10.1177/0278364919897292 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API record for the DOI (authors, journal, volume, pages, verbatim abstract, bronze-OA status).
open_access: Partial (S2 reports bronze OA at SAGE; the PDF endpoint refused my fetch).
contribution: The key structural result for controlling soft arms: under a **piecewise constant curvature (PCC)** assumption, soft-robot dynamics can be mapped *exactly* onto an equivalent rigid robot with elastic joints — which means the entire elastic-joint control literature (including De Luca's residual and Hogan's impedance) becomes importable. Presents the first closed-loop *dynamic* controllers for a continuous soft robot: trajectory tracking and **surface following**, both designed to preserve the robot's natural softness during interaction.
hard_numbers: none verified (abstract only; SAGE returned HTTP 403). The abstract reports analytic proofs, extensive simulation, and experiments on a physical planar soft robot, but no figures I could read.
design_relevance: This is your justification for treating each soft arm as an elastic-joint rigid arm in the controller, and for using PCC as the state parameterisation rather than a full Cosserat rod. "Surface following while preserving softness" is structurally the same problem as "maintain contact force against a torso a person is leaning on."
evidence_grade: B (top journal, important idea, but planar-only, single lab, and unverified numbers).
limitations: PCC assumes constant curvature per segment and breaks under exactly the load case you care about — a **concentrated external load mid-segment**, i.e. someone leaning on the middle of an arm. It is planar; your torso is spatial and must also handle gravity in a way a planar testbed never does. Model identification for a real soft arm is a semester of work by itself. ---

handle: SoftForceTracking — Tang, Xin, Wang & Laschi, 2024
citation: Z. Tang, W. Xin, P. Wang, C. Laschi, "Learning-Based Control for Soft Robot–Environment Interaction with Force/Position Tracking Capability," *Soft Robotics*, 11(5), 767–778, 2024.
source: https://doi.org/10.1089/soro.2023.0116 — verified via the Semantic Scholar Graph API record for the DOI (authors, journal, volume, pages, abstract).
contribution: Simultaneous **force and position** tracking on a soft manipulator with no prior model of either the robot's dynamics or the environment: probabilistic MPC feedforward plus a non-parametric learned feedback term, adapting online. Demonstrated against a **manikin**, which is the closest thing in this pile to your use case.
hard_numbers: none verified (paywalled; the abstract claims it outperformed comparable data-driven alternatives but gives no figures I could read).
design_relevance: The existence proof that force tracking on a soft arm against a human-shaped target is possible without a model — and simultaneously the warning about what it costs: a probabilistic MPC plus online non-parametric learning is not a senior-design deliverable. Cite it to justify the *goal*; do not cite it as a plan.
evidence_grade: C (right problem, right venue, but zero verified numbers, single platform, no human subjects — a manikin is not a person).
limitations: A manikin is passive, rigid-ish and does not push back, get startled, or shift its weight. Data-driven controllers trained on one environment degrade silently when the environment changes; on a robot a frail person leans on, a silent degradation is a safety event. Nothing in this approach is provably gentle. ---

handle: VICReview — Abu-Dakka & Saveriano, 2020
citation: F. J. Abu-Dakka, M. Saveriano, "Variable Impedance Control and Learning—A Review," *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 7, 590681, 2020.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2020.590681 — verified by fetching the full open-access article at Frontiers.
contribution: The map of the variable-impedance field, split into variable impedance *control* (VIC), *learning* (VIL) and *learning control* (VILC). Its most useful line for your team is the admission that **"stability in VIC is not a trivial problem"** — and that the two credible routes to a guarantee are passivity theory (no environment model needed) and Lyapunov constraints on the impedance matrices.
hard_numbers: **none reported** — verified by reading the full text; the paper is methodological taxonomy with no stiffness ranges, bandwidths or benchmark figures anywhere.
design_relevance: Use it to scope, not to build: it tells you that if you vary stiffness you must pair it with a passivity mechanism (→ TankVSC), and it lets you honestly say in your report that you surveyed the VIC landscape and deliberately chose the simplest rung.
evidence_grade: B (comprehensive, open, well-organised; it's a review, so it is evidence *about* the literature, not about hardware).
limitations: Rigid-manipulator-centric. Almost nothing on soft plants, nothing on human subjects, and no numbers at all — so it cannot settle any quantitative design question for you. ---

handle: RodControlReview — Alessi et al., 2024
citation: C. Alessi, C. Agabiti, D. Caradonna, C. Laschi, F. Renda, E. Falotico, "Rod models in continuum and soft robot control: a review," arXiv:2407.05886 (submitted 8 July 2024; revised 2026).
source: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2407.05886 — verified by fetching the arXiv abstract page (title, all six authors, dates, abstract).
contribution: Survey of Cosserat-rod and reduced-order rod theories specifically from a **control** standpoint — which rod formulations are cheap enough to sit inside a controller, and how they feed both model-based and learned control for manipulation and physical interaction.
hard_numbers: none reported (review).
design_relevance: Bounds your modelling ambition. It confirms the ladder PCC → piecewise-affine curvature → discrete Cosserat, with computational cost rising at each rung. For a senior-design build, this review's existence is the argument for stopping at the *bottom* rung: you do not need a Cosserat rod to command a stiffness.
evidence_grade: C (preprint, not peer-reviewed at the version I fetched; useful as a signpost, not as evidence).
limitations: A review of models, not of assistive control. No contact-safety content, no human data. Every rod model in it still requires material parameter identification on your actual hardware, which is the part that eats the schedule. --- Build a **joint-space impedance controller with gravity compensation, a commanded equilibrium posture, and a generalized-momentum residual watching for unexpected contact** — and nothing more clever than that. Hogan's result settles the top-level choice: your environment (a leaning human) is inertial, so the arm must behave as an impedance, and Keemink's flexibility analysis kills the admittance alternative outright, because structural compliance between your force sensor and your actuator is exactly the condition under which admittance control loses passivity — and that compliance is the entire point of your robot. Get your "commanded assistive force" from deflection against a known virtual stiffness (force = K · Δx) with a **characterised, calibrated pressure/tendon→force map**, not from a force-servo loop; ShoulderExosuit got a 40 % EMG reduction with a purely kinematics-triggered assist and no force feedback at all, and AAN-EMG shows **±6 N** was clinically meaningful on stroke patients, so a modest, open-loop-in-force assist is a defensible spec rather than a cop-out. Add exactly two safety mechanisms: a **hard saturation on commanded force/torque** sized to your injury budget, and a **scalar energy tank** gating any stiffness increase (TankVSC is ~20 lines and is the only thing in this pile that buys you a provable gentleness claim). For collision reaction, copy DLR-Reaction's *structure* — residual, threshold, switch to a reflex/admittance mode that lets the human push the arm away — but treat their numbers as unreachable: their 1 ms detection assumed a hard-real-time bus, and their real end-to-end latency was already 5–7 ms once comms were counted, so budget **20–50 ms** on realistic student hardware and say so in the report. Over-reach, to name it plainly: unified force-impedance control with energy tanks (UFIC), learned force/position tracking (SoftForceTracking), RL-based assist-as-needed (AR3n), and any Cosserat-rod model in the control loop are all graduate-thesis-scale and will consume your semester without producing a working demo. The single biggest evidence gap you must not paper over: **not one paper here validates interaction control on a freestanding soft torso that a person puts body weight into** — every human-subject result in this set is either a wearable grounded on the user's own skeleton or a rigid, bolted-down planar manipulandum, so your tipping/balance and sustained-quasi-static-lean cases are genuinely un-derisked by the literature and need their own bench test. Also be honest in the report that a momentum residual degrades from a force estimator to a crude change-detector on a soft plant, and that a slow lean is its worst-case input — which is precisely why the force saturation, not the residual, is your real safety guarantee.

handle: Cochrane-RAT — Mehrholz et al., 2018
citation: Mehrholz J, Pohl M, Platz T, Kugler J, Elsner B. Electromechanical and robot-assisted arm training for improving activities of daily living, arm function, and arm muscle strength after stroke. *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews* 2018;9(9):CD006876.
source: 10.1002/14651858.CD006876.pub5 — verified via eutils PMID 30175845 (PMCID PMC6513114). The Cochrane Library HTML/PDF returns 403 to automated fetch; the indexed record carries the full abstract including all effect sizes.
open_access: partial (abstract free; full review paywalled outside Cochrane subscription — PMC6513114 exists, check institutional access).
contribution: The single most authoritative synthesis: across 45 RCTs, robot/electromechanical arm training produces small but statistically reliable improvements in ADL, arm function and arm strength, with high GRADE quality and rare adverse events. It explicitly refuses to claim superiority over dose-matched conventional therapy.
hard_numbers: 45 trials, 1619 participants. ADL: SMD **0.31** (95% CI 0.09–0.52), p=0.0005, I²=59%, 24 studies, 957 participants, high-quality evidence. Arm function: SMD **0.32** (95% CI 0.18–0.46), p<0.0001, I²=36%, 41 studies, 1452 participants. Arm muscle strength: SMD **0.46** (95% CI 0.16–0.77), p=0.003, I²=76%, 23 studies, 826 participants. Dropout risk difference **0.00** (95% CI −0.02 to 0.02), I²=0%. Adverse events "rare". No force, torque or ROM figures.
design_relevance: This is the evidence base the team cites to justify the project existing at all — and the honesty constraint on every claim made about it. An SMD of ~0.3 is a *small* effect. It also sets the safety baseline: a device in this class is expected to produce essentially zero excess dropout and rare adverse events, which becomes a design requirement, not a nice-to-have.
evidence_grade: **A** (systematic review + meta-analysis of RCTs).
limitations: Authors themselves warn results must be read with caution because of variation in training intensity, duration, amount, device type, participant characteristics and outcome measures. Every trial is stroke-specific and therapist-supervised in a clinic. Nothing here transfers to an unsupervised care-home setting, and nothing here covers a *freestanding torso* that a person makes contact with — all included devices are grounded end-effector or exoskeleton machines with the patient seated and attended.

handle: RATULS — Rodgers et al., 2019
citation: Rodgers H, Bosomworth H, Krebs HI, van Wijck F, Howel D, Wilson N, et al. Robot assisted training for the upper limb after stroke (RATULS): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. *The Lancet* 2019;394(10192):51–62.
contribution: The largest, most pragmatic head-to-head test of upper-limb robot therapy. Robot-assisted training with MIT-Manus/InMotion did **not** beat an intensity-matched conventional therapy programme, and did not beat usual care, on the primary functional outcome. It did reduce impairment slightly versus usual care.
hard_numbers: n=770 randomised (robot 257, enhanced upper-limb therapy 259, usual care 254). Dose: **45 min/session, 3×/week, 12 weeks** (36 sessions); actual delivered median **23 h 28 min** robot, **24 h 40 min** EULT. Primary outcome (ARAT "success") at 3 months: robot 103/232 (**44%**), EULT 118/234 (**50%**), usual care 85/203 (**42%**); robot vs usual care adjusted OR **1.17** (98.3% CI **0.70–1.96**) — null. Fugl-Meyer motor, robot vs usual care: adjusted mean difference **2.79** (98.3% CI 0.66–5.01) at 3 months, **2.54** (0.07–5.06) at 6 months. Serious adverse events: 43 in 39 robot participants, 42 in 33 EULT, 29 in 20 usual care; **none related to the trial intervention**.
design_relevance: Sets the session protocol the team should default to (45 min × 3/week × 12 weeks ≈ 24 h) and sets the honest expectation ceiling. Also: the FM gain of ~2.8 points is *below* the clinically important difference (see #11), which the design review will notice if the team doesn't say it first.
evidence_grade: **A** (large multicentre RCT, blinded assessors).
limitations: Moderate-to-severe impairment, 1 week to 5 years post-stroke, four UK centres, supervised throughout. Participants, therapists and analysts unmasked for the intervention itself. Says nothing about elderly non-stroke users, postural support, or unsupervised use.

handle: ARMin-RCT — Klamroth-Marganska et al., 2014
citation: Klamroth-Marganska V, Blanco J, Campen K, Curt A, Dietz V, Ettlin T, et al. Three-dimensional, task-specific robot therapy of the arm after stroke: a multicentre, parallel-group randomised trial. *Lancet Neurology* 2014;13(2):159–166.
contribution: The definitive trial of an *exoskeleton* (ARMin) rather than an end-effector robot. Robot therapy beat conventional therapy on Fugl-Meyer — but by an amount the authors themselves call clinically questionable.
hard_numbers: n=77 enrolled, 73 analysed (38 robot, 35 conventional). Chronic (>6 months), moderate-to-severe arm paresis. Dose: **≥45 min, 3×/week, 8 weeks, 24 sessions**. Primary outcome FMA-UE: F=4.1, p=0.041, **mean difference 0.78 points (95% CI 0.03–1.53)**. No serious adverse events related to the study.
design_relevance: Confirms 45 min × 3/week as the field-standard session. More importantly it is the cleanest available statement that exoskeleton assistance produces a *sub-MCID* impairment change — the team must not promise motor recovery as its primary claim.
evidence_grade: **A** (multicentre RCT, masked assessors).
limitations: Chronic stroke only, n=77, therapists and patients unmasked, Swiss rehabilitation centres. 0.78 FM points is roughly one-fifth of the smallest clinically important difference.

handle: T-WREX-RCT — Housman, Scott & Reinkensmeyer, 2009
citation: Housman SJ, Scott KM, Reinkensmeyer DJ. A randomized controlled trial of gravity-supported, computer-enhanced arm exercise for individuals with severe hemiparesis. *Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair* 2009;23(5):505–514.
contribution: A **passive, purely elastic** gravity-balancing orthosis (five DOF, counterbalanced with elastic bands) delivered clinically real, sustained gains in severe hemiparesis with only ~4 minutes of therapist contact per session. This is the closest published analogue to a low-power compliant assistive arm.
hard_numbers: n=28 chronic stroke, moderate/severe hemiparesis. Dose: **twenty-four 1-hour sessions**; therapist assistance **≈4 min/session**. Fugl-Meyer at 6-month follow-up: T-WREX **+3.6 ± 3.9** vs tabletop control **+1.5 ± 2.7** points (p=0.04). Active reaching ROM and Motor Activity Log improved in both groups. Device is passive — no motor torque figure exists because there is no motor.
design_relevance: The single best argument in the literature that **you do not need high actuator torque to be clinically useful — you need arm-weight support plus feedback**. Also gives the supervision budget: ~4 min of human attention per 60 min session is achievable, which is the realistic target for a semi-autonomous device.
evidence_grade: **A** (RCT, blinded rater).
limitations: Small (n=28), chronic severe hemiparesis only, clinic-based with a therapist on site, no attempt at postural support or trunk contact. The absolute between-group difference (2.1 FM points) is well under the MCID.

handle: Dose-response — Lohse, Lang & Boyd, 2014
citation: Lohse KR, Lang CE, Boyd LA. Is more better? Using metadata to explore dose-response relationships in stroke rehabilitation. *Stroke* 2014;45(7):2053–2058.
source: 10.1161/STROKEAHA.114.004695 — verified via eutils PMID 24867924 (PMCID PMC4071164).
contribution: Meta-analysis/meta-regression across non-dose-matched RCTs: more scheduled therapy time predicts more improvement, independent of time since stroke.
hard_numbers: Pooled effect of higher vs lower dose **g = 0.35 (95% CI 0.26–0.45)**. Time scheduled for therapy was a significant independent predictor of improvement. Authors state that *time scheduled* is a poor dose proxy and that **active time in therapy or repetitions** would be preferable.
design_relevance: This is the project's real value proposition and it should be written into the requirements as such: a machine that is available for more hours than a therapist is the mechanism of benefit, not superior kinematics. It also tells the team what to instrument — **count repetitions and active time**, not session minutes.
evidence_grade: **A** (meta-analysis of RCTs).
limitations: Dose is confounded with attention and engagement; trials were not dose-matched by design, so the comparison is inherently unbalanced. Stroke only.

handle: MIT-MANUS — Krebs, Hogan, Aisen & Volpe, 1998
citation: Krebs HI, Hogan N, Aisen ML, Volpe BT. Robot-aided neurorehabilitation. *IEEE Transactions on Rehabilitation Engineering* 1998;6(1):75–87.
source: 10.1109/86.662623 — fetched PMC2692541 (full text); identity confirmed via NCBI esummary (PMID 9535526).
contribution: The origin document for impedance-controlled, backdrivable rehabilitation robotics, and the only place that states the *design rationale* for the end-effector force target in human terms.
hard_numbers: Endpoint force capability **0–45 N**; the stated design target was **28 N**, chosen because it "corresponds to the arm strength during elbow extension for a weak woman in seated position." Endpoint inertia **1 ± 0.33 kg**, max anisotropy 2:1. Endpoint friction **0.84 ± 0.28 N**. Achievable endpoint impedance **0–2 N/mm** as stated in the retrieved full text (secondary sources quote 0–8 N/mm for later builds — use 0–2 N/mm, that is what the 1998 paper says). Planar module 2 DOF, wrist module +3 DOF. Clinical trial: 20 patients (10 robot, 10 standard); FM-UE change **14.1 ± 9.7** vs **9.9 ± 11.2** (p=0.19, null); Motor Status shoulder/elbow **9.4 ± 5.9** vs **0.8 ± 3.8** (p=0.00065). Training: **4–5 h/week**, ~**1500 repetitions** of the task, ~7 weeks.
design_relevance: **This is the single most important number in this file.** The 28 N end-effector target is the only clinically-argued assistive-force spec in upper-limb rehab robotics, and 45 N is the field's de facto ceiling. A soft arm that can produce 25–30 N at the hand is in-spec; one that produces 5 N is not. The endpoint inertia (~1 kg) and friction (<1 N) numbers are the *transparency* budget — a soft arm that a patient must drag around is worse than no arm.
evidence_grade: **B** (hardware validated with patients; the embedded clinical trial is a small RCT but underpowered and the primary FM comparison was null).
limitations: Planar, seated, grounded end-effector. n=20. Impedance control on a rigid low-inertia linkage is a fundamentally different plant from a soft compliant arm — the transparency figures are an aspiration, not a transferable spec.

handle: ALS-exosuit — Proietti et al., 2023
citation: Proietti T, O'Neill C, Gerez L, Cole T, Mendelowitz S, Nuckols K, Hohimer C, Lin D, Paganoni S, Walsh C. Restoring arm function with a soft robotic wearable for individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. *Science Translational Medicine* 2023;15(681):eadd1504.
source: 10.1126/scitranslmed.add1504 — verified via eutils PMID 36724237.
open_access: no (abstract only; Harvard Biodesign hosts a preprint copy — check biodesign.seas.harvard.edu).
contribution: The state of the art in *soft* upper-limb assistance with real patients: a textile inflatable shoulder-elevation exosuit that is mechanically transparent when unpowered, works without training, and immediately expands active ROM in people with neuromuscular weakness.
hard_numbers: **150 g added per arm.** n=10 people with ALS; 2 followed over **6 months**. Immediate improvement in active ROM; reduced shoulder EMG and perceived exertion; increased object-holding endurance; restored basic ADL performance. Actuator torque is not stated in the abstract (**not verified** — a related Harvard shoulder actuator has been reported at ~16 Nm at 90° abduction and 136 kPa, but I could not retrieve a primary record confirming that figure, so the team must not cite it).
design_relevance: Proves the central premise: a soft, low-mass shoulder assist is clinically meaningful for weakness even when it provides *no* motor recovery. Sets the transparency requirement — the device must be near-zero-impedance when off. The "works with no training" result is the usability bar for an elderly user.
evidence_grade: **B** (hardware validated on patients; single-arm, no control group).
limitations: ALS, not stroke or frailty; n=10; supervised laboratory sessions; wearable rather than freestanding, so the reaction force goes into the wearer's own torso, not into a floor-standing base. The transparency claim depends on the suit being worn, which a freestanding torso cannot replicate.

handle: Scapular-stretch-robot — Isobe et al., 2026
citation: Isobe K, Hirokawa M, Suzuki Y, Kadone H, Shimizu Y, Suzuki K. Shoulder-wearable soft robot for assisting older adults in scapular stretching. *Wearable Technologies* 2026;7:e8.
source: 10.1017/wtc.2026.10044 — fetched PMC13280861 (full text).
contribution: The only retrieved study that applies a soft robot to **healthy older adults** for passive ROM/stretching (not stroke rehab), and the only one that publishes an explicit force safety envelope for that population.
hard_numbers: n=9 men, mean age **70.9 ± 2.6 y** (range 68–74). Target actuator-side cable tension **98.0–137.3 N (10–14 kgf)**; delivered force lower because of cable friction. Safety limit **F_max = F_ref + 19.6 N**. **Emergency stop within 25 ms.** Loading phase **≈8 s** (deliberately slower than the ~2 s of manual therapy), hold **≤5 s**, **10 stretches per session**. Robot-assisted stretch produced no significant difference from manual therapist stretching on scapula–spine distance; younger-adult comparison showed a 5.1 mm (7.1%) shortfall. Experimenter required within 2 m throughout.
design_relevance: The most directly transferable requirement source in this file for *this* project. It gives (a) an assistive force band for elderly passive ROM at the shoulder, (b) an explicit overload margin (+19.6 N over reference), (c) a **25 ms e-stop latency requirement**, and (d) a movement-speed requirement: assistive motion for older adults should be roughly **4× slower than manual therapy** — of order 8 s to load a stretch, not 2 s.
evidence_grade: **C** (pilot/feasibility, n=9, healthy older adults, no control condition beyond within-subject manual comparison).
limitations: Nine healthy men, all 68–74, no frailty, no pathology, no women. Wearable, not freestanding. Supervised with an operator within 2 m — explicitly *not* an unsupervised-care-setting result. Force is reported at the actuator, not at the skin interface, so the actual contact load on the shoulder is unknown.

handle: Soft-UL-review — Bardi et al., 2022
citation: Bardi E, Gandolla M, Braghin F, Resta F, Pedrocchi ALG, Ambrosini E. Upper limb soft robotic wearable devices: a systematic review. *Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation* 2022;19:87.
contribution: 69 soft upper-limb devices across 105 papers. The field is overwhelmingly single-DOF, bench-tested and immature; almost nothing has been tested on patients.
hard_numbers: 69 devices / 105 articles. Actuation: pneumatic **52%**, cable+DC motor **29%**, passive **6%**, SMA **6%**, spring blades **3%**, hybrid **4%**. DOF: single **56%**, two **28%**, three-plus **<16%**. Joint targets: elbow **51%**, shoulder **45%**, wrist **33%**, forearm **10%**. Tested on people with disability: **7 devices**; on healthy subjects: **50**. TRL: 3 → 9%, 4 → 45%, 5 → 30%, 5/6 → 10%, 6 → 6%. Tracking accuracy achieved: shoulder flexion RMSE **2.12°**, shoulder abduction **3.05°**, elbow flexion **2.9–4.9°**, wrist **<3°**. Hand/palm contact forces **did not exceed 2.2 N**. Interface pressure distribution peak **20–40 kPa**. One device flagged as too heavy at **6.5 kg**. Only one formal clinical trial found: 20 sessions, 15 stroke survivors, hybrid exosuit.
design_relevance: Two requirements fall straight out of it. (1) **Interface pressure at the skin must sit in the 20–40 kPa band or below** — that is the empirical envelope soft devices actually operate in. (2) The achievable joint-angle tracking accuracy for a soft arm is **2–5° RMSE**; do not write a ±1° spec. It also confirms the honest positioning: at TRL 4–5, this project is in the same bracket as almost the entire published field.
evidence_grade: **D** (systematic review of engineering literature, not of clinical trials).
limitations: Reviews wearables, not freestanding torsos. Only 7 of 69 devices ever met a patient. Says nothing about long-term skin tolerance, and the 20–40 kPa figure is a peak-pressure observation, not a validated safety threshold.

handle: ARMin-III-hardware — Nef, Guidali & Riener, 2009
citation: Nef T, Guidali M, Riener R. ARMin III — arm therapy exoskeleton with an ergonomic shoulder actuation. *Applied Bionics and Biomechanics* 2009;6(2):127–142.
source: 10.1080/11762320902840179 — metadata and abstract verified via Crossref API and the Semantic Scholar Graph API (both fetched); the full text is Gold OA CC-BY per Unpaywall, but every hosting mirror I tried (Wiley, T&F, Hindawi, IOS) returned **403** to automated retrieval.
open_access: yes (Gold OA, CC BY) — but the team must download it manually.
contribution: The mechanical design of the exoskeleton used in the Klamroth-Marganska RCT, including a shoulder actuation principle that moves the humeral head rather than assuming a fixed glenohumeral centre.
hard_numbers: **3 actuated DOF at the shoulder + 1 at the elbow**, plus an optional module for forearm pro/supination and wrist flexion/extension (6 actuated DOF total). Five devices manufactured. **Joint torque limits, velocities and ROM: not verified** — these are in Table 5 of the paper, which I could not retrieve. Do not cite a torque number for ARMin III until someone opens the PDF.
design_relevance: Sets the DOF allocation argument for a shoulder that must not fight the patient's scapulohumeral rhythm. A rigid exoskeleton needs 3 shoulder DOF plus humeral-head translation to avoid joint misalignment; a soft arm that only contacts the limb externally partly sidesteps this problem, which is a genuine argument in the project's favour and should be made explicitly.
evidence_grade: **D** (design/description paper; the clinical validation is entry #3).
limitations: Rigid exoskeleton, clinic-mounted, patient strapped in. Misalignment compensation is the central problem for exoskeletons and largely irrelevant to an external-contact soft assistant — cite it for the contrast, not the solution.

handle: FM-MCID — Page, Fulk & Boyne, 2012
citation: Page SJ, Fulk GD, Boyne P. Clinically important differences for the upper-extremity Fugl-Meyer Scale in people with minimal to moderate impairment due to chronic stroke. *Physical Therapy* 2012;92(6):791–798.
source: 10.2522/ptj.20110009 — verified via eutils PMID 22282773.
contribution: Anchor-based estimate of how much Fugl-Meyer change a therapist actually regards as meaningful.
hard_numbers: n=146. Estimated **CID for UE-FM: 4.25 to 7.25 points**, depending on the movement facet. ROC AUC 0.61–0.70.
design_relevance: The acceptance criterion. If the team ever runs an efficacy claim, the target is ≥4.25 FM points — which means **RATULS (2.79) and the ARMin trial (0.78) both fell short**, and the team should say so in the design review before the reviewer does.
evidence_grade: **B** (anchor-based psychometric study, not an RCT).
limitations: Mild-to-moderate chronic stroke only; anchor is the *treating therapist's* global rating, not the patient's; AUCs of 0.61–0.70 are weak discrimination.

handle: UL-MCID-early — Lang, Edwards, Birkenmeier & Dromerick, 2008
citation: Lang CE, Edwards DF, Birkenmeier RL, Dromerick AW. Estimating minimal clinically important differences of upper-extremity measures early after stroke. *Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation* 2008;89(9):1693–1700.
source: 10.1016/j.apmr.2008.02.022 — verified via eutils PMID 18760153 (PMCID PMC2819021).
contribution: MCIDs for the battery a clinic would actually run, estimated early after stroke, split by dominant/non-dominant side.
hard_numbers: n=52. Grip strength MCID **5.0 kg** (dominant) / **6.2 kg** (non-dominant). ARAT **12** / **17** points. Wolf Motor Function Test function score **1.0** / **1.2**. Motor Activity Log quality **1.0** / **1.1**. MCID indeterminate for composite strength, WMFT time and accelerometry duration of use.
design_relevance: Tells the team which instruments a clinic will use and what threshold each must clear. Note the ARAT MCID of 12–17 points is *far* above the ~5.7 figure that circulates in secondary sources — use 12–17 for early stroke and cite this paper. Also: accelerometry duration-of-use has **no** usable MCID, so don't build the evaluation plan around wear-time logging alone.
evidence_grade: **B** (anchor-based psychometric substudy of an RCT).
limitations: n=52, acute/subacute (9.5 → 25.9 days post-stroke), inpatient, single trial cohort. Authors state larger samples are needed and that MCIDs may shift with time post-stroke.

handle: Reps-observed — Lang et al., 2009
citation: Lang CE, MacDonald JR, Reisman DS, Boyd L, Jacobson Kimberley T, Schindler-Ivens SM, Hornby TG, Ross SA, Scheets PL. Observation of amounts of movement practice provided during stroke rehabilitation. *Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation* 2009;90(10):1692–1698.
source: 10.1016/j.apmr.2009.04.005 — verified via eutils PMID 19801058 (PMCID PMC3008558).
contribution: What conventional therapy actually delivers, measured by observation rather than claimed. It is very little.
hard_numbers: 312 observed PT/OT sessions, 7 sites. Task-specific functional UE movements occurred in only **51%** of sessions addressing the upper limb. Mean **32 repetitions/session (95% CI 20–44)**. Gait: 357 steps/session (95% CI 296–418). No patient or therapist factor explained the variance.
design_relevance: **This is the competitive benchmark.** The bar to beat is 32 upper-limb repetitions per session. Any device that can supervise 150+ repetitions in 45 minutes is delivering ~5× the practice dose of a human therapist, and *that* is the defensible claim — not better kinematics.
evidence_grade: **B** (prospective observational, convenience sample).
limitations: Convenience sample of 7 US sites in 2009; practice patterns may have shifted; observers counted repetitions with no standardised definition across movement categories.

handle: Rep-dose-feasibility — Birkenmeier, Prager & Lang, 2010
citation: Birkenmeier RL, Prager EM, Lang CE. Translating animal doses of task-specific training to people with chronic stroke in 1-hour therapy sessions: a proof-of-concept study. *Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair* 2010;24(7):620–635.
source: 10.1177/1545968310361957 — verified via eutils PMID 20424192 (PMCID PMC3235711).
contribution: 300+ repetitions per hour is feasible in chronic stroke without excess pain or fatigue, and produced a large ARAT gain.
hard_numbers: n=15 enrolled, 13 completed. Target **300+ repetitions/session (3 tasks × 100)**; achieved mean **322 repetitions/session**. Protocol: **1-hour sessions, 3×/week, 6 weeks (18 sessions)**. Attendance **97%**. Pain and fatigue ratings low. ARAT improved **+8 points** on average, maintained at 1 month. Impairment measure did **not** improve.
design_relevance: The repetition target for the requirements table: **300 repetitions/hour**, i.e. roughly **one assisted movement every 12 s** including rest. That is a hard cycle-time requirement for the arm — pneumatic fill/vent time, controller settling and re-positioning must all fit inside a ~12 s budget. Note this is ~10× the observed conventional dose (#13).
evidence_grade: **C** (single-arm proof-of-concept, n=13, no control group).
limitations: No control group; chronic stroke with sufficient residual function to complete task repetitions — a frail, severely impaired or cognitively impaired elderly user will not sustain 322 reps/hour. Impairment did not change, so the mechanism of the ARAT gain is unclear.

handle: Sarcopenia-EWGSOP2 — Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2019
citation: Cruz-Jentoft AJ, Bahat G, Bauer J, Boirie Y, Bruyère O, Cederholm T, et al. Sarcopenia: revised European consensus on definition and diagnosis. *Age and Ageing* 2019;48(1):16–31.
source: 10.1093/ageing/afy169 — verified via eutils PMID 30312372 and full text fetched from PMC6322506 (Table 3 cut-off points).
contribution: The consensus operational definition of sarcopenia, with numeric cut-offs — i.e. the quantitative definition of the user population's weakness.
hard_numbers: Grip strength **<27 kg (men) / <16 kg (women)**. Chair stand **>15 s for five rises**. Appendicular skeletal muscle **<20 kg (men) / <15 kg (women)**; ASM/height² **<7.0 (men) / <5.5 kg/m² (women)**. Gait speed **≤0.8 m/s**. SPPB **≤8**. Timed-Up-and-Go **≥20 s**. 400 m walk: non-completion or **≥6 min**.
design_relevance: Defines the user. A sarcopenic user generates **<27 kg / <16 kg** of grip — so any handle, grasp interface or "hold on here" affordance must work at forces well below that, and cannot rely on the user gripping to stay safe. The five-rise chair-stand cut-off (>15 s) sets the sit-to-stand timing the device must accommodate: assume **≥3 s per rise**, not the ~1.7–2 s of an able adult (see #16).
evidence_grade: **D** (consensus statement, though built on a large evidence base).
limitations: European reference populations; cut-offs are diagnostic thresholds, not engineering safety limits. Says nothing about tolerance to applied external load.

handle: STS-torques — Lau & Mombaur, 2024
citation: Lau JCL, Mombaur K. Can lower-limb exoskeletons support sit-to-stand motions in frail elderly without crutches? A study combining optimal control and motion capture. *Frontiers in Neurorobotics* 2024;18:1348029.
source: 10.3389/fnbot.2024.1348029 — fetched PMC11024314 (full text).
contribution: Optimal-control computation of the joint torques a sit-to-stand actually costs for a 50th-percentile elderly woman, and the finding that a current commercial exoskeleton (TWIN) is **under-actuated** for crutch-free STS.
hard_numbers: Hip torque **120.03 Nm** with exoskeleton / **95.79 Nm** without; knee **137.26 Nm** / **111.79 Nm**. Residual human contribution needed: hip **8.03 Nm**, knee **49.26 Nm**. TWIN motor capacity: hip **112 Nm**, knee **88 Nm** — insufficient. Motors required for full assistance: hip **≥121 Nm**, knee **≥140 Nm**. Phase durations: optimal-control lifting phase **1.67–2.00 s**; measured passive (no crutches) sitting **2.50 s** / lifting **1.80 s**. Peak crutch ground reaction force **330.3 N**; peak foot force (crutchless) **898.0 N**. Total modelled system mass 83.1 kg.
design_relevance: **The single most important reality check in this file for the postural-support ambition.** Full sit-to-stand assistance costs >120 Nm at the hip and >140 Nm at the knee. That is an order of magnitude beyond what a soft pneumatic upper body can produce, and it is at the *lower* limb, which this project does not even actuate. The honest scope for this project is *upper-body stabilisation and a handhold reaction force* — the ~330 N crutch reaction figure is the number that matters, because it is the load a freestanding torso would have to take through its base if a user pushes off it. **Design the base and torso structure to react ≥330 N applied at hand height without tipping**, and state explicitly that the device does not provide sit-to-stand lift.
evidence_grade: **C** (simulation/optimal control with a single-participant motion-capture pilot; the participant was 25 years old, not elderly).
limitations: One motion-capture subject, aged 25, experienced with the exoskeleton; the "frail elderly" is a de Leva-based anthropometric model, not a real patient. Sagittal plane.
