ARMin III joint torques — in the paper, but the PDF is unretrievable by tool; get it manually. Absolute maximum shoulder/elbow torque in Nm for older adults — O'Sullivan 2022 has it in the body text, not the abstract. Interface pressure *injury* thresholds for aged skin — no primary source retrieved; the 20–40 kPa figure is descriptive, not a limit. --- Robot-assisted upper-limb therapy does **not** beat conventional therapy when the two are matched for time, and the team should say that out loud in the first slide rather than have a reviewer say it in the last. RATULS — 770 patients, the biggest trial there is — found robot training no better than an intensity-matched therapy programme on the primary outcome (44% vs 50% success, OR 1.17, 98.3% CI 0.70–1.96), and the ARMin trial's win over conventional therapy was 0.78 Fugl-Meyer points, roughly a fifth of the 4.25-point minimum that a therapist would call meaningful. The Cochrane review's pooled effects (SMD 0.31–0.46) are real, high-GRADE, and small, and they are mostly comparisons against *less* therapy, not against *equal* therapy — which is the tell: Lohse's meta-regression (g=0.35) says the active ingredient is dose, and Lang's observational data says conventional therapy delivers a pitiful **32 upper-limb repetitions per session** while Birkenmeier showed **322 per hour** is achievable. That is the defensible thesis for this project — not better movement, more of it, cheaper, for more hours than a human will stand there — and it reframes the spec from "recover motor function" to "deliver 300 supervised repetitions an hour with a 4-minute human-attention budget." "Meaningful assistive force" is numerically modest and well within reach of soft actuation: **28 N at the hand** is the clinically-argued target (MIT-MANUS chose it as the elbow-extension strength of a weak seated woman), **45 N** is the ceiling, and assist-as-needed modulation happens in a **±6 N** band — meanwhile arm-weight support alone, with *zero* actuator torque, produced sustained gains in the T-WREX RCT, which is the strongest hint in this literature that the project should lead with gravity compensation (≈10 Nm shoulder, ≈3 Nm elbow, both INFERRED and both needing measurement) rather than trajectory-driving torque. Kill the sit-to-stand ambition now: crutch-free STS costs >121 Nm at the hip and >140 Nm at the knee, a commercial lower-limb exoskeleton already fails that test, and this project doesn't even actuate the legs — the honest scope is a stable handhold, and the structural requirement that falls out of it is that the torso and base react **≥330 N at hand height without tipping**. Design for a user who cannot grip (sarcopenia cut-offs are <27 kg men / <16 kg women, so the device must never depend on the user holding on), whose shoulder hurts about a third of the time after stroke, whose skin tears at 11.6% prevalence in long-term care — meaning cuff *shear* is the injury mode to engineer against, not peak normal pressure — and who needs assistive motion roughly **four times slower** than a therapist moves (8 s to load a stretch, not 2 s). Finally, note what every source in this file has in common and what the project does not: all of them were supervised, all of them were clinic- or lab-based, the Isobe protocol literally required an operator within 2 m with a 25 ms e-stop, and **not one retrieved study validates unsupervised assistive physical contact with a frail elderly person** — so the requirements table above is a *supervised-use* spec, and any claim about autonomous home or care-home operation is currently unsupported by clinical evidence. ---

handle: HRI Scale Database — Saad et al., 2026
citation: Saad, L., Roesler, E., Phillips, E., & Trafton, J. G. (2026). The human-robot interaction scale database. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 13, 1846413.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1846413 — **fetched the Frontiers full text** and the live database at http://hriscaledatabase.psychology.gmu.edu/
contribution: The first centralised, publicly browsable repository of HRI measurement scales, each scored against a 13-point psychometric development/validation guideline. It is the tool that settles the instrument argument in a design review instead of prolonging it.
hard_numbers: Paper reports 53 instruments across 12 constructs, collectively >73,000 citations; live site listed 47 scales in 11 categories when I fetched it (the site is updated after publication — cite the paper's numbers and check the site for current entries). **92% of HRI researchers have relied on non-validated custom scales.** Scale quality correlates with publication year, r = 0.56, p < 0.001. Quality ratings I pulled directly from the database pages: **Perceived Danger 100%, GAToRS 100%, RoSAS 85%, NARS 69%, Trust in Automation (Körber/TiA) 62%, Kamide Psychological Safety 54%, Trust Perception Scale-HRI 31%, Godspeed 23%.**
design_relevance: This is the defence for every instrument choice in the campaign. It also kills the "we'll write our own 10 questions" option outright — the team can point at the 92% figure and say that is exactly the failure mode they are avoiding.
evidence_grade: D (review/resource) — but operationally the highest-value item in this list.
limitations: Ratings score *reporting quality of the development paper*, not how well a scale works in your specific context. A 23% rating does not mean Godspeed produces garbage data; it means its development paper did not report what modern psychometric guidelines require. Almere/UTAUT are not in the database at all. ---

handle: Perceived Danger (PD) scale — Molan et al., 2025
citation: Molan, J., Saad, L., Roesler, E., McCurry, J. M., Gyory, N., & Trafton, J. G. (2025). The Perceived Danger (PD) Scale: Development and Validation. *2025 20th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)*, 420–428. Short form: Saad, L., Roesler, E., McCurry, J. M., Gyory, N., & Trafton, J. G. (2025). Development of the Perceived Danger-Short Form (PD-SF) Scale: Scale Reduction and Validation. *2025 34th IEEE RO-MAN*, 2178–2183.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/HRI61500.2025.10973898 and https://doi.org/10.1109/RO-MAN63969.2025.11217856 — **both verified via Crossref**; scale description and free scoring PDF **fetched** from http://hriscaledatabase.psychology.gmu.edu/social/2025/01/06/PD.html
open_access: no for the papers (IEEE); **yes for the instrument** — the administration-and-scoring PDF is a free download from the GMU database
contribution: A purpose-built instrument for "the anticipation of harmful consequences of the actual or imagined interaction with another entity" — i.e. the construct this project actually cares about, rather than a generic likeability proxy.
hard_numbers: 12 items, 4 subscales × 3 items: Affective States (nervousness, anxiety, stress), Physical Vulnerability (exposure to injury, injury severity, pain likelihood), Ominousness (menacing, threatening, intimidating), Cognitive Readiness (alertness, vigilance, caution). Quality rating 100% (all 13 guideline criteria met, including reported reliability and validity tests). **Cronbach's alphas and validation sample sizes: not stated on the database page I fetched — the team must pull them from the paper before quoting them.** A short form exists (PD-SF) for repeated within-session administration.
design_relevance: This is the primary DV for the approachability campaign. "Physical Vulnerability" and "Ominousness" map directly onto a freestanding torso with two arms that a person is expected to stand inside the reach envelope of. Use the full PD at pre/post and PD-SF between conditions.
evidence_grade: A (validated instrument, top-rated on the GMU guideline).
limitations: New (2025), so little third-party replication yet. Validation samples are almost certainly online/US undergraduate — I could not confirm any elderly validation. ---

handle: Godspeed Questionnaire Series — Bartneck et al., 2009
citation: Bartneck, C., Kulić, D., Croft, E., & Zoghbi, S. (2009). Measurement instruments for the anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence, and perceived safety of robots. *International Journal of Social Robotics*, 1(1), 71–81.
source: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12369-008-0001-3 — **verified via Semantic Scholar API**; subscale/alpha detail **fetched** from https://www.bartneck.de/publications/2009/measurementInstrumentsRobots/
open_access: partial — Springer hybrid (CC-BY-NC per Semantic Scholar); the author distributes the questionnaire itself free at bartneck.de
contribution: The de facto standard 5-index semantic-differential battery for robot perception. Its **Perceived Safety** index (3 items: anxious/relaxed, agitated/calm, quiescent/surprised) is the most-cited operationalisation of the exact thing this project claims to improve.
hard_numbers: 24 items total on 5-point semantic differentials. Anthropomorphism 5, Animacy 6, Likeability 5, Perceived Intelligence 5, **Perceived Safety 3**. Reported alphas: Anthropomorphism .856–.929; Likeability .842–.923; Perceived Intelligence .75–.769; Animacy .702. Translated into 19 languages. Free to use. **GMU guideline rating: 23%.**
design_relevance: Include the 3-item Perceived Safety index *for comparability* — most of the soft-robot papers in this list used it or something adapted from it, so it is how the team's numbers get compared to prior work. Do not make it the primary DV.
evidence_grade: A (validated instrument, enormous usage base) with a caveat: A for comparability, C for psychometric rigour by 2026 standards.
limitations: Developed pre-2010 without modern factor-validation reporting, hence the 23%. The 3-item safety index is short enough to be noisy. Semantic differentials confuse some older participants — pilot it. ---

handle: Robotic Social Attributes Scale (RoSAS) — Carpinella et al., 2017
citation: Carpinella, C. M., Wyman, A. B., Perez, M. A., & Stroessner, S. J. (2017). The Robotic Social Attributes Scale (RoSAS): Development and Validation. *Proceedings of the 2017 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI '17)*, 254–262. Independent re-validation: Pithayarungsarit, P., Saad, L., Trafton, J. G., & Roesler, E. (2025). A Systematic Validation of the Robotic Social Attributes Scale (RoSAS). *Proceedings of the 2025 ACM/IEEE HRI*, 1547–1552 (HRI 2025 honorable mention).
source: https://doi.org/10.1145/2909824.3020208 — **verified via Semantic Scholar API** (ACM DL returns 403 to automated fetches); scale detail **fetched** from http://hriscaledatabase.psychology.gmu.edu/social%20attributes/2024/06/12/RoSAS.html
contribution: 18-item scale with three factors — **Warmth, Competence, Discomfort** — grounded in the Fiske warmth/competence model of social perception. Crucially, the authors show Discomfort is *not* merely unfamiliarity, and that these attributions shift with robot appearance.
hard_numbers: 18 items, 3 subscales, 9-point frequency ratings of trait words. GMU guideline rating **85%** — the highest-rated general-purpose social-perception scale in HRI. One criterion failed: the initial sample-to-item ratio did not reach 10:1. Items are printed in the paper but the GMU database does **not** redistribute them pending author permission.
design_relevance: This is the approachability instrument. "Warmth" is the closest validated construct to what the team means by approachable; "Discomfort" catches the uncanny/creepy failure mode that a humanoid torso with two soft arms is genuinely at risk of. Pair with PD: PD measures *danger*, RoSAS measures *social welcome*. They are not the same thing and a compliant torso could plausibly move one without the other.
evidence_grade: A.
limitations: Validated on US online/undergraduate samples with robot *images*, not physical contact. No elderly validation that I could confirm. The 2025 systematic re-validation exists and the team should read it before assuming the 3-factor structure holds in their context — I verified that paper exists and won an honourable mention but could not fetch its findings. ---

handle: Softness, warmth and responsiveness in robot hugs — Block & Kuchenbecker, 2019
citation: Block, A. E., & Kuchenbecker, K. J. (2019). Softness, Warmth, and Responsiveness Improve Robot Hugs. *International Journal of Social Robotics*, 11(1), 49–64.
source: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12369-018-0495-2 — **verified via Crossref**; **full PDF fetched and text-extracted** from https://files.ait.ethz.ch/projects/HuggieBot/HuggieBot2018.pdf
open_access: partial — free author PDF at the ETH link above
contribution: The single cleanest causal test in this entire literature of whether adding compliance to a rigid robot changes perceived safety during real physical contact. A PR2 hugged people in Hard-Cold, Soft-Cold and Soft-Warm conditions.
hard_numbers: **n = 30** (14M/15F/1 other), **ages 21–54, M = 26.8, SD = 8.5**; 23 engineering students, 25 of 30 from technical backgrounds. **Within-subjects**, 12 randomised trials each (3 physical + 9 behavioural), order pre-randomised for up to 40 participants. Key results: covering the robot in foam **significantly raised perceived safety, F(2,58) = 5.28, p = 0.0078**, both soft conditions preferred over hard, **no significant difference between the two soft conditions**; Hard-Cold vs Soft-Cold was "close to the threshold of significance … interpreted with caution." Comfort during the hug needed foam **and** heat: F(2,58) = 3.17, **p = 0.049**, effect located between Hard-Cold and Soft-Warm. **No significant effect of any physical condition on how social or caring the robot was perceived. No physical condition made participants significantly happier.** Pre/post exposure: participants felt significantly more understood (p < 0.005), trusted the robot more (p < 0.005), liked its presence more (p < 0.005). Participants needed 2–3 practice hugs before being comfortable starting.
design_relevance: This is the load-bearing citation for "compliance improves perceived safety," and it is also the citation that bounds the claim. Copy its design: within-subjects, covered vs uncovered, same robot, same motion, perceived-safety DV. Also copy its practice-trial protocol — the acclimatisation period is a real experimental requirement, not politeness.
evidence_grade: B (controlled within-subjects, real physical contact, but small n and a heavily WEIRD/technical sample).
limitations: n = 30 young technical volunteers from the Penn engineering community — the least representative possible sample for an elderly-care claim. Hugging is not assistance. And note what softness did *not* buy: no gain in perceived sociality, caring, or happiness. ---

handle: Perceived safety for soft robotics in caregiving — Du Pasquier et al., 2025
citation: Du Pasquier, C., Grannen, J., Pan, C., Huber, S. L., Smith, A., Kennedy, M., Song, S., Sadigh, D., & Okamura, A. M. (2025). A Study of Perceived Safety for Soft Robotics in Caregiving Tasks. arXiv:2503.20916 [cs.RO].
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20916 — **fetched both the abstract page and the full HTML** at https://arxiv.org/html/2503.20916
contribution: A soft (positive + negative pressure) 3D-printed gripper performed a simulated bathing task — sweeping a towel along a participant's arm — and trust in robots was measured before and after.
hard_numbers: **n = 106, ages 18–89**, recruited at a robotics-centre launch event, Nov 2024. **Within-subjects pre/post**, 7-point Likert trust and familiarity items. Trust rated at ceiling (7) rose **21.3% → 39.6%**; low ratings (1–3) fell **14.8% → 2.8%**. The robotic arm moved to the participant's elbow and swept three times, so this is genuine physical contact. FEA-designed gripper showed a lower, more uniform pressure profile than a standard rigid gripper in bench tests. IRB approval stated. **No p-values, no effect sizes, no inferential statistics reported. No rigid-gripper control condition in the human study.**
design_relevance: Best available precedent for the exact study the team wants to run — contact with a soft end effector, wide age range, event-based recruiting, pre/post trust. Read it for the protocol, not for the conclusion.
evidence_grade: C (pilot; large n but uncontrolled and statistically unreported).
limitations: This design cannot separate "softness increased trust" from "any successful robot demo increases trust." The Block study shows exposure alone moves trust significantly (p < 0.005), which is very likely most of what happened here. Self-selected attendees at a robotics launch event are the most pro-robot sample imaginable. The paper's own claim that "soft robotics can enhance perceived safety and acceptance" is not supported by the design it reports. ---

handle: Perceived safety of soft-robot-hand motions — Wang et al., 2024
citation: Wang, Y., Wang, G., Ge, W., Duan, J., Chen, Z., & Wen, L. (2024). Perceived Safety Assessment of Interactive Motions in Human–Soft Robot Interaction. *Biomimetics*, 9(1), 58.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics9010058 — **fetched the PMC full text** at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10813124/
contribution: 15 interactive motions of a soft humanoid robotic hand executed on participants' forearms, rated for perceived safety. The finding that matters: **motion parameters, not material softness, drove the ratings.**
hard_numbers: **n = 30** (12M/18F), **ages 18–31, M = 21.63, SD = 5.37**. Custom **9-item, 5-point** scale (acceptance, reliability, emotional comfort, fluency, sense of security, sense of control, willingness to use, motion semantics, general safety), adapted from Akalin's perceived-safety framework. **Cronbach's alpha not reported.** Slow contact motions scored significantly higher than fast, **p < 0.01**. Negative semantic clarity correlated with reduced safety, **r = −0.661, p < 0.01**. High- vs moderate-acceptance participants, **t = −15.911, p < 0.01**; low vs high-moderate risk tolerance, **t = 3.485, p < 0.01**. Participants clustered as proactive (12), tech-savvy (4), conservative (6), cautious (8).
design_relevance: Direct evidence that the team's arm **speed profile and motion legibility** will dominate perceived safety over the fact that the arm is soft. Budget engineering effort accordingly: a slow, predictable, semantically obvious approach motion buys more perceived safety than another durometer drop.
evidence_grade: B (controlled, real contact, small n, unvalidated instrument).
limitations: Custom 9-item scale with no reliability reported — exactly the 92%-of-HRI-researchers failure mode. Ages 18–31, zero elderly participants. Chinese university sample. No rigid-hand control. ---

handle: User perceptions of soft robot arms and fingers for healthcare — Kim et al., 2016
citation: Kim, D. H., MacDonald, B., McDaid, A., Kawamura, S., Kim, H. J., Bean, E. T., Fraser, F., & Broadbent, E. (2016). User perceptions of soft robot arms and fingers for healthcare. *2016 25th IEEE International Symposium on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN)*, 1150–1155.
source: https://doi.org/10.1109/ROMAN.2016.7745253 — **verified via Crossref and Semantic Scholar**; the findings below are quoted from Rajashekhar V S & Prabhakar (2025), *Soft is Safe: Human-Robot Interaction for Soft Robots*, arXiv:2502.01256, which I **fetched and grepped** — I could not fetch the Kim paper itself (IEEE paywall)
contribution: Blindfolded participants performed tactile tasks with soft vs rigid vs human arms and fingers. **Soft arms were rated more human-like but more fragile than hard arms; overly soft fingers were perceived as creepy and less reliable.**
hard_numbers: **none confirmed** — I could not access the primary text, so sample size, ages and statistics are unverified. Treat the qualitative direction as secondhand until someone reads the PDF.
design_relevance: The counterweight to the whole "soft = approachable" thesis, and it comes from a healthcare-robotics group (Broadbent is a serious HRI/health researcher). Softness buys human-likeness and loses perceived reliability — and for an assistive device a patient leans on, **perceived reliability is part of perceived safety.** Design review will ask this question; better to have raised it first.
evidence_grade: C (primary numbers unverified by me; direction reported consistently in a PRISMA survey of 98 articles).
limitations: Everything above. Get the PDF through NYU's IEEE subscription before citing it in the report, and replace this entry with real numbers. ---

handle: Lay perceptions of soft vs rigid socially assistive robots — Fenn et al., 2026
citation: Fenn, J., Estadieu, L., Gorki, M., Monno, I., Tauber, F., Teichmann, J., Levy-Tzedek, S., Speck, T., Müller, O., & Kiesel, A. (2026). Informing robot design through early public engagement: lay perceptions of soft versus rigid socially assistive and rescue robots. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 13, 1741946.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1741946 — **fetched the PMC full text** at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13043413/ (Crossref-verified)
contribution: The largest sample comparing soft vs rigid robot perceptions, using Cognitive-Affective Maps. Soft-robot scenarios produced more positive evaluations — and the authors are unusually honest that their own design cannot rule out order effects.
hard_numbers: **n = 180** (218 recruited), German Prolific panel, Dec 2023. Emotional evaluation pre vs post: **F(1,178) = 14.68, p < .001, ηp² = .076**. Total concepts drawn: **F(1,178) = 250.05, p < .001, ηp² = .584**. Positively-rated concepts: **F(1,178) = 200.33, p < .001, ηp² = .530**; mean valence 0.19 (SD 0.47); 33% added no negative concepts. Qualitatively, soft robots gained concepts of safety, emotional comfort, adaptability — **and new concerns: fragility, emotional dependence, maintenance burden.**
design_relevance: Shows the *reputational* upside of softness is real at the level of public attitude, and simultaneously names the three objections the team will get in a design review. Also: the tiny effect size on emotional evaluation (ηp² = .076) next to the huge one on "number of concepts drawn" (ηp² = .584) tells you most of what happened was people elaborating more, not liking more.
evidence_grade: B (well-powered, but confounded by design; authors say so).
limitations: Authors list them: fixed rigid→soft order creating anchoring, information artifacts (participants echoing the scenario text), demand characteristics from visible map revision, German-only sample, and SAR scenarios that unintentionally emphasised special-needs users. **Scenario-based — no participant met a robot.** No elderly breakdown reported. ---

handle: Godspeed with 178 older adults (TIAGo) — Tobis et al., 2023
citation: Tobis, S., Piasek-Skupna, J., & Suwalska, A. (2023). The Godspeed Questionnaire Series in the Assessment of the Social Robot TIAGo by Older Individuals. *Sensors*, 23(16), 7251.
source: https://doi.org/10.3390/s23167251 — **fetched the PMC full text** at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10458894/ (Crossref-verified)
contribution: The reliability evidence that Godspeed actually works on an elderly sample — and the uncomfortable finding that **perceived safety scored significantly lower than likeability and perceived intelligence** for a mobile humanoid assistant.
hard_numbers: **n = 178 older adults, mean age 75.2 ± 9.6 (median 75); 62 participants (34.8%) aged ≥80**; 103 women; community and care-home residents. **Cronbach's alpha: Anthropomorphism .75, Animacy .87, Likeability .94, Perceived Intelligence .90, Perceived Safety .75, overall .90.** Anthropomorphism and Animacy significantly lower than the other subscales (p < 0.001); Likeability and Perceived Intelligence did not differ from each other but **both exceeded Perceived Safety (p < 0.001)**. Institutionalised participants rated Likeability (p < 0.05) and Perceived Safety (p < 0.001) *higher* than community dwellers. Age, gender, education and technology comfort had no significant effect.
design_relevance: Two things. (a) It licenses the team to use Godspeed with elderly participants and cite α ≥ .75 on every subscale in a 75-year-old sample — that is the strongest instrument-appropriateness argument available for this population. (b) It sets the realistic baseline: people can like a robot and rate it competent while still not feeling safe around it. Liking is not approachability.
evidence_grade: A (well-powered, elderly sample, instrument reliability reported).
limitations: Cross-sectional, single interaction, one robot (a rigid mobile manipulator, not a soft torso). Validation was internal consistency only — no factor confirmation. Ceiling effects on Likeability and Perceived Intelligence. Polish sample. **No soft/rigid comparison.** ---

handle: Older adults' attitudes and rejection — Pino et al., 2015
citation: Pino, M., Boulay, M., Jouen, F., & Rigaud, A.-S. (2015). "Are we ready for robots that care for us?" Attitudes and opinions of older adults toward socially assistive robots. *Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience*, 7, 141.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/fnagi.2015.00141 — **fetched the PMC full text** at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4512026/ (Crossref-verified)
contribution: The rejection paper the team needs on file. Older adults largely do not see themselves as users of assistive robots, and humanoid form specifically draws hostility.
hard_numbers: **n = 25, ages 58–86, M = 72.6**, 68% female; 10 with Mild Cognitive Impairment, 7 informal caregivers, 8 healthy older adults. Mixed questionnaire + 7 focus groups. **Healthy older adults' current adoption intention M = 0.13 / 3.0** — effectively zero. Future intention (M = 1.96) significantly exceeded current (M = 0.84), **Wilcoxon z = −3.08, p < 0.002**. Perceived usefulness: MCI 1.9/3.0, caregivers 1.86/3.0, **healthy older adults 1.13/3.0**. Privacy concerns in 56% of MCI participants; **47.9% of healthy older adults worried about machines replacing human contact.** Direct quote on humanoids: *"I'm against humanoid robots… what is the purpose of this ventriloquist dummy anyway?"*
design_relevance: Two hard constraints on the campaign. (a) Recruit the *right* elderly participants — healthy community-dwelling older adults will rate the device as "for someone else" and the data will say nothing. Target people with an actual functional need, or caregivers. (b) **Humanoid form is a liability, not an asset, with this population.** A freestanding torso with two arms is squarely in the shape this quote is attacking. The team should have a defensible reason the form is humanoid that is about biomechanics of assistance, not about approachability.
evidence_grade: C (qualitative + small-n survey) — but methodologically sound and widely cited.
limitations: n = 25, single French memory-clinic catchment, no robot contact (attitudes toward the concept). 2015, pre-Pepper-saturation. ---

handle: Taxonomy of factors influencing perceived safety + physiological/subjective measurement — Akalin et al., 2023 & 2022
citation: Akalin, N., Kiselev, A., Kristoffersson, A., & Loutfi, A. (2023). A Taxonomy of Factors Influencing Perceived Safety in Human–Robot Interaction. *International Journal of Social Robotics*, 15(12), 1993–2004. Companion study: Akalin, N., Kristoffersson, A., & Loutfi, A. (2022). Do you feel safe with your robot? Factors influencing perceived safety in human-robot interaction based on subjective and objective measures. *International Journal of Human-Computer Studies*, 158, 102744.
source: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12369-023-01027-8 and https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhcs.2021.102744 — **both verified via Crossref**; the 2022 paper's record **verified via Semantic Scholar API** (ScienceDirect returns 403)
open_access: 2023 paper — paywalled at Springer (repository copies circulate); **2022 paper — yes, hybrid CC-BY**
contribution: Perceived safety decomposes into six factors: **context of use, comfort, experience/familiarity with robots, trust, sense of control over the interaction, and transparent/predictable robot actions.** None of them is "material stiffness." The authors' framing line: *a robot that is safe by hardware and software design can still be perceived as unsafe.*
hard_numbers: 2022 study: **n = 27**, questionnaires plus physiological recording across varying robot behaviours. **Physiological signals were more predictive of perceived safety than facial expressions.** The 2023 taxonomy paper is a synthesis; I did not obtain its review corpus size.
design_relevance: This is the theoretical spine of the campaign and it reorients the design decision. If five of six levers are behavioural (control, transparency, predictability, familiarity, comfort) and one is contextual, then **the team's approachability gains will come from the interaction script and the motion profile, not from the silicone.** Concretely: give the participant a visible stop control, telegraph every motion, let them touch the arm before it moves.
evidence_grade: D (review) for the taxonomy; B for the n = 27 empirical companion.
limitations: n = 27 is underpowered for a six-factor model. Lab setting, no elderly participants confirmed. The taxonomy is a synthesis of a literature that is itself mostly WEIRD undergraduate studies. ---

handle: Robot speed and comfortable passing distance — Neggers et al., 2022
citation: Neggers, M. M. E., Cuijpers, R. H., Ruijten, P. A. M., & IJsselsteijn, W. A. (2022). The effect of robot speed on comfortable passing distances. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 9, 915972.
source: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2022.915972 — **fetched the Frontiers full text** (Crossref-verified)
contribution: Comfort as a quantified function of distance and speed, with a fitted model rather than a vibe.
hard_numbers: **Exp 1: n = 32** (17M/15F, M age 32.0, SD 16.3, **range 19–81**), 9 distances 50–130 cm × 2 sides × 2 sequences. **Exp 2: n = 22** (11M/11F, M age 23.9, SD 3.42, range 19–35), 4 speeds (**0.35, 0.8, 1.25, 1.7 m/s**) × 2 sides × 4 distances × 2 scenarios = 48 trials. Both **within-subjects**. Comfort follows an inverted Gaussian in distance; comfort level 6 corresponds to roughly **80 cm centre-to-centre**. Exp 1: distance F(8,66) = 128.71, p < .0001, η² = .50; sequence F(1,66) = 119.37, p < .0001, η² = .11; passing side n.s. (F(1,66) = 0.03, p = .86). Exp 2: distance F(3,940) = 110.23, p < .0001, η² = .26; **speed F(3,940) = 30.20, p < .0001, η² = .09**; scenario F(1,940) = 64.00, p < .0001, η² = .06. Higher speed → lower comfort; overtaking worse than passing.
design_relevance: Gives the team a defensible numeric envelope for the approach protocol and a template for a **behavioural** approachability measure (stop distance in cm) that is not a questionnaire. Note that speed's effect (η² = .09) is real but three times smaller than distance's — set the standoff first, then tune speed.
evidence_grade: A (well-powered within-subjects, modelled, one experiment spanning ages 19–81).
limitations: Mobile base passing a standing person, **not a stationary torso reaching toward a seated one** — the geometry the team cares about is different. Dutch lab sample. Exp 2 is all young adults. ---

handle: Physiological measurement of robot-induced anxiety — Kulić & Croft, 2007
citation: Kulić, D., & Croft, E. (2007). Physiological and subjective responses to articulated robot motion. *Robotica*, 25(1), 13–27. Companion: Kulic, D., & Croft, E. A. (2007). Affective State Estimation for Human–Robot Interaction. *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*, 23(5), 991–1000.
source: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0263574706002955 and https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2007.904899 — **both verified via Crossref**; abstract and sample size **fetched** from the Cambridge Core page
contribution: The origin of physiological perceived-safety measurement in HRI, and the result that safety-optimised motion planning measurably reduces reported anxiety.
hard_numbers: **n = 36 subjects.** Inputs: heart rate, perspiration rate (skin conductance), facial muscle contraction (corrugator EMG), mapped to a 2D valence–arousal space via fuzzy inference (Robotica) and an HMM (T-RO). Two planners compared: a nominal potential-field planner vs a safe planner minimising potential collision force along the path. **Subjects reported less anxiety and surprise with the safe planner.**
design_relevance: If the team wants an objective DV to complement questionnaires, this is the canonical precedent — and the two Kulić/Croft papers are the "physiological measures" half of what the assignment brief calls "Bartneck/Kulić & Croft perceived-safety measurement." (Kulić and Croft are also co-authors on the Godspeed paper, which is why the two lines converge.) **Practical read: skin conductance is the only one of these three signals a senior design team can instrument reliably and cheaply.**
evidence_grade: B (hardware-validated with 36 humans, no clinical population).
limitations: 2007 hardware, 2007 sensors. Participants *observed* robot motion — no physical contact. Individual differences in electrodermal response are large and require per-subject baselining; a team without a physiology-literate member will produce uninterpretable traces. No elderly participants. ---

handle: Attitude and acceptance instruments: NARS, GAToRS, Almere
citation: - NARS: Nomura, T., Suzuki, T., Kanda, T., & Kato, K. (2006). Measurement of negative attitudes toward robots. *Interaction Studies*, 7(3), 437–454. Companion: Nomura, T., Kanda, T., & Suzuki, T. (2006). Experimental investigation into influence of negative attitudes toward robots on human–robot interaction. *AI & Society*, 20(2), 138–150. - GAToRS: Koverola, M., Kunnari, A., Sundvall, J., & Laakasuo, M. (2022). General Attitudes Towards Robots Scale (GAToRS): A New Instrument for Social Surveys. *International Journal of Social Robotics*, 14(7), 1559–1581. - Almere: Heerink, M., Kröse, B., Evers, V., & Wielinga, B. (2010). Assessing acceptance of assistive social agent technology by older adults: the Almere model. *International Journal of Social Robotics*, 2(4), 361–375. Built on Venkatesh, V., Morris, M. G., Davis, G. B., & Davis, F. D. (2003). User acceptance of information technology: toward a unified view. *MIS Quarterly*, 27(3), 425–478.
source: 10.1075/is.7.3.14nom, 10.1007/s00146-005-0012-7, 10.1007/s12369-022-00880-3, 10.1007/s12369-010-0068-5, 10.2307/30036540 — **NARS, AI&Society, GAToRS and UTAUT verified via Crossref; Almere verified via Semantic Scholar API.** Scale details **fetched** from the GMU database pages for NARS and GAToRS.
open_access: NARS no; AI&Society no; **GAToRS yes (CC-BY)**; Almere yes (Springer hybrid CC-BY-NC); UTAUT no.
hard_numbers: **NARS:** 14 items, 3 subscales — S1 negative attitude toward interaction situations (6), S2 toward social influence of robots (5), S3 toward emotions in interaction (3); developed on 263 Japanese university students, confirmed on 240; a revised version reached **α = .80** after dropping 3 items; **GMU rating 69%**; items not redistributed by the GMU database. **GAToRS:** 20 items, 4 balanced subscales of 5 — Personal Positive, Personal Negative, Societal Positive, Societal Negative; **GMU rating 100%**; items listed publicly on the database page; paper is CC-BY. **Almere:** extends UTAUT with social-interaction constructs; explained **59–79% of variance in usage intentions and 49–59% of variance in actual use** across controlled and longitudinal studies in care settings. **Item count and per-construct alphas: not confirmed — Springer blocked every PDF route I tried. Do not quote an item count for Almere without opening the paper.**
design_relevance: Run **GAToRS** as the pre-exposure covariate. It is free, CC-BY, 20 items, 100%-rated, and balanced across personal/societal and positive/negative — which matters because a compliant care robot triggers societal-level reactions ("replacing carers") that a personal-level-only scale misses. Use Almere only if the team runs a multi-week deployment; it is an adoption model, not a first-impression instrument.
evidence_grade: A for all three as instruments.
limitations: NARS is Japanese-normed 2006 and superseded. GAToRS is Finnish-normed online panels. Almere's validation is Dutch elder-care and is about *sustained use*, which a two-session senior-design study cannot observe. ---

handle: Trust instruments and why to be careful with them — Jian et al., 2000; Schaefer, 2016
citation: Jian, J.-Y., Bisantz, A. M., & Drury, C. G. (2000). Foundations for an empirically determined scale of trust in automated systems. *International Journal of Cognitive Ergonomics*, 4(1), 53–71. Schaefer, K. E. (2016). Measuring Trust in Human Robot Interactions: Development of the "Trust Perception Scale-HRI." In *Robust Intelligence and Trust in Autonomous Systems* (pp. 191–218). Springer US.
source: https://doi.org/10.1207/S15327566IJCE0401_04 and https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-7668-0_10 — **both verified via Crossref**; quality assessments **fetched** from the GMU database trust pages. A free DTIC technical report of the Jian work exists at https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA395339.pdf.
open_access: Jian — partial (T&F paywall; DTIC report free). Schaefer — no.
hard_numbers: **Jian:** 12 items from a 3-phase word-elicitation/questionnaire/paired-comparison study; cluster analysis yielded the 12 factors; **the scale was never validated by the authors**; no reliability reported; **GMU rating 46%**, flagged for non-standard item generation and unreported factor structure. **Schaefer:** 156-item pool → 42 after SME content validation → **40-item pre/post scale scored 0–100% giving a percentage trust score**, plus a **14-item** SME-recommended subscale (the GMU auditors could identify only 11 of those 14 items in the chapter); six experiments in development; **GMU rating 31%** — missing construct definition, no confirmatory factor analysis, incomplete item transparency. Full items are inside the chapter text.
design_relevance: This is where the team should *resist* the obvious move. "Trust" is the word everyone reaches for, and the two standard trust scales are the two worst-rated instruments relevant to this project. If the claim is about approachability and perceived safety, measure those directly with PD and RoSAS. If a trust number is required for the report, use Schaefer's 14-item short form and state the 31% rating in a footnote rather than letting a reviewer find it.
evidence_grade: B (widely used, weakly validated).
limitations: Jian's scale was built for *automated systems* generally, not embodied robots that touch you; Schaefer's is functional-capability-weighted and explicitly may not capture feature-based (appearance, material) trust antecedents — which is precisely the variable this project manipulates. Neither has elderly norms. ---

handle: HuggieBot 2.0 / 3.0 — Block, Seifi, Hilliges, Gassert & Kuchenbecker, 2023 (ETH Zurich / MPI-IS)
citation: Block, A. E., Seifi, H., Hilliges, O., Gassert, R., & Kuchenbecker, K. J. (2023). In the Arms of a Robot: Designing Autonomous Hugging Robots with Intra-Hug Gestures. *ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction*, 12(2), 1–49.
source: 10.1145/3526110 — **fetched** the arXiv full text (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.09935) for hardware detail; publisher HTML (dl.acm.org) returned 403. Crossref record verified.
open_access: yes (arXiv preprint 2202.09935; ACM THRI is OA).
contribution: A custom, freestanding, human-sized hugging robot: two arms on a rigid V-shaped frame, a **custom inflated PVC torso ("HuggieChest")** that both softens the robot and senses contact, a face screen, and autonomous hug behaviours.
hard_numbers: 2 × **6-DOF Kinova JACO arms** mounted horizontally on a custom metal frame; **angle and torque sensors at every joint**; torso = two heat-sealed/glued sheet-PVC chambers, rear chamber instrumented with an Adafruit BME680 barometric pressure sensor + MAX4466 electret microphone amp, streaming to ROS at ~45 Hz; heating via two Thermophore MaxHeat pads (35.6 × 68.6 cm); arms covered in foam padding; arm speed limited in firmware and arms "can be mechanically overpowered by the user"; gesture classification 88% accuracy. Mass, reach, payload, assistive force: **not published**. Certification: **not published**. Human testing: **n = 32** (gesture corpus study) + **n = 16** (validation study) — healthy adults, not patients.
design_relevance: This is the closest existing thing to the proposed concept and it should be read line-by-line. Copy: the inflated-chamber-as-both-compliance-and-sensor trick (one pressure sensor + one microphone gives omnidirectional contact detection over a whole soft surface for ~$20 of parts); torque-threshold arm stopping as the "adjust to any body size" mechanism; firmware speed limits plus back-drivable arms as the safety story. Avoid: their arms are **rigid COTS Kinova units wearing foam**, i.e. they solved compliance at the *surface*, not in the *actuator* — if this project claims intrinsic compliance it must beat that, not match it.
evidence_grade: B (lab prototype, extensive hardware results, 48 human subjects, no patients).
limitations: The paper documents its own torso failure modes: seams tearing and the resealable inflation valve popping open, both of which "allow air to escape, change the feel of the robot's torso, and require re-inflation" — they rebuilt the chamber for 3.0 with heat seal + HH-66 vinyl cement. Front-chamber sensors picked up so much cross-talk they were deleted in 3.0. No assistive force of any kind is delivered or measured; this is an affective-touch machine, not a load-bearing one. ---

handle: King Louie (and "Grub") — Best, Wilson & Killpack, 2015 (BYU RAD Lab / Pneubotics–Otherlab)
citation: Best, C. M., Wilson, J. P., & Killpack, M. D. (2015). Control of a pneumatically actuated, fully inflatable, fabric-based, humanoid robot. In *2015 IEEE-RAS 15th International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids)*, 1133–1140.
source: 10.1109/HUMANOIDS.2015.7363495 — **fetched** the author PDF (http://radlab.byu.edu/uploads/4/4/7/0/4470886/humanoids_2015.pdf) and extracted the text directly.
open_access: partial (author-hosted PDF is free; IEEE version paywalled).
contribution: A **fourteen-DOF fully inflatable fabric humanoid** built by Pneubotics (an Otherlab affiliate), with a 1-DOF single-joint test article ("grub"). Structure *is* the pressurised bladder — there is no rigid skeleton. First published high-level control (MPC/LQR) for a fully inflatable soft humanoid.
hard_numbers: **14 DOF** total (two arms, 5 DOF each per the related literature, plus torso joint); construction entirely **ballistic nylon fabric with internal bladders**; main structural bladder pressurised **1–2 psi gauge (≈7–14 kPa)**; antagonistic joint actuators rated **0–25 psi gauge**, but the authors ran only **0–17 psi "because of pinching effects in the main chamber at higher pressures"**; demonstrated task = pick a board off a chair and place it in a box, **8/10 successes** using joint-space MPC. Mass, payload, contact force, reach: **not published in this paper**. Certification: none. Patient testing: **none**.
design_relevance: This is the existence proof that a freestanding, fully soft, dual-arm humanoid upper body can be built and controlled — so the project cannot claim that as novel. Copy: antagonistic pairs per joint on a common structural bladder; the low-pressure-structure / higher-pressure-actuator split. Avoid: assuming you can turn the actuator pressure up to spec — they lost a third of their pressure range to bladder pinching, which is exactly the failure that caps soft-arm force output.
evidence_grade: B (hardware prototype, quantitative control results).
limitations: No force, payload or safety numbers are reported at all — a soft humanoid with no published payload is not evidence that soft humanoids can assist anyone. Control is the contribution; capability is undemonstrated. Pneubotics as a commercial soft-robot arm venture did not produce a marketed assistive product. ---

handle: RIBA / RIBA-II / ROBEAR — Mukai et al., 2010–2015 (RIKEN-TRI, then RIKEN-SRK)
citation: Mukai, T., Hirano, S., Nakashima, H., Kato, Y., Sakaida, Y., Guo, S., & Hosoe, S. (2010). Development of a nursing-care assistant robot RIBA that can lift a human in its arms. In *2010 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)*, 5996–6001.
source: 10.1109/IROS.2010.5651735 (Crossref-verified). Specs **fetched** from RIKEN press releases: RIBA https://www.riken.jp/en/news_pubs/research_news/pr/2009/20090827/ ; RIBA-II https://www.riken.jp/en/news_pubs/research_news/pr/2011/20110802_2/ ; ROBEAR https://www.riken.jp/en/news_pubs/research_news/pr/2015/20150223_2/
open_access: no (IROS paper paywalled); press releases open.
contribution: The three-generation Japanese patient-transfer robot line — a bear-faced humanoid upper body on a wheeled base that physically picks a person up and moves them bed↔wheelchair. The only lineage in this table that actually lifts humans.
hard_numbers: **RIBA:** lifts a patient **up to 61 kg** bed→wheelchair and back; human-like arms with high-precision tactile sensors; **soft exterior of urethane foam**. **RIBA-II:** lifts **up to 80 kg**; added base and lower-back joints so it can crouch and lift from a futon at floor level; **Smart Rubber capacitance tactile sensor sheets** (first all-rubber capacitance tactile sensors) on arms and chest; arms described as high-rigidity / high-output-torque; mass **230 kg**. **ROBEAR:** mass **140 kg**; "actuator units with a very low gear ratio"; three sensor types including **torque sensors**; Smart Rubber capacitive tactile sensors. DOF for all three: **not published in the sources I could fetch**. Certification: **not published**. Patient testing: RIBA-II testing with partner nursing-care facilities was **planned**; for ROBEAR the RIKEN release states **"none have yet been deployed in care-giving facilities."**
design_relevance: This is the force target. 61–80 kg lift = **~600–785 N** of sustained assistive force. Copy: foam-over-structure plus full-coverage tactile skin on every surface that touches the patient; the Smart Rubber sheet-sensor idea is directly transferable to a soft torso. Avoid: the mass trajectory. They needed 230 kg of robot to lift 80 kg of person, then spent an entire generation getting back down to 140 kg and still shipped nothing.
evidence_grade: A for RIBA/RIBA-II (lifting real humans in demonstrations, care-facility partnership), B for ROBEAR.
limitations: RIKEN states plainly that the original RIBA had "functional limitations preventing commercialization." The **RIKEN-SRK Collaboration Center was closed at the end of March 2015**, one month after ROBEAR was announced; project lead Dr. Mukai moved to Meijo University; no unit was ever deployed in a care facility. Fifteen years, three generations, zero deployments — the most important negative result in this entire table. ---

handle: RoNA (Robotic Nursing Assistant) — Ding et al., 2014 (HStar Technologies) — *industry*
citation: Ding, J., Lim, Y.-J., Solano, M., Shadle, K., Park, C., Lin, C., & Hu, J. (2014). Giving patients a lift — the robotic nursing assistant (RoNA). In *2014 IEEE International Conference on Technologies for Practical Robot Applications (TePRA)*, 1–5.
source: 10.1109/TePRA.2014.6869137 (Crossref-verified). IEEE Xplore blocked automated fetch (HTTP 418); specs **fetched** from a secondary conference paper describing the system: http://ieomsociety.org/ieom_2015/papers/671.pdf (Mahrouche, IEOM 2015) — treat these numbers as second-hand.
open_access: no (primary); the secondary description is open.
contribution: A commercial-intent mobile patient-lift robot: humanoid upper torso with two lifting arms on a modified Segway holonomic base, nurse-teleoperated, intended to remove manual patient handling from nursing work.
hard_numbers: Lift capacity **up to 500 lb (≈227 kg)**, quoted elsewhere as 150 lb one arm / 250 lb two arms / up to 500 lb; actuation is a **Worm Series Elastic Actuator (WSEA)** — one large WSEA per arm provides primary shoulder lift, three small WSEAs form lower shoulder and elbow; **small WSEA torque capacity 678 N·m**, ~50% of the large unit's strength; lower arm is the patient contact surface and is specified for "increased force-fidelity and physical compliance"; also rated for transporting items **< 5 kg**. Total DOF, mass, reach: **not published in the sources I fetched**. Certification: **not published**. Patient testing: **not published / not verified**.
design_relevance: RoNA is the proof that **series elasticity scales to patient-lift torques** — 678 N·m in a compact worm-SEA module. It is also the only system here that explicitly partitions the arm into a high-force proximal segment and a compliant, high-fidelity distal segment that touches the patient. That proximal-stiff / distal-compliant split is a directly copyable architecture and it is the right answer to "how do you get force and safety in the same arm."
evidence_grade: C–B, **I** (industry prototype; no peer-reviewed patient trial found).
limitations: HStar Technologies never brought RoNA to market; there is no published clinical trial, no certification, and no independent verification of the 500 lb figure. Specs circulate only via the company and via secondary summaries — a warning about the reliability of industry numbers generally. ---

handle: Blower-powered soft inflatable joints / inflatable hugging robot — Niiyama, Seong, Kawahara & Kuniyoshi, 2021 (Univ. of Tokyo)
citation: Niiyama, R., Seong, Y., Kawahara, Y., & Kuniyoshi, Y. (2021). Blower-Powered Soft Inflatable Joints for Physical Human-Robot Interaction. *Frontiers in Robotics and AI*, 8, 720683.
source: 10.3389/frobt.2021.720683 — **fetched** https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/robotics-and-ai/articles/10.3389/frobt.2021.720683/full
contribution: Very-low-pressure, blower-inflated fabric joints with internal tendon drive, built specifically for physical human–robot interaction, demonstrated on an **inflatable hugging robot**.
hard_numbers: Operating pressure **50–300 Pa** (two orders of magnitude below King Louie); fabric ≈ **70 g/m² nylon**; range of motion **45–90°** depending on internal patch configuration; joint torque "proportional to internal pressure and to the square of the radius"; prototypes from **100 mm to 3 m**; demonstrated **5+ independent actuators** in one system; contact detection from a **single internal pressure sensor**; four contact patterns tested (strong hug, light hug, thumping, handshake). Mass, payload, assistive force: **not published**. Certification: none. Patient testing: **none**.
design_relevance: This is the honest ceiling-setter for "how soft can you go." At 50–300 Pa the structure is intrinsically incapable of hurting anyone and equally incapable of assisting anyone mechanically — the torque scaling law (∝ P·r²) tells the team exactly which knob to turn: if pressure must stay low for safety, **diameter is the only remaining lever**, and that is a torso-scale design decision, not an actuator-selection decision. Copy the single-internal-pressure-sensor contact detection. Copy the continuous-blower architecture (a puncture leaks instead of exploding).
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Authors state fabric hysteresis limits precision, buckling constrains maximum deflection, and scaling to larger systems needs further investigation. No force output, no payload, no human-subject protocol beyond contact-pattern demos. ---

handle: Soft robotic hand and arm system — Alspach, Kim & Yamane, 2018 (Disney Research)
citation: Alspach, A., Kim, J., & Yamane, K. (2018). Design and fabrication of a soft robotic hand and arm system. In *2018 IEEE International Conference on Soft Robotics (RoboSoft)*, 369–375.
source: 10.1109/ROBOSOFT.2018.8404947 (Crossref-verified) — **fetched** and text-extracted the Disney-hosted PDF (https://studios.disneyresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/Design-and-Fabrication-of-a-Soft-Robotic-Hand-and-Arm-System.pdf).
contribution: A **6-DOF conventionally-actuated arm** wrapped in air-filled force-sensing modules and an inflated outer cover, with a 3D-printed hand with air-filled force-sensing fingertips. Explicitly "soft skin on a hard robot" rather than a soft robot.
hard_numbers: **6 DOF** arm; **two air-filled force sensing modules** (heat-sealed polyurethane) on two links, each tubed to a pressure sensor for contact force feedback and passive impact absorption; inflated **polyethylene outer cover**, heat-sealed, with elastic relief features; internal projector displays through the translucent cover; arm dimensions given in the paper's kinematic figure (links of 214.6 mm and 373.15 mm, overall envelope 457.2 mm). Mass, payload, force range, reach: **not published**. Certification: none. Patient testing: **none** (validated by grasping a soft object and by bending the arm inside the cover).
design_relevance: The paper's own framing is the most useful thing in it: they cite King Louie, Grub, Sanan's inflatable manipulator and Marchese's soft continuum manipulator and then deliberately reject soft actuation because it "requires complex control schemes," choosing instead to outfit a hard robot with soft, easy-to-integrate sensing. That is the mainstream engineering position this project is arguing against, and the team should be able to answer it. Also note their earlier 3D-printed skin modules failed because the rubber-like material was porous and could not hold pressure for extended periods — a direct materials warning for any inflated torso.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: No force numbers, no payload, no human trial; the soft layer is cosmetic-plus-sensing, not load-bearing. Disney did not carry it into a product. ---

handle: GummiArm — Stoelen, de Azambuja, López Rodríguez, Bonsignorio & Cangelosi, 2022
citation: Stoelen, M. F., de Azambuja, R., López Rodríguez, B., Bonsignorio, F., & Cangelosi, A. (2022). The GummiArm Project: A Replicable and Variable-Stiffness Robot Arm for Experiments on Embodied AI. *Frontiers in Neurorobotics*, 16, 836772.
source: 10.3389/fnbot.2022.836772 — **fetched** https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurorobotics/articles/10.3389/fnbot.2022.836772/full
open_access: yes (CC BY; hardware CC BY-SA at github.com/GummiArmCE).
contribution: An open-source, 3D-printed, variable-stiffness arm driven by antagonistic composite rubber/nylon tendons — the open-source arm with the most variable-stiffness joints.
hard_numbers: **7+1 DOF**, **5 variable-stiffness antagonist joints**, scaled to 50th-percentile female anthropometry (upper arm ~300 mm, forearm+hand ~400 mm); **reach 0.7 m**; **total arm mass 3 kg** (v1.0 PLA), 1.1 kg below the shoulder; **payload 0.75 kg at rest pose, 0.45 kg at full extension**; tendons = Filaflex elastomer core twined with nylon thread, stiffness rising exponentially with elongation (R² = 0.94); stiffness modulated 0–100% co-contraction in real time; **material cost < $6,000** (~90% servos), structural plastic ~$20; ~77 h print time on a hobby FFF printer. Certification: none. Human testing: public exhibit 2016–2017 with **hundreds of handshakes per day** from random members of the public; 2 kg mass dropped from 1.3 m caused no structural damage; across five arms over six years **no Dynamixel servo was replaced due to mechanical failure**.
design_relevance: The single most useful number in this document for scoping: a well-engineered compliant anthropomorphic arm of realistic human scale carries **0.45 kg at full extension**. That is **~4.4 N**. Any assistive-force claim the team makes has to live between that and RIBA's ~600 N, and the team should decide now which end they are on. Copy: composite viscoelastic tendons (damping without metal springs, repairable in minutes), the co-contraction stiffness knob, and the "hundreds of uncontrolled handshakes" as a cheap, publishable safety-exposure protocol.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Authors are candid: payload "significantly lower than industrial manipulators" and insufficient for heavy manipulation; kinematic model degrades under load because the plastic flexes, so high gripper accuracy needs visual servoing; Dynamixel load sensing is slow and inaccurate; **composite tendons fail at their attachment points** and elastomer creep is expected with no long-term wear analysis done. ---

handle: PR2 as a robotic body surrogate — Grice & Kemp, 2019 (Georgia Tech)
citation: Grice, P. M., & Kemp, C. C. (2019). In-home and remote use of robotic body surrogates by people with profound motor deficits. *PLOS ONE*, 14(3), e0212904.
source: 10.1371/journal.pone.0212904 — **fetched** https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0212904
contribution: A web-based interface letting people with profound motor deficits operate a PR2 to perform self-care (feeding, face wiping, shaving, applying lotion) and household tasks, including a week-long in-home deployment.
hard_numbers: PR2 — omnidirectional base, vertically translating torso, **two 7-DOF arms** with grippers, pan/tilt head; **20 controllable DOF** through the interface (9 DOF during ARAT testing). Patient testing: **n = 15** participants with profound motor deficits (ARAT ≤ 9 both limbs; SMA n=6, MD n=3, SCI n=3, ALS n=1, arthrogryposis n=1, Dejerine-Sottas n=1), mean age 36.9 ± 8.7, operating remotely from across the US; plus **n = 1** expert user (Henry Evans, quadriplegia from brain-stem stroke) for a **7-day in-home deployment**, 22 h 30 min 50 s of use. 80% success on the simulated self-care task; mean 4:29 ± 1:55 per ARAT item vs ~5 s for able-bodied. Safety: dense foam padding around grippers and base, **fabric-based tactile sensing skin on arms and base**, adjusted gains for back-drivable arms, low-velocity motions, emergency run-stops with trained caregivers. Assistive force: **not published** (task is manipulation, not load bearing). Certification: **not published**.
design_relevance: The gold standard for how to run patient testing on a contact robot, and the source of a safety recipe the team can copy wholesale: foam + tactile skin + back-drivable low-gain arms + low velocity + a caregiver-held run-stop. Also the honest recruitment arithmetic: 37 prescreened → 15 completed.
limitations: The authors' own verdict: "The specific robotic hardware we used in our study is not sufficiently robust for longer-term use, nor is it cost-effective for consumers." The PR2 line is dead; Willow Garage closed in 2014; Kemp's response was to co-found Hello Robot around a far simpler, cheaper single-arm platform. Depth perception through the interface remained a hard problem, and participants could not grasp a 1 cm marble. ---

handle: HOBBIT PT2 — Bajones, Fischinger, Weiss, Vincze et al., 2018/2019 (TU Wien et al.)
citation: Bajones, M., Fischinger, D., Weiss, A., Wolf, D., Vincze, M., de la Puente, P., Körtner, T., Weninger, M., Papoutsakis, K., Michel, D., Qammaz, A., Panteleris, P., Foukarakis, M., & Adami, I. (2018). Hobbit: Providing Fall Detection and Prevention for the Elderly in the Real World. *Journal of Robotics*, 2018, 1754657. Companion field-trial paper: Bajones et al. (2019), *ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction*, 9(2), 1–27, doi:10.1145/3368554. Earlier prototype: Fischinger, D., et al. (2016), *Robotics and Autonomous Systems*, 75, 60–78, doi:10.1016/j.robot.2014.09.029.
source: 10.1155/2018/1754657 (Crossref-verified). Hardware and trial numbers **fetched** from the open companion chapter: https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/56864 (Vincze et al., doi:10.5772/intechopen.70453). Wiley and ACM HTML both returned 403.
open_access: partial (Journal of Robotics is OA but blocked automated fetch; the IntechOpen chapter is OA and fetchable).
contribution: A deliberately **low-cost** mobile service robot with a single arm for elderly fall prevention — picking objects off the floor so the user does not have to bend down — plus fall detection and emergency call. Multi-week autonomous deployment in real private homes.
hard_numbers: **Single arm** (users asked for two; one was built for cost reasons); **height 125 cm**, max width **56 cm at the shoulder**; RGB-D head camera (ASUS Xtion) plus a floor-parallel depth camera, pan/tilt active head; **safety edges/bumpers at the base and tablet mount**; **hardware BOM ≈ €16,000**, described as "more than a magnitude cheaper than other similar robots" and still unaffordable for the target users. Arm DOF, payload, mass: **not published in the fetched source**. Certification: **not published**. Patient testing: **18 primary users aged 75+** across Austria (7), Greece (4), Sweden (7), **3 weeks per household**, **372 days** total autonomous deployment; 16 secondary users.
design_relevance: The most brutally useful datum in the pass: **object pickup worked reliably on only 18% of the 372 deployment days**, while navigation ran at >98%. Manipulation in an unstructured home is where these systems die. If this project's assistive function depends on repeatable physical contact with a person in an uncontrolled environment, HOBBIT is the reliability baseline to beat, and 18% is the number to put in the design review.
evidence_grade: **A** (multi-week deployment with real elderly users in their own homes).
limitations: Reliability, not acceptance. Speech and gesture control underperformed; object pickup was unusable most of the time; the €16k BOM was still too expensive for the users it targeted; no commercial product resulted and the authors concede "considerable work ahead." ---

handle: Care-O-bot 3 / Care-O-bot 4 — Reiser et al., 2009 / Fraunhofer IPA — *industry + research*
citation: Reiser, U., Connette, C., Fischer, J., Kubacki, J., Bubeck, A., Weisshardt, F., Jacobs, T., Parlitz, C., Hägele, M., & Verl, A. (2009). Care-O-bot® 3 — creating a product vision for service robot applications by integrating design and technology. In *2009 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)*, 1992–1998.
source: 10.1109/IROS.2009.5354526 (Crossref-verified). Care-O-bot 4 specs **fetched** from the official technical-data page: https://www.care-o-bot.de/en/care-o-bot-4/technical-data.html
open_access: no (primary paper); vendor spec page open.
contribution: Fraunhofer IPA's flagship service/care robot line. Care-O-bot 4 is a modular mobile humanoid (base, torso, arms, sensor ring, head) with patented spherical neck and hip joints, buildable with zero, one, or two arms.
hard_numbers: **29 DOF**; arm **7 DOF**, reach **≈ 90 cm**, **payload 5 kg**, built from **Schunk PowerBall modules** (PRL100, ERB145, ERB115); total mass **140 kg**; footprint 72 × 72 × 158 cm; omnidirectional base max **1.1 m/s**; joint max velocity 200°/s; **3 safety laser scanners with a safety PLC**, **2-channel Safe-Torque-Off**, **2-channel wireless emergency stop**; 48 V Li-ion. Torque sensing and explicit compliance control: **not stated on the technical data page**. Certification: no certification number claimed on that page (safety *architecture* is described, not a certificate). Patient testing: **not published / not verified in this pass**.
design_relevance: This is what a professionally engineered, functionally safe care robot's safety architecture looks like, and it is entirely **extrinsic** — scanners, a safety PLC, dual-channel STO, wireless e-stop. Copy the STO + dual-channel e-stop as the baseline the project must at minimum match, because "it's soft" is not a substitute for a functional-safety chain. Note the payload: 5 kg per 7-DOF arm on a 140 kg robot.
limitations: Twenty-plus years and four generations without a care-market product. 140 kg of robot for a 5 kg arm payload. It remains a research/demonstration platform sold in small batches (the design is explicitly optimised for "economical small-batch production" in folded sheet metal), not a deployed assistive device. ---

handle: DLR LWR III → KUKA LBR iiwa — Albu-Schäffer, Haddadin, Ott, Stemmer, Wimböck & Hirzinger, 2007 — *research → industry*
citation: Albu-Schäffer, A., Haddadin, S., Ott, C., Stemmer, A., Wimböck, T., & Hirzinger, G. (2007). The DLR lightweight robot: design and control concepts for robots in human environments. *Industrial Robot: An International Journal*, 34(5), 376–385.
source: 10.1108/01439910710774386 (Crossref-verified). Specs **fetched** from https://www.dlr.de/en/rm/research/robotic-systems/arms/lwr-iii and https://www.kuka.com/en-de/products/robot-systems/industrial-robots/lbr-iiwa
contribution: The torque-sensing, impedance-controlled lightweight arm that defined physical human–robot interaction, and its commercial descendant, the first series-produced HRC-capable industrial robot.
hard_numbers: **7 DOF** (R-P-R-P-R-P-P); **mass 14 kg**, **payload 14 kg** (1:1 ratio); **max reach 936 mm**; **completely torque controlled**, joint control at 3 kHz; position / torque / impedance control modes; joint torque sensors on the Harmonic Drive flex spline. **(LBR iiwa, KUKA page):** two variants, **7 kg payload (R800)** and **14 kg payload (R820)**, reach **800–820 mm**, 7 axes, **joint torque sensors in all seven axes**, axis-specific torque accuracy **±2% of maximum torque**, IP54, described by KUKA as "the world's first series-produced sensitive, and therefore HRC-compatible, robot." Certification: **no ISO 10218 / ISO/TS 15066 number appears on the fetched page** — the HRC claim is made in prose. Patient testing: none.
design_relevance: The reference point for *active* compliance done properly: measure joint torque, close an impedance loop, get compliance you can retune in software. The key comparison for the team is that a rigid 14 kg arm with torque sensors carries 14 kg, while a 3 kg compliant tendon arm carries 0.45 kg. Intrinsic softness is not free — it costs roughly two orders of magnitude of payload-to-mass ratio, and the design review needs to state what is bought with that.
evidence_grade: B, **I** (iiwa).
limitations: For this project's purposes: no soft surface at all, no patient application, and the price/complexity of a torque-sensed harmonic-drive joint is out of reach for a senior design build. It also never entered care robotics — its market was industrial HRC. ---

handle: Rollin' Justin — Fuchs, Borst, Giordano et al., 2009 (DLR)
citation: Fuchs, M., Borst, C., Giordano, P. R., Baumann, A., Kraemer, E., Langwald, J., Gruber, R., Seitz, N., Plank, G., Kunze, K., Burger, R., Schmidt, F., Wimböck, T., & Hirzinger, G. (2009). Rollin' Justin — Design considerations and realization of a mobile platform for a humanoid upper body. In *2009 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)*, 4131–4137.
source: 10.1109/ROBOT.2009.5152464 (Crossref-verified). Specs **fetched** from https://www.dlr.de/en/rm/research/robotic-systems/humanoids/rollin-justin
contribution: A mobile **humanoid upper body** — the closest rigid analogue of the proposed architecture: a torso with two compliant-controlled 7-DOF arms and two four-finger hands on a variable-geometry wheeled base.
hard_numbers: **51 DOF** total — 8 platform, **2 × 7 arms**, 2 × 12 hands, 2 neck, **3 torso**; height **1.91 m**; mass **≈ 200 kg**; **payload 20 kg**; max speed 2 m/s; >60 min battery; **torque sensors in nearly all joints**; **compliant hierarchical whole-body control**; 2 IMUs, 2 stereo + 5 RGB-D cameras. Certification: **not published**. Patient testing: **none** — DLR's applications are household tasks and teleoperated astronaut assistance (including teleoperation from the ISS).
design_relevance: The direct rigid-world benchmark for "freestanding dual-arm upper body." A 3-DOF actuated torso is the feature most projects skip and Justin did not — if this project wants a compliant torso rather than a compliant pair of arms bolted to a post, Justin is the kinematic reference. The 200 kg / 20 kg ratio is the number to quote when someone suggests the soft version should match it.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: 200 kg, one-of-a-kind, no cost figure published, no human-contact or clinical application in seventeen years of operation. Compliance here is entirely software over stiff hardware. ---

handle: COMAN and WALK-MAN — Tsagarakis et al., 2013 / 2017 (IIT)
citation: Tsagarakis, N. G., Morfey, S., Medrano Cerda, G., Zhibin, L., & Caldwell, D. G. (2013). COMpliant huMANoid COMAN: Optimal joint stiffness tuning for modal frequency control. In *2013 IEEE ICRA*, 673–678. — and — Tsagarakis, N. G., Caldwell, D. G., Negrello, F., Choi, W., Baccelliere, L., Loc, V. G., Noorden, J., Muratore, L., Margan, A., Cardellino, A., Natale, L., & Mingo Hoffman, E. (2017). WALK-MAN: A High-Performance Humanoid Platform for Realistic Environments. *Journal of Field Robotics*, 34(7), 1225–1259.
source: 10.1109/ICRA.2013.6630645 and 10.1002/rob.21702 (both Crossref-verified). COMAN specs **fetched** from the IIT lecture slides https://www.ais.uni-bonn.de/Humanoid_Soccer_School/slides/HSS_13_Lecture_Tsagarakis.pdf (Tsagarakis, Humanoid Soccer School 2013, text-extracted). WALK-MAN specs **fetched** from https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/798389 (IIT press release for the 2017 revision). Wiley returned 403.
open_access: no (both papers); slides and press release open.
contribution: IIT's two generations of intrinsically compliant, series-elastic full humanoids — COMAN as the passive-compliance research platform, WALK-MAN as the disaster-response humanoid that operated in a post-earthquake scenario.
hard_numbers: **25 major DOF** (arms, legs, torso; excluding hands and neck/head); **intrinsic passive compliance** plus joint torque sensing and active compliance; SEA at the sagittal leg joints, torso pitch and yaw, and **shoulder flex/ext, shoulder abd/add and elbow flex/ext**; **arm = 3-DOF serial shoulder + 1-DOF elbow**; **3-DOF serial torso mechanism**; no cable transmissions; 2 × 6-DOF F/T sensors, IMU, battery, full body covers with internal wiring. COMAN height and total mass: **widely quoted as 0.95 m / 31 kg but I could not confirm either from a source I fetched — treat as unverified.** **WALK-MAN (2017 revision, IIT release):** height **1.85 m**, mass **102 kg** (down from 133 kg), shoulder width 62 cm, torso depth 31 cm; **32 motors and control boards**; **elastic joints**; **payload 10 kg per arm**, sustained for 10+ minutes (up from 7 kg per arm); 4 F/T sensors at hands and feet, 2 accelerometers; 1 kWh battery ≈ 2 h; Ergal 60% / magnesium alloy 25% / titanium, steel, plastics. The JFR paper's original WALK-MAN is 1.915 m / 132 kg. Certification: none. Patient testing: **none**.
design_relevance: COMAN's arm topology (3-DOF serial shoulder + 1-DOF elbow, with SEA at shoulder flex/ext, abd/add and elbow) is a proven minimal compliant-arm kinematic that a student team can actually build, and IIT's own slides admit the honest part: **"the tuning of the series passive elasticity still remains an experimental trial and error process and very little information on the methodologies used is available."** That is permission to tune empirically and a warning not to promise an optimal stiffness derivation. WALK-MAN's 10 kg/arm at 102 kg total is the current best-in-class payload-per-mass for an intrinsically compliant humanoid.
evidence_grade: B.
limitations: Disaster response, not care. No human-contact application, no patient testing, no certification, and both are unique research machines with no cost figure and no path to a care market. WALK-MAN's mass reduction from 133 → 102 kg to get from 7 → 10 kg per arm shows how expensive incremental force is on a compliant humanoid. ---

handle: Harvard soft inflatable shoulder exosuit — Zhou, Hohimer, Young et al., 2024 (Harvard Biodesign) — *competing approach*
citation: Zhou, Y. M., Hohimer, C. J., Young, H. T., McCann, C. M., Pont-Esteban, D., Civici, U. S., Jin, Y., Murphy, P., Wagner, D., Cole, T., Phipps, N., Cho, H., Bertacchi, F., Pignataro, I., et al. (2024). A portable inflatable soft wearable robot to assist the shoulder during industrial work. *Science Robotics*, 9(91), eadi2377.
source: 10.1126/scirobotics.adi2377 (Crossref-verified; science.org and the Harvard-hosted PDF both returned 403 to automated fetch — metadata and the headline numbers below were taken from the search-surfaced abstract text and Crossref, **not** from a page I successfully rendered. Flagged accordingly.)
contribution: A shirt-like textile pneumatic exosuit with integrated IMUs and a portable actuation unit that offloads the shoulder during overhead work.
hard_numbers: lower confidence** — not read off a fetched full text): up to **6.6 N·m** shoulder torque; adds **150 g per upper limb**; cycles assistance on/off up to **6×/min**; reduced agonist muscle activity (anterior/middle/posterior deltoid, biceps brachii) by up to **40%** with <7% ROM change and no increase in latissimus dorsi antagonist activity. Certification: **not published**. Patient testing: healthy participants in simulated industrial tasks (n **not verified**).
design_relevance: This is the competing answer to the same clinical problem and it is winning on the metric that matters. **6.6 N·m and 150 g per limb**, worn, beats every freestanding soft arm in this table on assistance-per-kilogram by orders of magnitude — because the wearer's own skeleton carries the load path and the robot only supplies torque. The team must be able to say why a freestanding torso is worth its mass penalty. The honest answers are: patients who cannot don a garment, tasks requiring bimanual external support, and contact that must not be anchored to a frail body. If the project cannot articulate one of those, the exosuit is simply the better design.
evidence_grade: B, and **I**-adjacent (Harvard Biodesign spins this technology out commercially).
limitations: Industrial, not clinical, in this paper. Requires a portable pneumatic unit and donning; assists one joint pair only. ---

handle: Harvard soft robotic wearable for ALS — Proietti, O'Neill, Gerez et al., 2023 (Harvard Biodesign / MGH) — *competing approach*
citation: Proietti, T., O'Neill, C., Gerez, L., Cole, T., Mendelowitz, S., Nuckols, K., Hohimer, C., Lin, D., Paganoni, S., & Walsh, C. (2023). Restoring arm function with a soft robotic wearable for individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. *Science Translational Medicine*, 15(681), eadd1504.
source: 10.1126/scitranslmed.add1504 (Crossref-verified: authors, journal, volume, issue, year all confirmed). Full text paywalled; headline results below come from the Harvard SEAS news page surfaced in search, **not** from a rendered paper — lower confidence, flagged.
contribution: A battery-powered, textile-based soft wearable assisting shoulder elevation and elbow extension, evaluated in people with ALS.
hard_numbers: battery-powered and cordless; detects residual arm motion and **calibrates in 30 s**; study with **10 participants** with ALS; improved range of motion, reduced fatigue, improved task performance. Torque, mass, actuator pressure: **not verified in this pass**. Certification: **not published**.
design_relevance: The only device in this whole table with a **clinical population, a quantified functional outcome, and a top-tier translational venue**. If the team wants an evidence-grade-A comparator for "assistive force delivered to rehabilitation patients by a soft robot," this is it — and it is a garment, not a humanoid. Copy the outcome-measure framing (ROM, fatigue, task performance, muscle activity) because that is what a clinical reviewer will ask for, and no freestanding soft system in this table reports any of it.
evidence_grade: **A** (patients), reported here at lower confidence on the numbers.
limitations: Assists an arm that still has residual motion; small n; single-joint-pair scope; no independent replication found in this pass. ---
